**Practice.** Say these aloud: **ένας φίλος, μια φίλη, ένα παιδί, έναν καφέ, μια μέρα**. Then say out loud, in Greek: *I want a coffee · I am a teacher · I have a car · I want a book*. Then say the difference between **Έχω ένα παιδί** and **Έχω παιδιά**.
Nominative and accusative:
The first case distinction, and the reason Greek word order can move. Two forms, one job each.

**A case is a form a noun takes according to its job in the sentence.** Greek has four — nominative, accusative, genitive and vocative — and this lesson is the first two, which cover most sentences.

**The nominative is the subject**: the one doing the verb, and the form a dictionary lists.

- **Ο δάσκαλος** γράφει. — The teacher is writing.

**The accusative is the object**: the one the verb is done to.

- Βλέπω **τον δάσκαλο**. — I see the teacher.

**Both words changed**: the article **ο** became **τον**, and the noun **δάσκαλος** became **δάσκαλο**. That is the whole mechanism, and it is why **Βλέπω τον δάσκαλο** and **Τον δάσκαλο βλέπω** mean the same thing.

**The article in both cases:**

| | Nominative | Accusative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Masculine** | ο / οι | τον / τους |
| **Feminine** | η / οι | την / τις |
| **Neuter** | το / τα | το / τα |

**Neuter never changes between the two**, singular or plural, which makes neuter nouns the easy ones: **Το παιδί τρώει** and **Βλέπω το παιδί**.

**The noun changes too, and how depends on its ending** — that is the next four lessons. The pattern for masculine **-ος**: **ο δάσκαλος** → **τον δάσκαλο**. The final **-ς** drops.

**Feminines mostly do not change in the singular**: **η γυναίκα** → **την γυναίκα**, **η πόλη** → **την πόλη**. Only the article moves.

**Where else the accusative is used**, and this is why it matters more than the object role alone:

1. **After nearly every preposition**: **σε, από, για, με, χωρίς** all take the accusative. **για τον φίλο μου** — for my friend.
2. **In expressions of time**: **την Κυριακή** — on Sunday. **τη Δευτέρα** — on Monday.
3. **With the weak object pronouns** — **με, σε, τον, την, το** — which have their own lesson.

**The final -ν on την and τον** is written and heard, and it is one of the places where the spelling track has a real question: *when* to keep it. For now, keep it before a vowel and before κ, π, τ, μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ, ξ, ψ, and you will be right nearly always.

**Practice.** Say these pairs aloud: **ο δάσκαλος / τον δάσκαλο · η γυναίκα / την γυναίκα · το παιδί / το παιδί**. Then make three sentences out loud: *I see the teacher · I see the woman · I see the child* — **βλέπω** is *I see*. Then say **για τον φίλο μου** and **την Κυριακή**.
Masculine nouns in -ος:
The first declension pattern, and the commonest masculine ending in the language.

**The pattern, with ο δάσκαλος — the teacher:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | ο δάσκαλος | οι δάσκαλοι |
| **Accusative** | τον δάσκαλο | τους δασκάλους |
| **Vocative** | δάσκαλε | δάσκαλοι |

**Three things happen.** The **-ς** drops in the accusative singular; the plural nominative is **-οι**; the plural accusative is **-ους**.

**And the stress moves.** **δάσκαλος** is stressed on the third syllable from the end, but **δασκάλους** has to move it forward — because the rule of limitation says the stress cannot be further back than the third syllable from the end, and the ending **-ους** counts. This is the rule from stage 1 doing real work.

- **ο άνθρωπος** → **τους ανθρώπους** · **ο δάσκαλος** → **τους δασκάλους**
- But **ο φίλος** → **τους φίλους**: no movement, because the stress was already within the limit.

**The vocative — the form for calling someone — is -ε**: **Γιώργο!**, **δάσκαλε!**, **φίλε!**. It is a real case and you will use it constantly with names, so it is worth noticing now even though stage 3 takes it properly.

**Words in this pattern**, and there are thousands: **ο φίλος** (friend), **ο δρόμος** (road), **ο κόσμος** (world), **ο άνθρωπος** (person), **ο αδελφός** (brother), **ο ουρανός** (sky), **ο θεός** (god), **ο χρόνος** (year, time), **ο καιρός** (weather, time), **ο λόγος** (word, reason).

**The -ος words that are not masculine.** A handful of common feminines — **η οδός** (street), **η νήσος** (island), **η μέθοδος** (method) — and a set of neuters — **το δάσος** (forest), **το μέρος** (part, place). Both are learnable sets and both are flagged in the deck.

**Why this pattern matters beyond itself.** It is the pattern of the masculine adjective too — **καλός, καλό, καλοί, καλούς** — so learning it once covers adjectives as well as nouns.

**Practice.** Say the full table aloud three times. Then decline **ο φίλος** and **ο άνθρωπος** out loud, both numbers, both cases, and check where the stress moves. Then say: **Βλέπω τον φίλο μου. · Βλέπω τους φίλους μου. · Οι άνθρωποι είναι καλοί.**
Masculine nouns in -ας and -ης:
The other two masculine patterns. Both are simpler than **-ος** because the stress does not move.

**ο πατέρας — the father:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | ο πατέρας | οι πατέρες |
| **Accusative** | τον πατέρα | τους πατέρες |
| **Vocative** | πατέρα | πατέρες |

**ο μαθητής — the pupil:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | ο μαθητής | οι μαθητές |
| **Accusative** | τον μαθητή | τους μαθητές |
| **Vocative** | μαθητή | μαθητές |

**The rule for both: drop the -ς in the singular accusative, and the plural is -ες for both cases.** Nominative and accusative plural are identical, which is half the work gone.

**Words in -ας**: **ο άντρας** (man), **ο πατέρας** (father), **ο χειμώνας** (winter), **ο μήνας** (month), **ο κανόνας** (rule), **ο γείτονας** (neighbour).

**Words in -ης**: **ο μαθητής** (pupil), **ο εργάτης** (worker), **ο ναύτης** (sailor), **ο επιβάτης** (passenger), **ο πολίτης** (citizen) — and a great many job words, because **-τής** is the Greek *-er*.

**Also in -ης**: a large set of first names — **ο Γιάννης**, **ο Κωστής**, **ο Μανώλης** — whose vocative is the bare stem: **Γιάννη!**, **Μανώλη!**. That is the form you will use most often, because calling someone by name is what you do first.

**The -έας and -ούς oddities.** **Ο ιερέας** (priest) and **ο καφές** (coffee) belong to small sub-patterns: **τον ιερέα / οι ιερείς**, **τον καφέ / οι καφέδες**. Both are high-frequency words for you specifically, so they are in the deck as whole patterns rather than as rules.

**Nouns of this group in the church:** **ο ιερέας** (priest), **ο ψάλτης** (chanter), **ο επίτροπος** (warden — an -ος word), **ο μαθητής** again in its scriptural sense of *disciple*.

**A useful habit from here on:** when you learn a masculine noun, say its plural out loud with it. **Ο πατέρας, οι πατέρες. Ο μαθητής, οι μαθητές.** Two seconds, and it settles the pattern before it can go wrong.

**Practice.** Say both tables aloud twice. Then decline **ο άντρας** and **ο εργάτης**. Then say out loud: **Βλέπω τον πατέρα μου. · Οι μαθητές είναι εδώ. · Γιάννη, τι κάνεις; · Θέλω έναν καφέ.**
Feminine nouns in -α and -η:
The feminine patterns, which are the easiest in the language in the singular and have one genuine trap in the plural.

**η γυναίκα — the woman:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | η γυναίκα | οι γυναίκες |
| **Accusative** | την γυναίκα | τις γυναίκες |

**η αδελφή — the sister:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | η αδελφή | οι αδελφές |
| **Accusative** | την αδελφή | τις αδελφές |

**The singular never changes.** Only the article moves — **η** to **την**. That is true of every feminine noun in Greek, and it means half the case system is free on this gender.

**The plural is -ες** for both of these, in both cases.

**Now the trap: a set of -η feminines pluralise in -εις.**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | η πόλη | οι πόλεις |
| **Accusative** | την πόλη | τις πόλεις |

**Which ones.** Abstract nouns, mostly, and they are extremely common: **η πόλη** (city), **η δύναμη** (strength, power), **η τάξη** (class, order), **η σκέψη** (thought), **η λύση** (solution), **η θέση** (position), **η κυβέρνηση** (government), **η άσκηση** (exercise), **η αίσθηση** (sense).

**The pattern behind it:** these are ancient third-declension nouns, and the **-σις** of the old language became **-ση** in the modern one while keeping its old plural. So a noun ending **-ση, -ξη** or **-ψη** almost always pluralises in **-εις** — which is a usable rule rather than a list.

**The stress moves in that plural too**, sometimes: **η κυβέρνηση** → **οι κυβερνήσεις**, by the rule of limitation again.

**The -ος feminines**, from the last lesson: **η οδός** (street), **η νήσος** (island), **η μέθοδος** (method). They decline like the masculine **-ος** nouns but take feminine articles — **η οδός, την οδό, οι οδοί, τις οδούς** — which looks strange and is regular. **Οδός** is on every street sign in Greece.

**The church words in this group:** **η εκκλησία** (church), **η Λειτουργία** (the Liturgy), **η εικόνα** (icon), **η Παναγία** (the Mother of God), **η προσευχή** (prayer), **η αγάπη** (love), **η νηστεία** (fast), **η Ανάσταση** (the Resurrection — an **-ση** noun, so **οι Αναστάσεις**).

**Practice.** Say all three tables aloud. Then decline **η μέρα**, **η φίλη** and **η τάξη** out loud. Then say: **Βλέπω την γυναίκα. · Οι πόλεις είναι μεγάλες. · Η εκκλησία είναι εδώ. · Πάω στην εκκλησία.**
Neuter nouns in -ο, -ι and -μα:
The easiest gender, because the nominative and accusative are always identical. Three patterns and no case changes to learn.

**το βιβλίο — the book:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. and acc.** | το βιβλίο | τα βιβλία |

**το παιδί — the child:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. and acc.** | το παιδί | τα παιδιά |

**το μάθημα — the lesson:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. and acc.** | το μάθημα | τα μαθήματα |

**Neuter nouns never distinguish subject from object.** **Το παιδί βλέπει το βιβλίο** — the child sees the book — relies entirely on word order, exactly as English does. So with neuters, Greek is briefly an English-shaped language.

**The -ι plural is -ια**, and it is one syllable more: **παιδί** → **παιδιά**, **σπίτι** → **σπίτια**, **τραπέζι** → **τραπέζια**. The stress moves to the ending in some and not in others, and the deck carries each word's plural.

**The -μα plural inserts -ατ-**: **μάθημα** → **μαθήματα**, **όνομα** → **ονόματα**, **πρόβλημα** → **προβλήματα**, **σώμα** → **σώματα**, **αίμα** → **αίματα**. Always, with no exceptions worth learning as such — and the stress stays where it was.

**Words in each pattern:**

- **-ο**: το βιβλίο, το δώρο (gift), το θέατρο, το αυτοκίνητο (car), το δέντρο (tree), το πρόσωπο (face, person)
- **-ι**: το παιδί, το σπίτι (house), το ψωμί (bread), το κρασί (wine), το νερό is **-ό** and behaves like **-ο**
- **-μα**: το μάθημα, το όνομα (name), το πρόβλημα, το κύμα (wave), το ρεύμα (current), το πνεύμα (spirit)

**The fourth neuter pattern — -ος** — is the one that looks masculine: **το δάσος** (forest) → **τα δάση**, **το μέρος** (part, place) → **τα μέρη**, **το έθνος** (nation) → **τα έθνη**. A small, common set, and stage 3 takes it.

**-άκι is the diminutive and it is always neuter**, as stage 2's gender lesson said: **το παιδάκι, το σπιτάκι, το καφεδάκι, το ψωμάκι**. Greeks use these constantly, including about adults and including affectionately, and learning to hear the ending is worth more than learning any individual diminutive.

**Church words here:** **το κερί** (candle), **το τέμπλο** (icon screen), **το αντίδωρο** (the blessed bread given out), **το Ευαγγέλιο** (the Gospel), **το μνημόσυνο** (memorial service), **το πνεύμα** (spirit), **το σώμα** (body), **το όνομα** (name — and *name day*, which matters socially more than birthdays do).

**Practice.** Say the three tables aloud. Then give the plural of: **το δώρο, το σπίτι, το όνομα, το κρασί, το πρόβλημα**. Then say: **Τα παιδιά είναι εδώ. · Θέλω ψωμί και κρασί. · Πώς είναι το όνομά σου;**
The noun system, in one table:
A consolidation lesson. Every pattern from the last four lessons, side by side, so that the shape of the whole system is visible at once.

| | Masc. -ος | Masc. -ας | Masc. -ης | Fem. -α | Fem. -η | Fem. -ση | Neut. -ο | Neut. -ι | Neut. -μα |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | ο δάσκαλος | ο πατέρας | ο μαθητής | η γυναίκα | η αδελφή | η πόλη | το βιβλίο | το παιδί | το μάθημα |
| **Acc. sg.** | τον δάσκαλο | τον πατέρα | τον μαθητή | την γυναίκα | την αδελφή | την πόλη | το βιβλίο | το παιδί | το μάθημα |
| **Nom. pl.** | οι δάσκαλοι | οι πατέρες | οι μαθητές | οι γυναίκες | οι αδελφές | οι πόλεις | τα βιβλία | τα παιδιά | τα μαθήματα |
| **Acc. pl.** | τους δασκάλους | τους πατέρες | τους μαθητές | τις γυναίκες | τις αδελφές | τις πόλεις | τα βιβλία | τα παιδιά | τα μαθήματα |

**What the table shows, in five observations:**

1. **Masculines are the only gender that changes in the singular** — the **-ς** drops. Feminines and neuters do not change at all.
2. **Only -ος masculines have a distinct accusative plural** (**-ους**). Everything else has nominative and accusative plural identical.
3. **Neuters never distinguish the two cases at all.**
4. **The article does more work than the noun.** In most of this table it is **ο/τον/οι/τους** and **η/την/οι/τις** that tell you the case, not the ending.
5. **So learning the article's forms cold is worth more than learning any noun pattern**, and that is the single highest-return memorisation in Greek grammar.

**The article, by itself, for the two cases you now know:**

| | Masc. | Fem. | Neut. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | ο | η | το |
| **Acc. sg.** | τον | την | το |
| **Nom. pl.** | οι | οι | τα |
| **Acc. pl.** | τους | τις | τα |

**Eight forms, three of them repeats.** Say them in that order, down the columns, until they come without thinking — it is twelve cells and it unlocks every noun in the language.

**What is still missing**: the genitive (*of the*) and the vocative (*calling someone*), which are stage 3, and the **Forms track** opens there with the whole thing as reference tables.

**Practice.** Cover the big table and rebuild it out loud from the nine headwords. Then say the article table, down each column, five times. Then take ten nouns from the deck and say each one's four forms.
έχω — I have:
The second verb, and the model for the biggest verb class in the language.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **έχω** | *ého* | I have |
| **έχεις** | *éhis* | you have |
| **έχει** | *éhi* | he / she / it has |
| **έχουμε** | *éhume* | we have |
| **έχετε** | *éhete* | you have (plural or polite) |
| **έχουν** | *éhun* | they have |

**The endings are the pattern**: **-ω, -εις, -ει, -ουμε, -ετε, -ουν**. Those six endings fit several thousand Greek verbs, and the next lesson is about using them on anything.

**έχουν is often said and written έχουνε**, with an extra syllable. Both are standard; the longer one is more colloquial.

**What it takes: the accusative**, like every object in Greek.

- **Έχω ένα βιβλίο.** — I have a book.
- **Έχεις τον αριθμό του;** — Do you have his number?
- **Δεν έχω χρόνο.** — I have no time.

**έχω is not used for age.** English *I am thirty* and Greek **είμαι τριάντα χρονών** both use *be*, so that one is easy; but note **χρονών** is a genitive plural, which is stage 3.

**Nor for the perfect tense, yet.** Greek does build a perfect with **έχω** — **έχω γράψει** (*I have written*) — and it needs the perfective stem, which is stage 4. For now **έχω** is simply *to have*.

**Useful set phrases with έχω:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν έχω χρόνο.** | I have no time. |
| **Έχεις δίκιο.** | You are right. (*you have right*) |
| **Δεν έχει σημασία.** | It does not matter. (*it has no meaning*) |
| **Τι έχεις;** | What is wrong with you? |
| **Έχει ζέστη.** | It is hot. (*it has heat* — common alongside κάνει ζέστη) |

**είμαι and έχω together** carry an enormous amount of ordinary conversation, and between them you can already say who you are, how you are, what you have and what you do not.

**Practice.** Say the six forms aloud five times, then the six endings alone five times. Then say out loud: *I have a book · you have time · we have two children · they have a house · I do not have the number*. Then the five set phrases, until **δεν έχει σημασία** comes out without thinking.
Verbs in -ω: the present tense:
The first conjugation, the largest in the language, and the one whose endings you already know from **έχω**.

**The pattern, with γράφω — I write:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **γράφω** | I write | stress on the stem |
| **γράφεις** | you write | |
| **γράφει** | he / she / it writes | |
| **γράφουμε** | we write | |
| **γράφετε** | you write (pl./polite) | |
| **γράφουν** | they write | |

**The defining feature of this class: the stress stays on the stem** and never moves to the ending. **γράφω, γράφεις, γράφουμε** — all stressed on *γρά-*.

**Verbs in this class**, and this is a starter set worth having now:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **γράφω** | I write | **διαβάζω** | I read |
| **βλέπω** | I see | **ακούω** | I hear, I listen |
| **θέλω** | I want | **ξέρω** | I know |
| **πίνω** | I drink | **τρώω** | I eat (slightly irregular) |
| **κάνω** | I do, I make | **παίρνω** | I take, I get |
| **πηγαίνω / πάω** | I go | **έρχομαι** | I come (a passive-form verb, stage 4) |
| **μένω** | I live, I stay | **δουλεύω** | I work |
| **μαθαίνω** | I learn | **καταλαβαίνω** | I understand |

**The present tense covers both English presents.** **Γράφω** is *I write* and *I am writing* — Greek has no separate continuous form, and whether something is habitual or happening now is left to context or to a time word.

**It also does the near future in speech**: **Αύριο πάω στην Αθήνα** — *tomorrow I am going to Athens*. English does the same thing, so this needs no effort.

**The one thing to get right from the start: the stress.** Because the stress is written, a verb with the stress in the wrong place is a misspelling as well as a mispronunciation. **γράφουμε**, not *γραφούμε*.

**Where the endings are heard**, which matters for listening: the difference between **γράφει** (*he writes*) and **γράφεις** (*you write*) is one final *s*, and it is the commonest thing to mishear in a sentence. Listening for final **-ς** is a real skill and it is worth practising deliberately.

**Practice.** Conjugate **θέλω, βλέπω, κάνω** and **μένω** aloud, all six persons. Then say: *I want a coffee · do you want a coffee? · we live in York · they work here · I do not understand*. Then say **γράφει** and **γράφεις** ten times alternately and listen to the difference.
Verbs in -άω and -ώ: the second class:
The second conjugation, smaller than the first and containing some of the commonest verbs in the language. Its distinguishing feature is that the stress is on the ending.

**Group B1 — αγαπάω / αγαπώ (I love).** Two sets of forms, both correct, used interchangeably:

| | Long form | Short form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | αγαπάω | αγαπώ |
| you | αγαπάς | αγαπάς |
| he/she/it | αγαπάει | αγαπά |
| we | αγαπάμε | αγαπούμε |
| you (pl.) | αγαπάτε | αγαπάτε |
| they | αγαπάνε | αγαπούν |

**The long forms are the everyday spoken ones**; the short forms are more formal and more written. Mixing them is normal and nobody will blink.

**Verbs in B1**: **αγαπάω** (love), **μιλάω** (speak), **ρωτάω** (ask), **απαντάω** (answer), **γελάω** (laugh), **περνάω** (pass), **ξεχνάω** (forget), **πεινάω** (be hungry), **διψάω** (be thirsty), **φοράω** (wear), **χαλάω** (break, spoil).

**Group B2 — μπορώ (I can).** One set of forms, with **-εί-** through the middle:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| μπορώ | I can |
| μπορείς | you can |
| μπορεί | he / she / it can |
| μπορούμε | we can |
| μπορείτε | you can (pl./polite) |
| μπορούν | they can |

**Verbs in B2**: **μπορώ** (can), **μιλώ** also appears here, **οδηγώ** (drive), **τηλεφωνώ** (telephone), **ευχαριστώ** (thank), **παρακαλώ** (please, beg), **συμφωνώ** (agree), **αργώ** (be late), **προχωρώ** (go forward), **ζω** (live — slightly irregular), **ακολουθώ** (follow).

**ευχαριστώ and παρακαλώ are verbs**, which is worth noticing: *I thank* and *I beg*. That is why **παρακαλώ** is both *please* and *you are welcome* and *can I help you?* — it is a verb doing social work.

**How to tell which class a verb is in: listen to where the stress falls in the *I* form.** **γράφω** — stem. **αγαπώ**, **μπορώ** — ending. That is the whole test, and it is why the stress mark matters.

**The deck stores every verb with its class**, because the class decides every other form — and from stage 4, with its perfective stem too, which is the real heart of the Greek verb.

**Practice.** Conjugate **μιλάω** (both ways) and **μπορώ** aloud. Then say: *I speak Greek a little · can you speak more slowly? · I am hungry · I forget the words · thank you very much*. Then say **γράφω / αγαπώ / μπορώ** and name each one's class by where the stress is.
δεν — how Greek says not:
Negation, which is one short word in front of the verb — and a second word you need for commands and wishes.

**δεν goes before the verb.** Nothing else moves.

- **Δεν ξέρω.** — I do not know.
- **Δεν είμαι Έλληνας.** — I am not Greek.
- **Δεν έχω χρόνο.** — I have no time.
- **Δεν καταλαβαίνω.** — I do not understand.

**It goes before the weak pronouns too**, which cluster in front of the verb: **Δεν το ξέρω** — *I do not know it*. **Δεν μου αρέσει** — *I do not like it*.

**No helper verb and no *do*.** English needs *do not*; Greek needs one word and no rearrangement.

**The final -ν is heard and it assimilates**, as stage 1's digraph lesson said: **δεν ξέρω** comes out *δeŋ-gzéro*, **δεν πειράζει** as *δem-birázi*. The spelling never changes.

**δε is a shorter form**, used before some consonants and common in writing and speech both: **δε θέλω**. Keep **δεν** and you will always be right.

**μην is the other negative**, and it is used for:

1. **Commands.** **Μην το κάνεις!** — Do not do that.
2. **Wishes and the subjunctive.** **Να μην πας** — *that you not go* — which is stage 4's territory.
3. **On signs.** **Μην καπνίζετε** — no smoking.

**So: δεν for statements, μην for telling someone not to.** That split is reliable and it is the whole distinction.

**όχι is the word for "no"**, and it is not used in front of verbs:

- **Όχι, δεν θέλω.** — No, I do not want to.
- **Όχι εγώ.** — Not me.

**And the double negative is normal and correct.** Greek, like Spanish, piles negatives up rather than cancelling them:

- **Δεν ξέρω τίποτα.** — I do not know anything. (*literally: I do not know nothing*)
- **Δεν ήρθε κανείς.** — Nobody came.
- **Δεν πάω πουθενά.** — I am not going anywhere.

**τίποτα** (nothing, anything), **κανείς** (nobody, anybody) and **πουθενά** (nowhere, anywhere) all need **δεν** with them. Leaving it out is the error; keeping it is correct.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **Δεν ξέρω. · Δεν καταλαβαίνω. · Δεν έχω χρόνο. · Δεν θέλω τίποτα. · Μην το κάνεις.** Then negate five sentences you made in the verb lessons. Then say **δεν ξέρω** and **δεν πειράζει** at speed and let the final -ν do what it wants.
Questions, and the question words:
How Greek asks. The word order does not change, so the question words and the voice do all the work.

**A yes/no question is the statement with a rising voice** and the Greek question mark:

- **Είσαι καλά.** — You are well. → **Είσαι καλά;** — Are you well?
- **Θέλεις καφέ;** — Do you want coffee?
- **Μιλάς ελληνικά;** — Do you speak Greek?

**Nothing is inverted and nothing is added.** No *do*, no auxiliary, no reordering. This is one of the genuinely easy things in Greek.

**The question words:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **τι;** | what? | **Τι κάνεις;** |
| **ποιος, ποια, ποιο;** | who? which? | **Ποιος είναι;** |
| **πού;** | where? | **Πού είσαι;** |
| **πότε;** | when? | **Πότε έρχεσαι;** |
| **πώς;** | how? | **Πώς σε λένε;** |
| **γιατί;** | why? | **Γιατί όχι;** |
| **πόσο;** | how much? | **Πόσο κάνει;** |
| **πόσοι, πόσες, πόσα;** | how many? | **Πόσα παιδιά έχεις;** |

**ποιος inflects**, because it is really an adjective: **ποιος άντρας** (which man), **ποια γυναίκα**, **ποιο παιδί**, and in the accusative **ποιον, ποια, ποιο**. So *who do you see?* is **Ποιον βλέπεις;**

**πόσο against πόσα.** **Πόσο** is *how much* and does not change: **Πόσο κάνει;** — how much does it cost? **Πόσος/πόση/πόσο** agrees when it modifies a noun, and **πόσοι/πόσες/πόσα** is *how many*: **Πόσα χρόνια;** — how many years?

**The accented ones are the question words.** From stage 1: **πού** and **πώς** with accents are *where?* and *how?*; **που** and **πως** without are *that/who* and *that*. The accent is the only difference and it is not optional:

- **Πού είσαι;** — Where are you?
- **Ο άντρας που είδα** — the man **that** I saw
- **Πώς σε λένε;** — What is your name?
- **Ξέρω πως είναι καλά.** — I know **that** he is well.

**The most useful questions to have cold this week:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πώς σε λένε;** / **Πώς σας λένε;** | What is your name? (familiar / polite) |
| **Από πού είσαι;** | Where are you from? |
| **Τι κάνεις;** / **Τι κάνετε;** | How are you? |
| **Πόσο κάνει;** | How much is it? |
| **Τι είναι αυτό;** | What is this? |
| **Πώς το λένε στα ελληνικά;** | How do you say it in Greek? |
| **Μπορείς να μιλάς πιο αργά;** | Can you speak more slowly? |
| **Δεν καταλαβαίνω. Συγγνώμη.** | I do not understand. Sorry. |

**The last three are the survival set.** Learn them before anything else in this lesson — they are what turn a conversation you are losing into one you can stay in.

**Practice.** Say the eight question words aloud, five times. Then ask eight questions out loud using one of each. Then say the survival set until **Πώς το λένε στα ελληνικά;** comes out in one piece.
Adjectives, and agreement:
An adjective in Greek changes to match its noun — in gender, in number and in case. Three agreements, every time.

**The commonest pattern, -ος / -η / -ο**, with καλός (good):

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | καλός | καλή | καλό |
| **Acc. sg.** | καλό | καλή | καλό |
| **Nom. pl.** | καλοί | καλές | καλά |
| **Acc. pl.** | καλούς | καλές | καλά |

**It is the noun endings you already know.** Masculine like **δάσκαλος**, feminine like **αδελφή**, neuter like **βιβλίο**. Nothing new to learn — the same twelve endings doing a second job.

- **ο καλός δάσκαλος** · **η καλή γυναίκα** · **το καλό παιδί**
- **οι καλοί δάσκαλοι** · **τις καλές γυναίκες** · **τα καλά παιδιά**

**The adjective goes before the noun**, as in English, and between the article and the noun: **ο μεγάλος δρόμος**.

**After είμαι it still agrees**, with whatever it describes:

- **Ο δρόμος είναι μεγάλος.** — The road is big.
- **Η πόλη είναι μεγάλη.** — The city is big.
- **Τα παιδιά είναι καλά.** — The children are well.

**Which is why "καλά" is the answer to "τι κάνεις;"** — it is a neuter plural, meaning *good things*, used adverbially. **Είμαι καλά** rather than *είμαι καλός*, because you are reporting on how things are rather than on your moral character.

**The adverb is the neuter plural**, in fact, as a rule: **καλός** → **καλά** (well), **γρήγορος** → **γρήγορα** (quickly), **σιγανός** → **σιγανά** (quietly). One of the tidiest rules in the language.

**A starter set of adjectives:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **καλός** | good | **κακός** | bad |
| **μεγάλος** | big, large, old (of people) | **μικρός** | small, young |
| **νέος** | new, young | **παλιός** | old (of things) |
| **ωραίος** | lovely, nice | **άσχημος** | ugly |
| **ακριβός** | expensive | **φτηνός** | cheap |
| **εύκολος** | easy | **δύσκολος** | difficult |
| **ζεστός** | hot | **κρύος** | cold |
| **γεμάτος** | full | **άδειος** | empty |

**Two patterns beyond this one** exist — **-ύς/-ιά/-ύ** as in **γλυκός**... in fact **πλατύς, πλατιά, πλατύ** — and the irregular **πολύς, πολλή, πολύ** (much, many), which is so common it is worth memorising now: **πολλά παιδιά** (many children), **πολύ καλά** (very well), **πολλή δουλειά** (a lot of work). Stage 3 takes the rest.

**Practice.** Say the καλός table aloud twice. Then put **μεγάλος** with **δρόμος, πόλη, σπίτι** in both numbers. Then say: **Η Ελλάδα είναι ωραία. · Τα παιδιά είναι μικρά. · Είναι πολύ ακριβό. · Πολλά παιδιά είναι εδώ.**
The personal pronouns, and when Greek us:
Greek has words for *I*, *you* and the rest — and leaves them out almost all the time. Knowing when to use them is as important as knowing them.

**The strong forms:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **εγώ** | I | **εμείς** | we |
| **εσύ** | you (one, familiar) | **εσείς** | you (plural or polite) |
| **αυτός / αυτή / αυτό** | he / she / it | **αυτοί / αυτές / αυτά** | they (m / f / n) |

**Normally they are omitted**, because the verb ending already says who:

- **Είμαι εδώ.** — I am here.
- **Μιλάς ελληνικά;** — Do you speak Greek?

**So when are they used?** Four cases, all of them about emphasis:

1. **Contrast.** **Εγώ** πάω, **εσύ** μένεις. — *I* am going, *you* are staying.
2. **Emphasis on the person.** **Εγώ** δεν ξέρω. — *I* do not know.
3. **Alone, with no verb.** **Ποιος θέλει καφέ; — Εγώ.** — Who wants coffee? — Me.
4. **After **και** and **ούτε**.** Και **εγώ** — me too. (In speech: **κι εγώ**.)

**Using them in every sentence is the clearest grammatical mark of a foreigner** — more noticeable than a wrong case ending, because it makes every sentence sound insistent.

**The third person doubles as "this".** **Αυτός** is both *he* and *this one*, and Greek uses it where English would use a name or *he*: **Αυτός είναι ο φίλος μου** — *this is my friend*. It inflects like an adjective and has its own lesson next.

**The accusative strong forms** — for emphasis as an object — are **εμένα, εσένα, αυτόν/αυτήν/αυτό, εμάς, εσάς, αυτούς/αυτές/αυτά**:

- **Εμένα** ρώτησε, όχι εσένα. — He asked *me*, not you.

**But the everyday object pronouns are the weak ones** — **με, σε, τον, την, το, μας, σας, τους** — which go before the verb and have their own lesson in this stage. **Με βλέπει** is *he sees me*; **εμένα βλέπει** is *it is me he sees*.

**There is no word for "it" as a subject.** English *it is raining* and *it is three o'clock* have no pronoun in Greek at all: **βρέχει**, **είναι τρεις**.

**Practice.** Say the six strong forms aloud. Then say these out loud, with the pronoun only where it belongs: *I am here · I do not know, but he does · who wants coffee? — me · I am going, you are staying · we are Greek, they are not*. Then say five sentences about yourself with no pronoun at all.
αυτός and εκείνος — this and that:
Pointing at things, which you will do constantly before you have the vocabulary to name them.

**αυτός — this, and he.** It inflects like an adjective:

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | αυτός | αυτή | αυτό |
| **Acc. sg.** | αυτόν | αυτήν | αυτό |
| **Nom. pl.** | αυτοί | αυτές | αυτά |
| **Acc. pl.** | αυτούς | αυτές | αυτά |

**εκείνος — that, over there.** Same endings: **εκείνος, εκείνη, εκείνο**.

**The one rule that matters: with a noun, the article stays.**

- **αυτός ο άντρας** — this man. Literally *this the man*.
- **αυτή η γυναίκα** — this woman.
- **αυτό το παιδί** — this child.
- **εκείνο το σπίτι** — that house.

**Leaving the article out is wrong** and it is the commonest error English speakers make here, because English has no article in *this man*.

**Without a noun it stands alone:**

- **Αυτό είναι.** — That is it.
- **Τι είναι αυτό;** — What is this?
- **Αυτός είναι ο φίλος μου.** — This is my friend.
- **Πόσο κάνει αυτό;** — How much is this?

**The neuter is what you point with.** When you do not know a word — which at this stage is most of the time — **αυτό** plus a gesture does the job: **Θέλω αυτό, παρακαλώ.** — I want this, please. That sentence will get you through a bakery today.

**εδώ and εκεί** — here and there — go with them naturally: **αυτό εδώ** (this one here), **εκείνο εκεί** (that one there).

**A third, more formal pair** exists — **ούτος**, **τούτος** — and **τούτος** is alive in dialect and in Cyprus. Standard modern speech uses **αυτός** and **εκείνος** and nothing else.

**The emphatic repeat** is worth hearing: **αυτός ο ίδιος** (this very one), **ο ίδιος** (the same, himself). **Ο ίδιος ο παπάς** — the priest himself.

**Practice.** Say the αυτός table aloud. Then say these out loud: **Τι είναι αυτό; · Αυτό εδώ, παρακαλώ. · Αυτός ο άντρας είναι ο πατέρας μου. · Εκείνη η γυναίκα είναι η μητέρα μου. · Πόσο κάνει αυτό;** Then point at five things in the room and name each with **αυτό** plus whatever noun you know.
υπάρχει — there is:
Greek has a separate verb for *there is* and *there are*, and it is not **είμαι**.

**υπάρχει** — there is. **υπάρχουν** — there are.

- **Υπάρχει ένα πρόβλημα.** — There is a problem.
- **Υπάρχουν πολλά παιδιά εδώ.** — There are many children here.
- **Δεν υπάρχει χρόνος.** — There is no time.
- **Υπάρχει εκκλησία στο χωριό;** — Is there a church in the village?

**It agrees with what there is** — singular for one thing, plural for several — which is the opposite of English, where *there is* and *there are* follow the same rule but the *there* never changes.

**The verb means "to exist"** in its own right: **Ο Θεός υπάρχει** — God exists. That is the same word doing the plainer job, and in a theological conversation it is the word you will want.

**The spoken alternative: έχει.** Colloquially, **έχει** is used impersonally for *there is*:

- **Έχει κόσμο σήμερα.** — There are a lot of people today. (*κόσμος* = world, and also *crowd*)
- **Έχει ψωμί;** — Is there any bread?
- **Δεν έχει νερό.** — There is no water.

**Both are correct.** **Υπάρχει** is the standard and slightly more formal; **έχει** is what you will hear in a shop. Learn to recognise both and use whichever comes out.

**είμαι cannot do this job.** *There is a church here* is not **είναι μια εκκλησία εδώ** — that means *a church is here*, which is odd in the same way the English would be odd. Use **υπάρχει**.

**Where it is useful immediately:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Υπάρχει...;** | Is there...? |
| **Δεν υπάρχει πρόβλημα.** | There is no problem. |
| **Υπάρχει κάτι άλλο;** | Is there anything else? |
| **Έχει καφέ;** | Is there coffee? |
| **Πού υπάρχει φαρμακείο;** | Where is there a pharmacy? |

**Practice.** Say the five phrases aloud, five times. Then say out loud: *there is a problem · there are many people · there is no time · is there bread? · is there a church here?* Then say **Ο Θεός υπάρχει** and notice it is the same verb.
μου, σου, του — saying whose:
Possession, which Greek does with a short word after the noun — and which is one of the first things you will need.

**The possessives:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **μου** | my | **μας** | our |
| **σου** | your (one, familiar) | **σας** | your (plural or polite) |
| **του** | his, its | **τους** | their |
| **της** | her | | |

**They go after the noun, and the article stays:**

- **ο φίλος μου** — my friend. Literally *the friend of me*.
- **η μητέρα μου** — my mother.
- **το όνομά μου** — my name.
- **τα παιδιά μας** — our children.
- **το σπίτι τους** — their house.

**The article is not optional.** *Φίλος μου* without the article means something different and usually wrong; **ο φίλος μου** is the normal form.

**The second accent, from stage 1, appears here**: when the noun is stressed on its third-from-last syllable, adding the pronoun forces a second accent:

- **το όνομα** → **το όνομά μου** · **ο δάσκαλος** → **ο δάσκαλός μου** · **το μάθημα** → **το μάθημά μου**

**They are the same words as the genitive weak pronouns**, which is exactly what they are — *of me, of you, of him*. That is why stage 3's genitive lesson will look familiar.

**του and της matter.** **του** is *his*, **της** is *her*, and both are *of it* depending on the noun's gender. **Ο πατέρας του** is *his father*; **ο πατέρας της** is *her father*. The difference is one letter and it carries all the information.

**Family words, which is where this gets used most:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ο πατέρας** / **ο μπαμπάς** | father / dad | **η μητέρα** / **η μαμά** | mother / mum |
| **ο αδελφός** | brother | **η αδελφή** | sister |
| **ο γιος** | son | **η κόρη** | daughter |
| **ο παππούς** | grandfather | **η γιαγιά** | grandmother |
| **ο άντρας** | man, husband | **η γυναίκα** | woman, wife |
| **ο θείος** | uncle | **η θεία** | aunt |
| **ο νονός** | godfather | **η νονά** | godmother |

**The last pair matters at church**, and more than it does in English: a godparent is a real family relationship in Greek practice, and **ο νονός μου** is said the way *my uncle* is.

**δικός μου is the emphatic form** — *mine, my own*: **Αυτό είναι δικό μου** (this is mine), **ο δικός μου φίλος** (my own friend). It inflects like an adjective.

**Practice.** Say the seven possessives aloud. Then say out loud, with the article: *my friend · my mother · her father · their house · our children · my name*. Then say five of the family words with **μου**, checking the second accent on **ο δάσκαλός μου** and **το όνομά μου**.
Prepositions: σε, από, για, με:
Four words that do most of the work of English's two dozen prepositions — and all of them take the accusative.

**σε — in, at, to, on.** The most overloaded word in Greek:

- **Είμαι στο σπίτι.** — I am at home.
- **Πάω στην εκκλησία.** — I am going to church.
- **Το βιβλίο είναι στο τραπέζι.** — The book is on the table.
- **Μένω στην Αγγλία.** — I live in England.

**One word for in, at, to and on**, and the difference is left to context and to the verb. That is a simplification for you and a thing to get used to.

**από — from, of, than, by:**

- **Είμαι από την Αγγλία.** — I am from England.
- **Από πού είσαι;** — Where are you from?
- **ένα ποτήρι από γυαλί** — a glass made of glass
- **Είναι πιο μεγάλος από μένα.** — He is bigger than me.

**για — for, about, to:**

- **Αυτό είναι για σένα.** — This is for you.
- **Μιλάμε για το μάθημα.** — We are talking about the lesson.
- **Φεύγω για την Αθήνα.** — I am leaving for Athens.

**με — with, by:**

- **Έρχομαι με τον φίλο μου.** — I am coming with my friend.
- **Πάω με το αυτοκίνητο.** — I am going by car.
- **καφές με γάλα** — coffee with milk

**More, all with the accusative**: **χωρίς** (without), **μετά** (after), **πριν** (before), **προς** (towards), **κατά** (against, during), **μέχρι** (until), **σαν** (like, as), **παρά** (despite, to — in telling the time).

**Every one of them takes the accusative**, which is why the accusative matters more than its name suggests: it is not only the object case, it is the after-a-preposition case, and that is most of its daily work.

- **για τον φίλο μου** · **με την μητέρα μου** · **από το σπίτι** · **χωρίς ζάχαρη**

**σε merges with the article**, which is the next lesson, and it is compulsory rather than optional: **σε** + **το** is always **στο**, never two words.

**The strong pronouns follow prepositions**, not the weak ones: **για μένα** (for me), **με σένα** (with you), **από αυτόν** (from him). **Για με** is wrong.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **στο σπίτι, στην εκκλησία, από την Αγγλία, για σένα, με γάλα, χωρίς ζάχαρη**. Then say out loud: *I am from England · I live in York · this is for you · I am coming with my friend · coffee with milk, without sugar*.
στον, στη, στο — σε plus the article:
The one contraction in Greek that you must get right, because it is compulsory and it appears in almost every sentence about where anything is.

**σε and the definite article always merge:**

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Singular** | στον | στη / στην | στο |
| **Plural** | στους | στις | στα |

- **σε + τον δρόμο** → **στον δρόμο** — in the road
- **σε + την εκκλησία** → **στην εκκλησία** — to church
- **σε + το σπίτι** → **στο σπίτι** — at home
- **σε + τα παιδιά** → **στα παιδιά** — to the children

**Never written as two words.** *Σε το σπίτι* is simply wrong.

**στη or στην?** Both are correct and the choice is the final-ν rule, which the Spelling track takes properly. The short version: keep the **-ν** before a vowel and before **κ, π, τ, μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ, ξ, ψ** — so **στην Αθήνα**, **στην πόλη**, but **στη Θεσσαλονίκη**, **στη μητέρα**. Keeping it always is a very minor error; dropping it always is slightly more noticeable.

**With a name, the article is still there**: **στον Γιώργο** (to George), **στη Μαρία** (to Maria), because Greek keeps the article with names.

**Where it turns up constantly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **στο σπίτι** | at home |
| **στη δουλειά** | at work |
| **στην εκκλησία** | at / to church |
| **στο σχολείο** | at school |
| **στην Ελλάδα** | in Greece |
| **στην Αθήνα** | in Athens |
| **στα ελληνικά** | in Greek |
| **στον δρόμο** | in the street, on the way |

**στα ελληνικά** is how you say *in Greek*, and it is a neuter plural: **Πώς το λένε στα ελληνικά;** — the sentence from the question lesson.

**από merges too, informally**: **απ' το σπίτι**, **απ' την Αθήνα** — with an apostrophe, exactly as stage 1's punctuation lesson described. **Για** and **με** do not merge.

**Practice.** Say the six merged forms aloud, five times. Then say: *at home · at work · to church · in Greece · in Greek · in the street*. Then make five sentences out loud with **πάω** (I go) and five with **είμαι** plus a place.
Where things are:
The place words, which go with **σε** and turn *the book is on the table* into something you can say about anything in a room.

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **πάνω σε** | on, on top of | **κάτω από** | under |
| **μέσα σε** | inside | **έξω από** | outside |
| **δίπλα σε** | next to | **κοντά σε** | near |
| **μπροστά από** | in front of | **πίσω από** | behind |
| **ανάμεσα σε** | between | **γύρω από** | around |
| **απέναντι από** | opposite | **μακριά από** | far from |

**Notice which take σε and which take από.** There is no rule worth deriving; they are learned as units, and the deck stores each as a whole phrase.

- **Το βιβλίο είναι πάνω στο τραπέζι.** — The book is on the table.
- **Η γάτα είναι κάτω από την καρέκλα.** — The cat is under the chair.
- **Μένω δίπλα στην εκκλησία.** — I live next to the church.
- **Το φαρμακείο είναι απέναντι από την τράπεζα.** — The pharmacy is opposite the bank.

**And they merge with the article**, exactly as **σε** does: **πάνω στο**, **δίπλα στην**, **μέσα στα**.

**Several of them stand alone as adverbs**, without a following noun:

- **Είμαι μέσα.** — I am inside.
- **Έλα κάτω.** — Come down.
- **Πάμε έξω.** — Let's go out.
- **Είναι εκεί πάνω.** — It is up there.

**The direction words:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **εδώ** | here | **εκεί** | there |
| **αριστερά** | left | **δεξιά** | right |
| **ευθεία** | straight on | **πίσω** | back |
| **πάνω** | up | **κάτω** | down |

**Which gives you directions, and asking for them:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πού είναι...;** | Where is...? |
| **Είναι δεξιά.** | It is on the right. |
| **Πηγαίνετε ευθεία.** | Go straight on. |
| **Στρίψτε αριστερά.** | Turn left. |
| **Είναι κοντά;** | Is it near? |
| **Είναι μακριά.** | It is far. |

**Practice.** Say the twelve place phrases aloud. Then describe five things in the room you are in — *the book is on the table, the chair is next to the door* — out loud, in Greek. Then ask and answer: **Πού είναι η εκκλησία; — Είναι δίπλα στο σχολείο.**
με, σε, τον — the object pronouns:
The short pronouns that stand in for a noun as the object of a verb. They go **before** the verb, which is the thing English speakers have to get used to.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **με** | me | **μας** | us |
| **σε** | you | **σας** | you (pl./polite) |
| **τον / την / το** | him / her / it | **τους / τις / τα** | them (m / f / n) |

**Before the verb, always, in a statement:**

- **Με βλέπει.** — He sees me.
- **Σε ξέρω.** — I know you.
- **Τον ξέρω.** — I know him.
- **Την αγαπώ.** — I love her.
- **Το θέλω.** — I want it.
- **Μας περιμένουν.** — They are waiting for us.

**They go before δεν as well** — or rather, δεν goes first and the pronoun sits between it and the verb:

- **Δεν το ξέρω.** — I do not know it.
- **Δεν τον βλέπω.** — I do not see him.

**After a command, they go behind:**

- **Πες μου!** — Tell me!
- **Δώσε το!** — Give it!
- **Πάρε τα!** — Take them!

**So the order flips with the mood of the verb**, and that is the only complication: before a statement, after a command. Greek grammar calls these **clitics** — words that cannot stand alone and attach to the verb.

**Two pronouns together: indirect first, then direct.**

- **Μου το δίνει.** — He gives it to me. (*to me it he-gives*)
- **Σου το λέω.** — I am telling you it.
- **Δώσε μου το.** — Give it to me.

**The indirect object uses the genitive forms**, which are the possessives you just learned: **μου, σου, του, της, μας, σας, τους**. So **μου** is both *my* and *to me*, and position tells you which: after a noun it is possessive, before a verb it is *to me*.

- **ο φίλος μου** — my friend
- **μου μιλάει** — he speaks to me

**The strong forms are for emphasis**, as the pronoun lesson said: **Εμένα ρώτησε** (he asked *me*), **Σε εμένα το έδωσε** (he gave it to *me*).

**Three sentences to have cold**, because they are the ones you will use most:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν το ξέρω.** | I do not know it. |
| **Πες μου.** | Tell me. |
| **Μου αρέσει.** | I like it. — and that is the next lesson. |

**Practice.** Say the two sets aloud. Then say out loud: *I know him · I love her · I want it · he sees me · they are waiting for us · I do not know it*. Then the command forms: **Πες μου · Δώσε το · Πάρε τα**. Then **Μου το δίνει** and **Δώσε μου το**, and notice the order flipping.
μου αρέσει — liking things:
How Greek says *I like*, which is not with a verb meaning *like*. It is worth its own lesson because the structure is backwards from English and it is extremely common.

**The verb is αρέσω — to be pleasing.** So *I like coffee* is literally *coffee is pleasing to me*:

- **Μου αρέσει ο καφές.** — I like coffee.
- **Σου αρέσει η Ελλάδα;** — Do you like Greece?
- **Του αρέσει το ψωμί.** — He likes bread.

**The thing liked is the subject**, so the verb agrees with **it**, not with you:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μου αρέσει ο καφές.** | I like coffee. (one thing → αρέσει) |
| **Μου αρέσουν τα παιδιά.** | I like children. (several → αρέσουν) |

**Getting that agreement right is the whole lesson.** *Μου αρέσει τα παιδιά* is the standard learner error.

**The person goes in the weak genitive** — the same **μου, σου, του, της, μας, σας, τους** from the last two lessons:

- **Μου αρέσει** — I like · **Σου αρέσει** — you like · **Του αρέσει** — he likes
- **Της αρέσει** — she likes · **Μας αρέσει** — we like · **Σας αρέσει** — you like · **Τους αρέσει** — they like

**With a verb after it, use να**: **Μου αρέσει να διαβάζω** — *I like reading*. **να** plus a verb is the Greek infinitive-substitute and it is stage 4's subject; this is a preview you can use immediately.

**The negative is δεν in front of the pronoun**: **Δεν μου αρέσει** — I do not like it.

**Other verbs work the same way**, and they are all common:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **μου φαίνεται** | it seems to me |
| **μου λείπει** | I miss it / him (*it is lacking to me*) |
| **μου πάει** | it suits me |
| **μου χρειάζεται** | I need it |
| **μου πονάει** | it hurts (me) — **μου πονάει το κεφάλι** |
| **με πειράζει** | it bothers me (this one takes the accusative) |

**Δεν μου αρέσει** and **δεν με πειράζει** are both worth having cold, and **δεν πειράζει** on its own is the extremely useful *never mind, it does not matter*.

**Practice.** Say the seven persons aloud with **αρέσει**. Then say out loud: *I like coffee · I like children · do you like Greece? · she likes the house · I do not like it · I like reading*. Then say **Μου λείπει** and **Δεν πειράζει** five times each.
Politeness: εσύ and εσείς:
The fork that runs through every verb in the language, and the one social mistake worth not making at church.

**Greek has two ways of saying *you*:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **εσύ**, with the singular verb | one person, familiar |
| **εσείς**, with the plural verb | several people — **or** one person, politely |

- **Τι κάνεις;** — How are you? (a friend)
- **Τι κάνετε;** — How are you? (someone older, someone new, several people)

**Everything agrees with the choice:**

| Familiar | Polite |
| --- | --- |
| **Γεια σου** | **Γεια σας** |
| **Πώς σε λένε;** | **Πώς σας λένε;** |
| **Είσαι καλά;** | **Είστε καλά;** |
| **Θέλεις καφέ;** | **Θέλετε καφέ;** |
| **Το σπίτι σου** | **Το σπίτι σας** |
| **Πες μου** | **Πείτε μου** |

**When to use the plural**, and the Greek convention is a little looser than the French or German one:

- **Anyone noticeably older than you**, until they tell you otherwise.
- **Anyone you have just met**, in a formal setting.
- **Shopkeepers, officials, doctors, teachers** — though in a small shop the singular comes quickly.
- **The priest.** Always, until he says otherwise.

**When the singular is right:** friends, people your age in an informal setting, children, and anyone who has used it to you first.

**The switch happens fast and it is usually offered**: **Πες μου "εσύ"** — *call me "you"* — or simply by the other person using the singular. Greeks are less formal than the grammar suggests, and in a parish hall you will be on **εσύ** with most people within a few weeks.

**Addressing the priest.** **Πάτερ** is the vocative of **πατέρας** and it is how you address him — **Πάτερ, καλημέρα**. In the third person, **ο πατέρας** or **ο παπάς** (informal, affectionate, and not rude), or **ο ιερέας** (formal). Depending on rank there are formal styles — **Παναγιώτατε** for the Patriarch, **Σεβασμιώτατε** for a bishop — and getting those right matters at the moment it arises; **Πάτερ** covers the parish priest.

**The safe default for you, this year: εσείς with adults you do not know, εσύ when invited.** Over-politeness in Greek is a trivial error and under-politeness is a noticeable one.

**Practice.** Say every pair in the table aloud, both columns. Then say five sentences to an imagined friend, then the same five to an imagined priest. Then say **Πάτερ, καλημέρα. Τι κάνετε;** until it is automatic.
Numbers 20 to 100, and prices:
The rest of the numbers you need daily, and the two sentences that get you through a shop.

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 20 | είκοσι | 70 | εβδομήντα |
| 30 | τριάντα | 80 | ογδόντα |
| 40 | σαράντα | 90 | ενενήντα |
| 50 | πενήντα | 100 | εκατό |
| 60 | εξήντα | 1000 | χίλια |

**Compounds are just the two words, in order**, with no joining word and no hyphen:

- **είκοσι ένα** — 21 · **τριάντα πέντε** — 35 · **εξήντα εφτά** — 67 · **ενενήντα εννιά** — 99

**And 1, 3, 4 still inflect inside a compound**: **είκοσι μία ώρες** (21 hours, feminine), **τριάντα τρία παιδιά** (33 children, neuter).

**Above a hundred**: **εκατό** on its own, **εκατόν** before another number — **εκατόν είκοσι** (120). Then **διακόσια** (200), **τριακόσια** (300), **τετρακόσια**, **πεντακόσια**, **εξακόσια**, **εφτακόσια**, **οχτακόσια**, **εννιακόσια**, **χίλια** (1000).

**The hundreds and thousands inflect for gender**: **διακόσιες γυναίκες**, **διακόσια παιδιά**. Not urgent; useful to recognise.

**Money.** The currency is **το ευρώ**, and it does not inflect: **ένα ευρώ, δύο ευρώ, είκοσι ευρώ**. Cents are **τα λεπτά**.

- **δύο ευρώ και πενήντα** — €2.50
- **τρία ευρώ** — €3
- Prices are written **2,50 €** — comma for the decimal, as stage 1's punctuation lesson said.

**The shop sentences:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πόσο κάνει;** | How much is it? |
| **Πόσο κάνουν;** | How much are they? |
| **Πόσο κοστίζει;** | How much does it cost? (more formal) |
| **Θέλω ένα...** | I want a... |
| **Θα ήθελα...** | I would like... (politer; the form is stage 6) |
| **Ένα κιλό, παρακαλώ.** | A kilo, please. |
| **Μισό κιλό.** | Half a kilo. |
| **Αυτό, παρακαλώ.** | This one, please. |
| **Τίποτα άλλο, ευχαριστώ.** | Nothing else, thanks. |
| **Δώστε μου την απόδειξη.** | Give me the receipt. |

**Ordinals**, briefly, because dates and floors need them: **πρώτος** (1st), **δεύτερος**, **τρίτος**, **τέταρτος**, **πέμπτος**, **έκτος**, **έβδομος**, **όγδοος**, **ένατος**, **δέκατος**. They inflect like adjectives, and they are the words behind **η Δευτέρα** (Monday — the second day), **η Τρίτη**, **η Τετάρτη**, **η Πέμπτη**.

**Practice.** Count by tens to 100, aloud. Then say these numbers: 21, 35, 48, 67, 99, 120, 500. Then say the shop sentences five times each. Then price five things in the room in euros, out loud.
Telling the time:
One table and three patterns, and the numbers go feminine because **ώρα** is feminine.

**The question and the answer:**

- **Τι ώρα είναι;** — What time is it?
- **Είναι τρεις.** — It is three o'clock.
- **Είναι μία.** — It is one o'clock. (**μία**, feminine)
- **Είναι δώδεκα.** — It is twelve.

**The numbers used are the feminine ones**, because the hours are **ώρες**: **μία, δύο, τρεις, τέσσερις, πέντε…** — so 3 and 4 are **τρεις** and **τέσσερις**, not **τρία** and **τέσσερα**.

**The minutes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **τρεις και δέκα** | ten past three |
| **τρεις και τέταρτο** | quarter past three |
| **τρεις και μισή** | half past three |
| **τρεις και είκοσι πέντε** | twenty-five past three |
| **τέσσερις παρά είκοσι** | twenty to four |
| **τέσσερις παρά τέταρτο** | quarter to four |

**και** for past, **παρά** for to. Exactly the English structure, with the hour named first both ways.

**Half past is και μισή**, with the feminine **μισή** agreeing with **ώρα**.

**The 24-hour clock is used in writing** — timetables, tickets, notices — and said as plain numbers: **στις δεκαπέντε και τριάντα**.

**At what time: στις**, with the accusative plural of the article:

- **στις τρεις** — at three · **στις πέντε και μισή** — at half past five
- **στη μία** — at one (singular, because **μία** is one)

**The parts of the day**, which Greeks attach constantly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το πρωί** | the morning |
| **το μεσημέρι** | midday, the early afternoon |
| **το απόγευμα** | the late afternoon |
| **το βράδυ** | the evening |
| **τη νύχτα** | the night |

- **στις εννιά το πρωί** — at nine in the morning
- **στις εφτά το βράδυ** — at seven in the evening

**το μεσημέρι is a real institution** — roughly 2 to 5 pm, when shops close and people rest, and when you do not telephone anyone.

**Church times**, which is why this lesson has a particular use for you: the Sunday Liturgy is usually **στις δέκα** or **στις δέκα και μισή**, the Orthros before it from about **στις οχτώ και μισή**, and Saturday Vespers **στις έξι** or **στις εφτά το βράδυ**. The notice board will give you the exact times in writing, in the numerals you already read.

**Practice.** Say the time table aloud. Then say the current time, then ten random times. Then say: *at three · at half past five · at nine in the morning · at seven in the evening*. Then read the next service time off a notice and say it out loud.
Days, months and the church year:
The calendar words, and the small set of feast-day greetings that will be said to you before you can answer them.

**The days**, all feminine except Saturday:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **η Δευτέρα** | Monday | *the second* |
| **η Τρίτη** | Tuesday | *the third* |
| **η Τετάρτη** | Wednesday | *the fourth* |
| **η Πέμπτη** | Thursday | *the fifth* |
| **η Παρασκευή** | Friday | *preparation* |
| **το Σάββατο** | Saturday | *Sabbath* |
| **η Κυριακή** | Sunday | *the Lord's day* |

**The names are a week that starts on Sunday** — Monday is the second day — and two of them are explicitly Christian: **Παρασκευή** is the day of preparation, and **Κυριακή** is the day of the Lord. You are learning a calendar that was named by the Church, which is a useful thing to notice early.

**On a day: the accusative with no preposition.**

- **τη Δευτέρα** — on Monday · **την Κυριακή** — on Sunday · **το Σάββατο** — on Saturday

**The months**, all masculine:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Ιανουάριος** | January | **Ιούλιος** | July |
| **Φεβρουάριος** | February | **Αύγουστος** | August |
| **Μάρτιος** | March | **Σεπτέμβριος** | September |
| **Απρίλιος** | April | **Οκτώβριος** | October |
| **Μάιος** | May | **Νοέμβριος** | November |
| **Ιούνιος** | June | **Δεκέμβριος** | December |

**Dates use the genitive of the month** — which is stage 3 — so for now learn the shape as a phrase: **στις 14 Οκτωβρίου**, **την 1η Μαΐου**. Note **Μαΐου** with its diaeresis and accent, from stage 1.

**The seasons**: **η άνοιξη** (spring), **το καλοκαίρι** (summer), **το φθινόπωρο** (autumn), **ο χειμώνας** (winter).

**The feasts you will meet first**, with the greeting that goes with each:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Χρόνια πολλά!** | *Many years!* — for name days, birthdays and feasts. The most useful greeting in Greek life. |
| **Καλά Χριστούγεννα** | Happy Christmas |
| **Καλή Χρονιά** | Happy New Year |
| **Καλή Σαρακοστή** | A good Lent — said as Lent begins |
| **Καλή Ανάσταση** | said in Holy Week, before Easter |
| **Χριστός Ανέστη!** — **Αληθώς Ανέστη!** | Christ is risen — truly he is risen. The Paschal exchange, for forty days. |
| **Καλό Πάσχα** | Happy Easter |
| **Καλή εβδομάδα** | a good week — said on a Monday |
| **Καλό μήνα** | a good month — said on the first |

**Name days matter more than birthdays.** Everyone named for a saint celebrates on that saint's day, people say **χρόνια πολλά** to them, and the parish knows whose day it is. Learning the names of the saints in your parish is learning when to say it.

**Χριστός Ανέστη is not Modern Greek** — it is the older form, kept as a formula, and it is the clearest everyday example of the point stage 1 made: the liturgical language survives inside modern speech as set phrases.

**Practice.** Say the seven days aloud, then the twelve months. Then say: *on Monday · on Sunday · in May · in the summer*. Then say all nine greetings aloud, and learn **Χρόνια πολλά** first.
At church: the words you will hear first:
The vocabulary of the parish — not of the service, which is the later curriculum, but of the building, the people and the Sunday around it.

**The building and what is in it:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **η εκκλησία** | the church | **ο ναός** | the church, the temple (formal) |
| **το τέμπλο** | the icon screen | **η εικόνα** | the icon |
| **το κερί** | the candle | **το κηροπήγιο** | the candle stand |
| **το θυμίαμα** | the incense | **ο σταυρός** | the cross |
| **το Ευαγγέλιο** | the Gospel book | **το αναλόγιο** | the chanter's stand |
| **ο νάρθηκας** | the narthex | **το Ιερό** | the sanctuary |
| **το παγκάρι** | the candle desk at the door | **το αντίδωρο** | the blessed bread given out |

**The people:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ο ιερέας** | the priest (formal) | **ο παπάς** | the priest (everyday, affectionate) |
| **Πάτερ** | Father — how you address him | **ο επίσκοπος** | the bishop |
| **ο ψάλτης** | the chanter | **το παιδί του Ιερού** | the altar server |
| **η πρεσβυτέρα** | the priest's wife | **ο επίτροπος** | the parish warden |
| **ο νονός** / **η νονά** | godfather / godmother | **η ενορία** | the parish |

**The services, by name**, which is what the notice board lists:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **η Θεία Λειτουργία** | the Divine Liturgy |
| **ο Όρθρος** | Matins, before the Liturgy |
| **ο Εσπερινός** | Vespers |
| **η Παράκληση** | the Supplication service |
| **το μνημόσυνο** | the memorial service |
| **η βάπτιση** | the baptism |
| **ο γάμος** | the wedding |
| **η Μεγάλη Εβδομάδα** | Holy Week |

**The things people say, which is the actual point of this lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλή Κυριακή!** | A good Sunday to you |
| **Χρόνια πολλά!** | Many years — name days and feasts |
| **Ο Θεός να σε/σας έχει καλά.** | God keep you well |
| **Να ζήσεις!** | Long life to you — at a birthday or a wedding |
| **Καλή δύναμη!** | Strength to you — in Lent, or to someone with a hard job on |
| **Δόξα τω Θεώ.** | Glory to God — said constantly, and an old form |
| **Με το καλό.** | roughly *may it go well* — on leaving or beginning something |
| **Περαστικά!** | Get well soon |
| **Συλλυπητήρια.** | My condolences |

**Two of those are not Modern Greek** — **Δόξα τω Θεώ** is a dative, which the modern language no longer has, and **Ο Θεός να σε έχει καλά** keeps an older shape. They survive as formulas, like **Χριστός Ανέστη**, and you use them without analysing them. That is exactly how Greeks use them too.

**What to do with this lesson practically.** Learn the people and the greetings first — they are what Sunday actually requires. The building words come by looking at the building. The service names come off the notice board.

**Practice.** Say the nine phrases aloud, five times each, and have **Καλή Κυριακή** and **Χρόνια πολλά** ready for this week. Then name five things in your own church in Greek. Then read the notice board and find the service names on it.
Ordering a coffee: your first real excha:
Everything in stage 2, used in the one transaction you will have most often. Learn this whole exchange as a unit.

**The coffees, because the names are not optional:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ελληνικός καφές** | Greek coffee, boiled in a briki, grounds in the cup |
| **σκέτος** | without sugar |
| **μέτριος** | with a little sugar |
| **γλυκός** | sweet |
| **φραπέ** | instant coffee shaken cold with ice — the summer default |
| **φρέντο εσπρέσο** | cold espresso, shaken |
| **φρέντο καπουτσίνο** | the same with cold milk foam |
| **ζεστός** / **κρύος** | hot / cold |
| **με γάλα** / **χωρίς γάλα** | with / without milk |
| **για εδώ** / **για πάνω** | to drink here / to take away |

**The exchange:**

— **Καλημέρα!**
— **Καλημέρα. Τι θα πάρετε;** *(What will you have?)*
— **Έναν ελληνικό μέτριο, παρακαλώ.**
— **Κάτι άλλο;** *(Anything else?)*
— **Ένα κουλούρι. Πόσο κάνει;**
— **Δύο ευρώ και πενήντα.**
— **Ευχαριστώ.**
— **Παρακαλώ. Καλή σας μέρα!**

**What is in that, grammatically**, all of it from this stage: **έναν** is the masculine accusative of the indefinite article, because **καφές** is masculine and it is the object of an unspoken *I want*. **Μέτριο** agrees with it in gender and case. **Πόσο κάνει** is the price question. **Παρακαλώ** is doing its third job — *you are welcome*.

**Θα πάρετε** is a future, which is stage 6 — recognise it, do not analyse it.

**The short version, if the full one deserts you:** point and say **Αυτό, παρακαλώ.** Then **Ευχαριστώ.** That works everywhere and it is not rude.

**Other everyday orders**, built the same way:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ένα νερό, παρακαλώ.** | A water, please. |
| **Μια μπύρα.** | A beer. |
| **Ένα τοστ.** | A toasted sandwich. |
| **Δύο σουβλάκια με πίτα.** | Two souvlaki in pita. |
| **Έναν φραπέ γλυκό με γάλα.** | A sweet frappé with milk. |
| **Τον λογαριασμό, παρακαλώ.** | The bill, please. |

**The social fact worth knowing.** Coffee in Greek life is an hour, not a drink — **πάμε για καφέ** is an invitation to sit down with someone, and it is how most friendships in a parish are actually conducted. Being able to accept it, and to order once you are there, is a more useful piece of Greek than any amount of grammar.

**Practice.** Read the exchange aloud, both parts, five times. Then order five different things out loud. Then say **Πάμε για καφέ;** — and be ready for a yes.
Shadowing, and how to do it:
The single most effective speaking exercise available without another person, and ten minutes of it a day is worth more than an hour of silent study.

**What it is.** You play a short piece of Greek audio and speak along with it, at the same time, matching the speed, the rhythm and the intonation as closely as you can. Not repeating after — speaking **with**.

**Why it works.** Three things improve at once: the mouth learns to make Greek sequences at Greek speed, the ear learns the rhythm, and the chunks of language go in as wholes rather than as assembled words. It is also the only exercise that makes you speak faster than your grammar can keep up with, which is the point.

**The method:**

1. **Pick ten to twenty seconds of audio** you understand completely. Understanding first, shadowing second.
2. **Listen twice** without speaking.
3. **Read the text while listening**, if you have it.
4. **Speak along, with the text**, several times.
5. **Speak along without the text.**
6. **Then speak it alone**, from memory, at the same speed.

**Ten minutes, on the same ten seconds, is correct.** The exercise is repetition of a tiny piece, not coverage.

**What to shadow at this stage:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pimsleur** | already built this way — answer out loud, do not skip the speaking prompts |
| **Language Transfer** | pause and say every answer aloud before the student on the recording does |
| **Super Easy Greek** | short, subtitled, and at a real speed |
| **The lesson examples here** | read aloud, then shadow the Forvo recording of the same word |
| **A Greek song** | genuinely useful, and the lyrics are on stixoi.info |

**What to listen for in your own voice:**

- **The stress on the right syllable** — the thing Greek marks and you are learning to hear.
- **Full vowels**, with no English mumble in the unstressed ones.
- **One tap on the ρ.**
- **The rhythm of the whole phrase** rather than the correctness of each word.

**The embarrassment is the exercise.** Shadowing feels ridiculous, especially the first week, and it is the reason most learners never do it — which is also why it works so well for the ones who do. Nobody is listening.

**Where it pays off.** The gap between knowing a phrase and being able to say it at speed is the gap that keeps people silent at church. Shadowing closes exactly that gap, and nothing else does.

**Practice.** Take ten seconds of Super Easy Greek, or one Pimsleur exchange. Do the six steps on it, for ten minutes. Then do the same ten seconds again tomorrow.
Writing, from the first week:
Three sentences a day, by hand, in Greek letters. It is a small habit and it does several things nothing else does.

**Why write at all**, when the goal is talking to people:

1. **It forces the endings.** Speaking lets you mumble past a case ending; writing does not.
2. **It makes the spelling a question.** Which *i*? Which *o*? That is the Spelling track's subject and writing is where it gets tested.
3. **It makes the grammar explicit.** A sentence you can write is a sentence you understand; one you can only say may be a memorised chunk.
4. **It is the slowest and most deliberate form of practice**, which is why it catches what the others miss.

**The habit: three sentences a day, by hand.** About yourself, about the day, about what you did and what you want. Not translations of English — sentences you compose in Greek with the grammar you have.

**Starting material**, from this stage alone:

- **Είμαι ο [name]. Είμαι από την Αγγλία. Μένω στο York.**
- **Σήμερα πάω στην εκκλησία.**
- **Έχω δύο παιδιά. Τα παιδιά μου είναι μικρά.**
- **Μου αρέσει ο ελληνικός καφές.**
- **Δεν ξέρω πολλά ελληνικά, αλλά μαθαίνω.**

**That last sentence is worth memorising** as a sentence: *I do not know much Greek, but I am learning.* It is the single most useful thing to be able to say for the next year, and people answer it warmly.

**Then correct yourself.** Write the three sentences, then go back over them asking three questions: is every noun's gender right, is every ending right, is every accent there. That self-check is most of the value.

**Where to get corrections.** The dictionary at greek-language.gr for the inflection tables; Lexiscope for any form you are unsure of; and the deck, which will tell you which spelling a word takes. There is no teacher in this curriculum, so checking is a habit rather than a service.

**Keep them.** A notebook or a file, dated. In three months the first page becomes the clearest evidence of progress you will have, and that matters more than it sounds in a long route.

**Typing counts for some of it**, since you set the keyboard up in stage 1 — but handwriting at least some of it is better, for the reason stage 1's handwriting lesson gave.

**Practice.** Write three sentences now, by hand, about today. Then check each one for gender, endings and accents. Then do the same tomorrow.
Reading: the school readers:
What to read at the end of stage 2, which is written for Greek six-year-olds and is therefore exactly right.

**ebooks.edu.gr is the whole resource** — every Greek state school textbook, free, in PDF and in a browser reader. The ones you want:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γλώσσα Α΄ Δημοτικού** | Language, first year of primary. Short sentences, present tense, enormous illustrations. |
| **Ανθολόγιο Α΄–Β΄ Δημοτικού** | the reader — stories, poems and rhymes for the first two years |
| **Γλώσσα Β΄ Δημοτικού** | the second year, which is the right target by the end of stage 3 |

**Why children's school material rather than a graded reader for foreigners.** It is free, there is a mountain of it, it is written by people whose job is teaching reading, and it is real Greek rather than constructed Greek. The vocabulary is a child's, which means it is concrete and high-frequency — exactly the words you want first.

**The one drawback**, and it is worth knowing: it assumes a child who already speaks Greek, so the grammar is not graded the way a textbook for foreigners would grade it. You will meet a past tense in week one. Read past it.

**How to read at this level:**

1. **Read aloud.** Always, at this stage. Reading Greek silently this early builds a reader and not a speaker.
2. **Do not look everything up.** One or two words a page, the ones that block the sentence.
3. **Reread.** The same page three times is better than three pages once.
4. **Stop when it stops being comprehensible**, and go back a level.

**The other free reading at this level:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The church notice board** | short, repetitive, weekly, and the vocabulary you most want |
| **Signs and labels**, from stage 1 | still working |
| **Children's books**, if anyone in the parish has any to lend | |
| **Greek Wikipedia's simple articles** | harder than they look; keep for stage 3 |
| **Song lyrics on stixoi.info** | with the song playing |

**What not to read yet:** newspapers, Greek Wikipedia proper, anything from the Church beyond the notice board. All of them are stage 8 and beyond, and attempting them now produces a page of dictionary lookups and no reading.

**The target for the end of stage 2** is a page of **Γλώσσα Α΄ Δημοτικού** read aloud, understood, without stopping more than once or twice.

**Practice.** Download **Γλώσσα Α΄ Δημοτικού** today. Read its first two pages aloud. Note how many words blocked you — then read the same pages again tomorrow and notice the number drop.
Review: stage 2:
The end of stage 2, which is the A1 level. What should be true, and what stage 3 does.

**What should now be true:**

- **είμαι** and **έχω**, all six persons, cold.
- The three genders, and the habit of learning every noun with its article.
- The definite article in all four nominative and accusative forms, said without thinking.
- **ένας / μία / ένα**, and **έναν** before a masculine object.
- Nominative against accusative: what each is for, and that prepositions take the accusative.
- The noun patterns: masculine **-ος, -ας, -ης**; feminine **-α, -η** and the **-ση** plurals in **-εις**; neuter **-ο, -ι, -μα**.
- Verbs in **-ω**, and the second class in **-άω/-ώ** and **-ώ/-είς**, with the stress telling you which.
- **δεν** for statements, **μην** for commands, and the double negative being correct.
- Questions by intonation alone, and the eight question words — with **πού/που** and **πώς/πως** distinguished by the accent.
- Adjectives agreeing in gender, number and case, and the adverb being the neuter plural.
- The strong pronouns, used only for emphasis.
- **αυτός** and **εκείνος**, with the article kept: **αυτό το παιδί**.
- **υπάρχει** and **υπάρχουν** for *there is*, and **έχει** in speech.
- The possessives after the noun, with the second accent where it is needed.
- The weak object pronouns before the verb and after a command.
- **μου αρέσει** against **μου αρέσουν**, and the family of verbs like it.
- **σε, από, για, με**, and **στον / στη / στο** merged.
- The place words, and giving simple directions.
- **εσύ** against **εσείς**, and **Πάτερ** for the priest.
- Numbers to a thousand, prices, and the shop sentences.
- The time, the days, the months, the seasons, and nine feast-day greetings.
- The parish vocabulary: the building, the people, the services, and what people say.
- Ordering a coffee, start to finish.
- Three habits running: shadowing, three written sentences a day, and reading the school readers aloud.

**What stage 2 deliberately did not do.** No genitive, no past tense, no future, no subjunctive, and no aspect. Every verb has been in the present, and that is why everything so far has been about now.

**What stage 3 does.** The cases, properly: the genitive — *of*, possession, and a great deal else — the vocative, the full declension of adjectives and pronouns, comparatives, and the **Forms track** opening with all of it as reference tables. By the end of it the noun system is complete and you can say what belongs to whom.

**And the Spelling track should already be running.** If it is not, start Spelling 1 now: it pairs with this stage, and the endings you have just learned are exactly what it drills.

**Practice.** Go down the list. Then hold a two-minute conversation with yourself out loud, using only stage 2 grammar: who you are, where you are from, what you have, what you like, where you are going on Sunday.
What the Spelling track is for:
**Spelling track, module 1 of 5. Run this module alongside stage 2**, at about one of these lessons for every three or four route lessons.

**The problem, stated once more.** Greek is read in one direction and spelled in the other. Given the letters you can always say the word; given the sound you cannot always write it, because five vowel sounds share about a dozen spellings and which one a word takes is a historical fact.

**What this track does about it.** Three things, in order of how much they pay:

1. **The endings.** Most of the *i*, *e* and *o* decisions in any Greek sentence are in word endings, and endings are decided by **grammar**, not by history. **-ει** is a verb, **-η** is a feminine noun, **-οι** is a masculine plural. That is a rule, it covers most of the problem, and it is this module.
2. **The patterns in stems.** Not rules, but strong tendencies and recognisable families — the **-ση** nouns, the **ευ-** words, the doubled consonants.
3. **The word-by-word remainder**, which is the deck's job.

**Why drill rather than read.** You asked for drills and the subject deserves them: spelling is recall, not understanding. Reading about **ει** against **η** teaches you nothing you cannot already see; writing fifty words from dictation and checking them teaches you exactly where your gaps are.

**The drill, and it is the same every time:**

1. **Read a list of words aloud.**
2. **Cover them.**
3. **Write them from memory, by hand, with their accents.**
4. **Check, and mark only the wrong ones.**
5. **Rewrite the wrong ones three times each.**
6. **Do the same list again tomorrow**, then in three days, then in a week.

**Ten minutes, and only the words you got wrong.** A list you can already spell is wasted time.

**Where the words come from:** the deck, which carries a spelling card for any word whose *i* or *o* is not predictable, and the three sentences a day from stage 2, which is where your own errors appear.

**What the track covers, module by module:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Spelling 1** | the *i*, *e* and *o* spellings, the endings, final **-ν**, the accent rules, diaeresis and syllables |
| **Spelling 2** | the noun and adjective endings in full, including the genitive, and the **-ση / -ξη / -ψη** family |
| **Spelling 3** | the verb endings in every tense, the augment, and the perfective stems' spellings |
| **Spelling 4** | doubled consonants, the **ευ-** and **αυ-** families, prefixes, and compounds |
| **Spelling 5** | abbreviations, numerals, punctuation in full, capitalisation, and handwriting at speed |

**Practice.** Take ten words you have already learned — from the deck — and do the six-step drill on them now. Note which ones you got wrong. Those are the only ones that matter.
The i sounds: ι η υ ει οι:
Five spellings, one sound, and the first thing to do is separate what is decided by grammar from what has to be memorised.

**The sound is *i* in all of these**: **ι, η, υ, ει, οι** — and **υι**, which is rare enough to ignore.

**Where grammar decides, and it is most of them:**

| Ending | Spelling | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| verb, 3rd person singular | **-ει** | γράφει, θέλει, μπορεί |
| verb, 2nd person singular | **-εις** | γράφεις, θέλεις |
| feminine noun, singular | **-η** | η πόλη, η αδελφή, η αγάπη |
| feminine adjective, singular | **-η** | καλή, μεγάλη, ωραία — and η |
| masculine noun, nominative plural | **-οι** | οι δάσκαλοι, οι φίλοι |
| **-ση / -ξη / -ψη** noun, plural | **-εις** | οι πόλεις, οι τάξεις, οι σκέψεις |
| neuter noun, singular | **-ι** | το παιδί, το σπίτι, το κερί |
| diminutive | **-άκι** | το παιδάκι, το καφεδάκι |

**Learn that table as rules and the endings stop being guesswork.** It is the highest-value page in this track.

**Where the stem has to be memorised**, with the commonest examples in each spelling:

- **ι**: είμαι, πίνω, ίδιος, ιστορία, φίλος, πολιτική, κίνηση
- **η**: ήλιος, μήνας, ημέρα, κήπος, ζωή, νίκη, ψυχή
- **υ**: μύτη, ύψος, γυναίκα, κύριος, φύλλο, θυμάμαι, σύμφωνα
- **ει**: είναι, εικόνα, ειρήνη, κλειδί, παιδεία, θείος
- **οι**: οικογένεια, οικία, ποιος, κοιτάζω, κοινός, ανοίγω

**Two patterns worth having**, because they cover a lot of words at once:

1. **Words with a clear English cousin usually keep the ancient spelling**, and the English spelling preserves it. **Ψυχή** → *psychology*, so **υ**. **Ιστορία** → *history*, so **ι**. **Ειρήνη** → *Irene*, so **ει**. **Οικονομία** → *economy*, so **οι**. This is a genuinely reliable trick for the educated vocabulary, which is a large slice of Greek.
2. **The -ια / -εια endings on abstract nouns**: **οικογένεια, παιδεία, αλήθεια, ιστορία**. The **-εια** ones usually come from an adjective; the **-ια** ones from a noun. A tendency rather than a rule, and worth noticing.

**The accent does not help with the spelling** — it says where the stress is and nothing about which *i*.

**Practice.** Drill the eight-row grammar table until you can say which spelling each ending takes without looking. Then do the six-step drill on these twenty words: **πόλη, παιδί, φίλοι, γράφει, γράφεις, πόλεις, γυναίκα, εικόνα, οικογένεια, ήλιος, μύτη, ψυχή, είναι, κλειδί, μήνας, σπίτι, ιστορία, ειρήνη, καφεδάκι, τάξεις**.
The e sounds: ε and αι:
Two spellings, one sound, and this one is much smaller than the *i* problem — because **ε** is the default and **αι** is a short list.

**ε is the normal spelling.** If you have no reason to think otherwise, write **ε**.

**Where αι appears, and it is mostly grammar again:**

| | |
