**Notice how short the irregular perfectives are**: **δω, πω, πάω, φάω, πιω, βρω, μπω, βγω**. They are monosyllables, and that is because they are the oldest verbs in the language, worn down by three thousand years of use — exactly as English's irregular verbs are its commonest ones.

**The monosyllables conjugate with the stress on the ending:**

- **δω, δεις, δει, δούμε, δείτε, δουν**
- **πω, πεις, πει, πούμε, πείτε, πουν**
- **φάω, φας, φάει, φάμε, φάτε, φάνε**

**How to learn them, and this is the method that works:** always say both halves. Never **βλέπω** alone — **βλέπω, να δω**. Never **λέω** — **λέω, να πω**. The deck stores every verb as a pair and the card asks for both.

**Ten minutes a day on this list for a fortnight** settles the first twenty, and they are the twenty that appear in every conversation you will have.

**Practice.** Say all twenty of the first list as pairs, aloud, five times: **βλέπω — να δω**, **λέω — να πω**, and so on. Then cover the perfective column and produce it. Then conjugate **δω** and **πω** in all six persons.
Why Greek has no infinitive:
Ancient Greek had one. The modern language lost it, and what replaced it is the construction you will use in every other sentence.

**There is no word for *to write*.** No form of the verb corresponds to English *to go*, *to eat*, *to be*. Where English uses an infinitive, Greek uses **να** plus a fully conjugated verb:

| English | Greek | Literally |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I want **to go** | **Θέλω να πάω** | I want that I go |
| I can **speak** Greek | **Μπορώ να μιλήσω ελληνικά** | I can that I speak |
| I must **leave** | **Πρέπει να φύγω** | it is necessary that I leave |
| It is easy **to learn** | **Είναι εύκολο να μάθεις** | it is easy that you learn |
| I like **reading** | **Μου αρέσει να διαβάζω** | it pleases me that I read |

**The second verb agrees with its own subject**, which is usually the same as the first verb's:

- **Θέλω να πάω** — I want to go. (I want, I go)
- **Θέλεις να πας;** — Do you want to go? (you want, you go)
- **Θέλω να πας.** — I want **you** to go. (I want, you go)

**That last one is the structural gift.** English needs *I want you to go* — an infinitive with a different subject, which is awkward and which many languages cannot do at all. Greek simply conjugates the second verb for whoever is doing it, and the whole class of English sentences like *I want him to come* becomes **Θέλω να έρθει**.

**And it means the aspect choice appears in every one of these sentences**, because **να** is followed by either stem:

- **Θέλω να διαβάζω** — I want to read, as an ongoing activity
- **Θέλω να διαβάσω** — I want to read this, once, now

**Where English uses an *-ing* form**, Greek again uses **να**:

- **Μου αρέσει να μαγειρεύω.** — I like cooking.
- **Σταμάτησε να μιλάει.** — He stopped talking.
- **Άρχισα να μαθαίνω ελληνικά.** — I started learning Greek.

**The old infinitive survives in two places**, both of which you will see:

1. **Inside the perfect tenses**, where **έχω γράψει** uses a frozen old infinitive form — stage 6.
2. **In fixed learned expressions**, mostly church and legal: **Δόξα τω Θεώ** is not one, but **το ειπείν**, **εν τω ποιείν** and similar appear in liturgical texts and in the older register.

**So: the next lesson is να itself**, which is the single most frequent word in Greek after the article and **και** — and every one of its uses needs the aspect decision.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **Θέλω να πάω · Μπορώ να μιλήσω · Πρέπει να φύγω · Μου αρέσει να διαβάζω · Θέλω να έρθεις**. Then say five sentences of your own with **θέλω να** and five with **πρέπει να**.
να, and what it does:
The most useful particle in Greek. It introduces a verb, it carries no meaning of its own, and it appears in roughly every third sentence.

**The uses, and they all look the same grammatically:**

**1. After a verb that needs a second verb** — the infinitive-replacement from the last lesson:

- **Θέλω να πάω** · **Μπορείς να μιλήσεις;** · **Ξέρω να κολυμπάω** (I know how to swim)

**2. As a command or a request, softened:**

- **Να προσέχεις!** — Take care! (habitually)
- **Να μου τηλεφωνήσεις.** — Call me.
- **Να πάμε;** — Shall we go?

**3. As a wish or a blessing**, which is where Greek is at its most idiomatic:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Να ζήσεις!** | Long life to you — at a birthday or wedding |
| **Να χαίρεσαι τα παιδιά σου.** | May you enjoy your children — said to parents |
| **Ο Θεός να σε έχει καλά.** | God keep you well |
| **Να με συγχωρείς.** | Forgive me |
| **Καλά να περάσεις!** | Have a good time |
| **Να 'σαι καλά!** | Bless you — the everyday thank-you-plus-blessing |

**Those are not a special grammar.** They are **να** plus a verb, used as a wish, and Greek uses them constantly — they are much of the warmth of the language and they are the register of the parish hall.

**4. For purpose, with για:**

- **Πάω στην εκκλησία για να προσευχηθώ.** — I go to church in order to pray.
- **Μαθαίνω ελληνικά για να μιλάω με τους φίλους μου.** — I am learning Greek in order to talk to my friends.

**5. In a subordinate clause after certain words**: **πριν να** (before), **χωρίς να** (without), **αντί να** (instead of), **μέχρι να** (until).

**The negative is μην**, not δεν:

- **Θέλω να μην πας.** — I want you not to go.
- **Να μην ξεχάσεις!** — Do not forget!
- **Πριν να φύγεις** — before you leave

**The aspect choice is in every one of these.** **Να** plus the imperfective is ongoing or repeated; **να** plus the perfective is a single complete act:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Να προσέχεις** | be careful — always, generally |
| **Να προσέξεις** | be careful — this once, now |
| **Θέλω να διαβάζω** | I want to read — as a habit |
| **Θέλω να διαβάσω** | I want to read it — once, through |

**Which is why να has waited until this stage**: it cannot be taught without aspect, and aspect cannot be practised without it.

**The weak pronouns go between να and the verb**: **να μου πεις**, **να το κάνεις**, **να μου το δώσεις**.

**Practice.** Say the six blessings aloud, five times each — they are the ones you will use at church. Then say: **Θέλω να πάω · Να μην ξεχάσεις · Πάω για να προσευχηθώ · Να μου τηλεφωνήσεις**. Then make five wishes for five different people, out loud.
The subjunctive with the imperfective:
**να** plus the present stem: the ongoing, repeated or general version. One form, and a clear meaning.

**The forms are the present tense with να in front:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **να γράφω** | that I write, to write (ongoing) |
| **να γράφεις** | |
| **να γράφει** | |
| **να γράφουμε** | |
| **να γράφετε** | |
| **να γράφουν** | |

**Nothing new to learn.** If you can conjugate the present, you can form this.

**What it means: the action as a process or a habit.**

- **Μου αρέσει να διαβάζω.** — I like reading. (an ongoing activity)
- **Θέλω να μαθαίνω κάτι κάθε μέρα.** — I want to learn something every day. (repeated)
- **Πρέπει να τρώμε λαχανικά.** — We should eat vegetables. (in general)
- **Μπορείς να μιλάς πιο αργά;** — Can you speak more slowly? (for the rest of this conversation)

**That last one is worth dwelling on**, because it is a sentence you already know. **Να μιλάς** rather than **να μιλήσεις** because you want the slow speech to continue — you are not asking for one slow sentence. If you said **Μπορείς να μιλήσεις πιο αργά;** it would mean *could you say that one thing again, slowly*. Both are correct and they ask for different things.

**The five situations that take the imperfective after να:**

1. **Habits and repetition** — **κάθε μέρα, πάντα, συνήθως, συχνά**
2. **General truths** — **Πρέπει να προσέχουμε.**
3. **Ongoing states** — **Θέλω να ζω στην Ελλάδα.**
4. **Continuous processes** — **Άρχισε να βρέχει.** (it began to rain, and continues)
5. **Verbs that imply continuation** — **συνεχίζω να**, **εξακολουθώ να**

**The adverbs are your signal.** If **κάθε μέρα, πάντα, συνήθως, συχνά, ποτέ, όλη την ώρα, συνέχεια** is in the sentence, the verb after **να** is almost certainly imperfective.

**With the negative μην:**

- **Να μην καπνίζεις.** — Do not smoke. (ever, as a rule)
- **Προσπαθώ να μην τρώω γλυκά.** — I try not to eat sweets.

**Where beginners go wrong**: using the imperfective because it is the form they know. If in doubt, ask whether the action is a single complete event — and if it is, the next lesson's form is the right one.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **Μου αρέσει να διαβάζω · Πρέπει να τρώμε καλά · Μπορείς να μιλάς πιο αργά; · Να μην καπνίζεις**. Then say five habits of yours with **θέλω να** or **πρέπει να** plus the imperfective, each with a time adverb.
The subjunctive with the perfective:
**να** plus the perfective stem: one complete action, seen as a whole. This is the form you will use most.

**The forms are the perfective stem with the present endings:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **να γράψω** | that I write, to write (once) |
| **να γράψεις** | |
| **να γράψει** | |
| **να γράψουμε** | |
| **να γράψετε** | |
| **να γράψουν** | |

**And with the irregular pairs**, which is where it gets real:

- **να δω, να δεις, να δει, να δούμε, να δείτε, να δουν** — to see
- **να πω, να πεις, να πει, να πούμε, να πείτε, να πουν** — to say
- **να πάω, να πας, να πάει, να πάμε, να πάτε, να πάνε** — to go
- **να φάω, να φας, να φάει, να φάμε, να φάτε, να φάνε** — to eat

**What it means: the action complete, once, as a single event.**

- **Θέλω να πάω στην Ελλάδα.** — I want to go to Greece. (one trip)
- **Πρέπει να φύγω.** — I must leave. (now, once)
- **Μπορώ να σε βοηθήσω;** — Can I help you? (with this thing)
- **Να μου τηλεφωνήσεις.** — Call me. (once, when you can)
- **Θέλω να δω τον πατέρα Γιώργο.** — I want to see Father George.

**This is the default.** Most of the time, when you want to do something, you want to do it once and finish — so most **να** clauses take the perfective, and a learner who always used the perfective would be right more often than one who always used the imperfective.

**The signals that call for it:**

1. **A single occasion** — now, tonight, tomorrow, once.
2. **A result or a completion** — **Θέλω να τελειώσω** (I want to finish).
3. **A specific object** — **να διαβάσω το βιβλίο** (to read *the* book, through).
4. **After verbs of trying, managing, deciding** — **προσπάθησα να βρω**, **κατάφερα να μάθω**, **αποφάσισα να πάω**.
5. **After πριν, μέχρι, όταν, αν** with a single event.

**The clearest contrasts, to say aloud:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Θέλω να μάθω ελληνικά.** | I want to learn Greek. (and get there) |
| **Θέλω να μαθαίνω ελληνικά.** | I want to be learning Greek. (as an ongoing part of life) |
| **Πρέπει να πάω στην εκκλησία.** | I must go to church. (this Sunday) |
| **Πρέπει να πηγαίνω στην εκκλησία.** | I ought to go to church. (regularly) |
| **Να μου πεις.** | Tell me. (this) |
| **Να μου λες.** | Keep telling me. (generally) |

**Those pairs are the whole lesson.** Say them aloud until the difference is audible rather than analysed, because that is how the choice eventually gets made at speaking speed.

**Practice.** Say the six contrast pairs aloud, five times. Then say these: **Θέλω να πάω στην Ελλάδα · Πρέπει να φύγω · Μπορώ να σε βοηθήσω; · Να μου τηλεφωνήσεις · Θέλω να δω τον πατέρα**. Then take five verbs from the pair list and make a **θέλω να** sentence with the perfective of each.
The aspect decision, in practice:
A working procedure for choosing a stem, and the honest account of how long it takes to become automatic.

**The question to ask, every time: is this one complete event, or is it ongoing?**

**Complete → perfective.** Ongoing, repeated or habitual → imperfective.

**The decision tree, for when the question is not obvious:**

1. **Is there a time adverb?** **κάθε μέρα, πάντα, συνήθως, συχνά, συνέχεια** → imperfective. **τώρα, αύριο, μια φορά, απόψε** → usually perfective.
2. **Is there a definite object?** *the* book, *this* letter → usually perfective. A general one — *books*, *letters* → usually imperfective.
3. **Does the sentence have an endpoint?** **μέχρι τις πέντε, ως το τέλος** → perfective.
4. **Is the verb about starting or continuing?** **αρχίζω να, συνεχίζω να** → imperfective, because what follows goes on.
5. **Is it a single request?** → perfective. **A standing instruction?** → imperfective.
6. **Still unsure?** Use the perfective. It is the commoner choice and the less marked one.

**The verbs that take one or the other almost always:**

| Almost always imperfective after it | Almost always perfective after it |
| --- | --- |
| **μου αρέσει να** | **θέλω να** (usually) |
| **ξέρω να** (know how to) | **πρέπει να** (usually) |
| **αρχίζω να** | **μπορώ να** (usually) |
| **συνεχίζω να** | **προσπαθώ να** |
| **μαθαίνω να** | **αποφασίζω να** |
| **συνηθίζω να** | **ξεχνάω να** |

**Those are tendencies, not rules** — every one of them can take the other stem with a different meaning. But they are reliable enough to lean on while the instinct builds.

**What the mistake sounds like.** Using the imperfective where a Greek would use the perfective makes you sound as though you are describing a habit when you meant an event: **Θέλω να τρώω** for *I want to eat* sounds like *I want to be an eater*. It is comprehensible and faintly odd. The reverse error — perfective where imperfective belongs — sounds abrupt. Neither is a disaster.

**How long it takes.** Months to be mostly right, years to be automatic. It is the one feature of Greek that keeps catching advanced learners, and it is also the feature that most marks out someone who has really learned the language.

**The drill that works**, and it is worth ten minutes a day through this stage: take a verb pair and make two sentences, one with each stem, and say what each means. **Γράφω: θα γράφω γράμματα κάθε βδομάδα / θα γράψω ένα γράμμα απόψε.** Twenty pairs is twenty minutes and it does more than any amount of reading about it.

**Practice.** Do the drill on ten pairs from the irregular list. Then take five sentences from your reading that have **να** in them and say why each stem was chosen. Then make the six-question decision tree into a habit by applying it out loud five times.
θέλω να, μπορώ να, πρέπει να:
The three verbs that take **να** most often, and the sentences they build. With these you can express want, ability and obligation about anything.

**θέλω να — I want to:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Θέλω να πάω.** | I want to go. |
| **Θέλεις να έρθεις;** | Do you want to come? |
| **Δεν θέλω να φύγω.** | I do not want to leave. |
| **Θέλω να μου πεις.** | I want you to tell me. |

**And the polite form, which is a conditional and worth having as a phrase now:**

- **Θα ήθελα να…** — I would like to… **Θα ήθελα έναν καφέ.** — I would like a coffee.

**μπορώ να — I can, I may:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μπορώ να σε βοηθήσω;** | Can I help you? |
| **Μπορείς να μιλάς πιο αργά;** | Can you speak more slowly? |
| **Δεν μπορώ να έρθω.** | I cannot come. |
| **Μπορεί να βρέξει.** | It may rain. (impersonal) |

**μπορεί να, impersonal, is how Greek says *maybe***: **Μπορεί να είναι εδώ** — he may be here. Extremely common, and it is **μπορεί** fixed in the third person.

**πρέπει να — I must, I should:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πρέπει να φύγω.** | I must go. |
| **Πρέπει να πας στον γιατρό.** | You must go to the doctor. |
| **Δεν πρέπει να το κάνεις.** | You must not do that. |
| **Τι πρέπει να κάνω;** | What should I do? |

**πρέπει never changes**, as stage 3 said: the person is in the second verb. **Πρέπει να πάω, πρέπει να πάμε, πρέπει να πάνε.**

**The others in the same family:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ξέρω να** | know how to — **Ξέρω να μαγειρεύω** |
| **μαθαίνω να** | learn to |
| **προσπαθώ να** | try to |
| **αποφασίζω να** | decide to |
| **αρχίζω να** | begin to |
| **σταματάω να** | stop doing |
| **ελπίζω να** | hope to |
| **φοβάμαι να** | be afraid to |
| **προτιμώ να** | prefer to |
| **αξίζει να** | it is worth — **Αξίζει να το δεις** |

**The word order with pronouns**: the pronoun goes after **να** and before the verb — **Θέλω να σου πω**, **Μπορείς να μου το δώσεις;**, **Πρέπει να το κάνω**.

**Negating: δεν on the first verb, μην on the second**, depending on what you are negating:

- **Δεν θέλω να πάω.** — I do not want to go.
- **Θέλω να μην πάω.** — I want not to go. (a different thing)

**Practice.** Say ten sentences with **θέλω να**, ten with **πρέπει να** and ten with **μπορώ να**, all about today and tomorrow — and choose the stem deliberately each time. Then say **Θα ήθελα** three times, and use it next time you order something.
The future with θα:
One particle, two futures. **θα** plus the perfective is the simple future and the one you will use most.

**The forms: θα plus the perfective stem.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **θα γράψω** | I will write |
| **θα γράψεις** | |
| **θα γράψει** | |
| **θα γράψουμε** | |
| **θα γράψετε** | |
| **θα γράψουν** | |

**With the irregular pairs:**

- **θα πάω** — I will go · **θα δω** — I will see · **θα πω** — I will say
- **θα φάω** — I will eat · **θα έρθω** — I will come · **θα πάρω** — I will take

**What it means: one complete action in the future.**

- **Θα πάω στην εκκλησία την Κυριακή.** — I will go to church on Sunday.
- **Θα σου τηλεφωνήσω αύριο.** — I will call you tomorrow.
- **Θα το κάνω.** — I will do it.
- **Δεν θα έρθω.** — I will not come.

**θα is not a verb.** It does not change, it has no forms, and it goes directly before the verb — after **δεν** and after any weak pronouns:

- **Δεν θα το κάνω.** — I will not do it.
- **Θα σου το δώσω.** — I will give it to you.
- **Δεν θα σου το πω.** — I will not tell you it.

**Where θα came from**, which makes it easier to remember: it is a worn-down **θέλω να** — *I want that*. Spanish and English do the same thing with *will*, which was once a verb of wanting.

**The present tense also does the near future**, as stage 2 said, and Greeks use it constantly:

- **Αύριο πάω στην Αθήνα.** — Tomorrow I am going to Athens.
- **Τι κάνεις το βράδυ;** — What are you doing tonight?

**So θα is not obligatory for the future** when a time word makes it clear — exactly as in English.

**θα with the imperfective is the other future**, and the next lesson.

**θα also builds the conditional** — **θα ήθελα** (I would like), **θα πήγαινα** (I would go) — by combining with the past tenses. That is stage 6, and **θα ήθελα** is worth using as a phrase from today.

**The future of είμαι and έχω**, which have no perfective stem, so they use the only stem they have:

- **θα είμαι, θα είσαι, θα είναι…** — I will be
- **θα έχω, θα έχεις, θα έχει…** — I will have

**Practice.** Say ten things you will do tomorrow, out loud, with **θα** plus a perfective. Then negate five of them. Then say: **Θα σου τηλεφωνήσω · Δεν θα το κάνω · Θα σου το δώσω · Θα είμαι εκεί**.
The continuous future:
**θα** plus the imperfective: what you will be doing, or will do repeatedly. Less common than the simple future and necessary for a whole class of sentences.

**The forms: θα plus the present.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **θα γράφω** | I will be writing, I will write (regularly) |
| **θα γράφεις** | |
| **θα γράφει** | |

**What it means**, in its three uses:

**1. An action in progress at a future moment:**

- **Αύριο στις δέκα θα δουλεύω.** — Tomorrow at ten I will be working.
- **Θα σε περιμένω στο καφενείο.** — I will be waiting for you at the café.

**2. A repeated or habitual future action:**

- **Θα πηγαίνω στην εκκλησία κάθε Κυριακή.** — I will go to church every Sunday.
- **Θα μαθαίνω ελληνικά όλη μου τη ζωή.** — I will be learning Greek all my life.

**3. A future state or a general intention:**

- **Θα είμαι εδώ.** — I will be here. (είμαι has only this stem)
- **Θα μένουμε στην Αθήνα.** — We will be living in Athens.

**The contrast, said aloud, is the lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Θα γράψω ένα γράμμα.** | I will write a letter. (and finish it) |
| **Θα γράφω γράμματα.** | I will write letters. (as a practice) |
| **Θα φάω.** | I will eat. (a meal, now) |
| **Θα τρώω.** | I will be eating. (when you arrive) |
| **Θα διαβάσω το βιβλίο.** | I will read the book. (through) |
| **Θα διαβάζω.** | I will be reading. (occupied in it) |

**The adverbs decide it, usually.** **κάθε μέρα, πάντα, συνέχεια, όλη την ώρα, συνήθως** pull the imperfective; **αύριο, απόψε, σε μια ώρα, μια φορά** pull the perfective — though *tomorrow* can take either, depending on whether you mean a single act or an all-day activity.

**Where English needs extra words**, Greek has the stem:

- *I will be working* → **θα δουλεύω**
- *I will keep writing* → **θα γράφω**
- *I will have written* → that is the future perfect, **θα έχω γράψει**, and it is stage 6

**One idiom worth having**: **θα δούμε** — *we will see*, said constantly, with the perfective. And **θα δεις** — *you'll see*.

**Practice.** Say the six contrast pairs aloud. Then say five sentences about what you will be doing tomorrow at a specific time, and five about what you will do regularly from now on. Then say **θα δούμε** and mean it.
The imperative: telling someone to do so:
Commands. Greek has a real imperative form, and it comes in both aspects — which means two commands for every verb.

**The perfective imperative: one action, now.** This is the everyday command.

| | Singular | Plural / polite |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **γράφω** | γράψε | γράψτε |
| **διαβάζω** | διάβασε | διαβάστε |
| **ανοίγω** | άνοιξε | ανοίξτε |
| **παίρνω** | πάρε | πάρτε |
| **δίνω** | δώσε | δώστε |
| **λέω** | πες | πείτε |
| **έρχομαι** | έλα | ελάτε |
| **πηγαίνω** | πήγαινε | πηγαίνετε |
| **τρώω** | φάε | φάτε |
| **βλέπω** | δες | δείτε |
| **μπορώ** | — | — |

**The pattern for regular verbs**: the perfective stem with **-ε** in the singular and **-τε** in the plural — **γράψε, γράψτε**. With the stress moving back in the singular: **διάβασε**, not *διαβάσε*.

**έλα and ελάτε are the two to have cold.** *Come!* — and they are used constantly, including as *come on*, *come now*, and as a general attention-getter.

**The imperfective imperative: keep doing it, or do it always.**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **γράφω** | γράφε | γράφετε |
| **διαβάζω** | διάβαζε | διαβάζετε |
| **προσέχω** | πρόσεχε | προσέχετε |

**It is less common** and it has a specific flavour: a standing instruction rather than a request.

- **Πρόσεχε!** — Be careful! (as a general warning, continuously)
- **Πρόσεξε!** — Watch out! (now, this)
- **Διάβαζε κάθε μέρα.** — Read every day.
- **Διάβασε αυτό.** — Read this.

**The weak pronouns come after the imperative**, as stage 2 said:

- **Πες μου!** — Tell me! · **Δώσε το!** — Give it! · **Πάρε τα!** — Take them!
- **Δώσε μου το!** — Give it to me! — indirect first, as always.

**And the stress may need a second accent**: **δώσε μού το** in careful writing, by the rule from the Spelling track.

**The polite imperative is the plural**, which is also the plural command — so **γράψτε** is both *write* (to several people) and *write, please* (to one person politely). Context decides, and with a stranger or the priest you use it.

**Softening a command.** Greek commands can sound blunt, and the usual softeners are:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **…, παρακαλώ** | please |
| **Μπορείς να…;** | Can you…? |
| **Να μου πεις.** | the να form, which is gentler than the imperative |
| **Έλα, πες μου.** | *come on, tell me* — the conversational opener |

**Practice.** Say the eleven perfective imperatives aloud, both numbers. Then say: **Πες μου! · Δώσε μου το! · Έλα εδώ! · Πρόσεχε! · Διάβασε αυτό.** Then give five commands politely with **μπορείς να** instead.
Negative commands, and ας:
How to tell someone **not** to do something, and how to say *let's*.

**The negative command is μην plus the subjunctive form** — not the imperative. The imperative has no negative in Greek.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μην πας!** | Do not go! (this once) |
| **Μην πηγαίνεις!** | Do not go! (as a rule) |
| **Μην το κάνεις!** | Do not do that! |
| **Μην ξεχάσεις!** | Do not forget! |
| **Μη μου το λες.** | Do not tell me that. |

**The aspect choice is live here too**, and it is clearer than almost anywhere:

- **Μην καπνίζεις** — do not smoke, ever, as a habit
- **Μην καπνίσεις** — do not smoke this cigarette, now

**So the signs say Μην καπνίζετε**, because it is a standing prohibition — and now you can see why that form was chosen.

**μη and μην** are the same word; **μην** before a vowel or κ, π, τ, μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ, ξ, ψ and **μη** elsewhere, by the final-ν rule.

**ας — let's, let me, let him:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ας πάμε.** | Let's go. |
| **Ας δούμε.** | Let's see. |
| **Ας το κάνω εγώ.** | Let me do it. |
| **Ας έρθει.** | Let him come. |
| **Ας μην πάμε.** | Let's not go. |

**να does the same job** and is commoner in speech for the first person plural:

- **Να πάμε;** — Shall we go?
- **Πάμε!** — Let's go! — the plain present, used as an invitation, and the most frequent version of all.

**πάμε is worth noting specially.** It is the present tense of **πάω** in the first person plural and it does duty as *let's go*, *shall we go*, *come on* and *off we go*. You will hear it ten times a day.

**Softening and strengthening:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μην ανησυχείς.** | Do not worry. |
| **Μη φοβάσαι.** | Do not be afraid. |
| **Μην πειράζει** — no: **Δεν πειράζει.** | Never mind. — note it is δεν here, because it is a statement |
| **Σε παρακαλώ, μην…** | Please do not… |

**That δεν πειράζει against μην is worth the pause.** **Δεν πειράζει** is a statement — *it does not matter* — so it takes **δεν**. **Μην πειράζεις τον σκύλο** is a command — *do not tease the dog* — so it takes **μην**. Same verb, two particles, and the difference is statement against command, exactly as stage 2's negation lesson said.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **Μην πας! · Μην το κάνεις! · Μην ξεχάσεις! · Μην ανησυχείς · Ας πάμε · Πάμε!** Then give five prohibitions with **μην** — one habitual, one single-occasion — and say which is which.
The past: Greek's two past tenses:
Greek has two simple past tenses, and the difference between them is aspect — the same distinction you have been making in the future and the subjunctive, now where English also marks it.

| | Built from | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The aorist** | the **perfective** stem | I did it, once, complete |
| **The imperfect** | the **imperfective** stem | I was doing it, I used to do it |

- **έγραψα** — I wrote (and finished)
- **έγραφα** — I was writing, I used to write

**The names are worth knowing** because every grammar uses them: **αόριστος** (aorist, meaning *unbounded* — a historical accident of naming) and **παρατατικός** (imperfect, meaning *extending*).

**English has the same distinction and only sometimes marks it.** *I wrote* and *I was writing* are both available; *I used to write* adds habituality. So this is the one place where your English instincts help rather than hinder.

**Both tenses use the same endings**, which is the good news:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **-α** | I |
| **-ες** | you |
| **-ε** | he / she / it |
| **-αμε** | we |
| **-ατε** | you (pl.) |
| **-αν** | they |

**So the only question is which stem** you attach them to — exactly as with **θα** and **να**.

**The pair, side by side:**

| | Aorist | Imperfect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | έγραψα | έγραφα |
| you | έγραψες | έγραφες |
| he/she/it | έγραψε | έγραφε |
| we | γράψαμε | γράφαμε |
| you (pl.) | γράψατε | γράφατε |
| they | έγραψαν | έγραφαν |

**Note the ε- at the front of four forms and not the other two.** That is the **augment**, and it is there to carry the stress — a stress rule rather than a meaning. It has its own lesson shortly.

**Which you will use more: the aorist, by a long way.** Most of what you say about the past is a sequence of completed events — *I went, I saw, I said* — and that is the aorist. The imperfect is for background, description and habit.

**The one-sentence summary to carry:** the aorist tells the story, the imperfect paints the scene.

**Practice.** Say both columns of the table aloud. Then say these pairs and give the English of each: **έγραψα / έγραφα · είδα / έβλεπα · πήγα / πήγαινα · έφαγα / έτρωγα**. Then say three things you did yesterday — all aorists.
The aorist: how it is formed:
The commonest past tense in the language, built from the perfective stem you already know.

**The recipe: perfective stem + the past endings.**

**γράφω → γράψ- → έγραψα:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **έγραψα** | I wrote |
| **έγραψες** | you wrote |
| **έγραψε** | he / she / it wrote |
| **γράψαμε** | we wrote |
| **γράψατε** | you wrote |
| **έγραψαν** | they wrote |

**More, by the three sound rules from the perfective-stem lesson:**

| Present | Perfective | Aorist |
| --- | --- | --- |
| διαβάζω | διαβάσ- | **διάβασα** |
| αγοράζω | αγοράσ- | **αγόρασα** |
| ανοίγω | ανοίξ- | **άνοιξα** |
| δουλεύω | δουλέψ- | **δούλεψα** |
| τρέχω | τρέξ- | **έτρεξα** |
| κλείνω | κλείσ- | **έκλεισα** |
| ακούω | ακούσ- | **άκουσα** |

**And the second conjugation, with -ησ-:**

| Present | Aorist |
| --- | --- |
| αγαπάω | **αγάπησα** |
| μιλάω | **μίλησα** |
| ρωτάω | **ρώτησα** |
| τηλεφωνώ | **τηλεφώνησα** |
| μπορώ | **μπόρεσα** |
| ευχαριστώ | **ευχαρίστησα** |

**The stress rule, which is the only tricky part**: the aorist is stressed on the **third syllable from the end** wherever the word is long enough — **διάβασα, αγόρασα, τηλεφώνησα** — and that is why short verbs need the augment to give them a third syllable.

**So:**

- **γράψα** would have only two syllables, so **έγραψα** — the **ε-** supplies the third.
- **γράψαμε** already has three, so no augment.

**Which is the whole explanation of why the augment comes and goes** inside one tense, and it is a stress rule rather than a grammatical one.

**The negative is δεν**, as always: **Δεν έγραψα. Δεν πήγα. Δεν το είδα.**

**The weak pronouns still go before the verb**: **Το έγραψα. Μου το είπε. Δεν τον είδα.**

**What it is used for:**

1. **A single completed action**: **Πήγα στην εκκλησία.**
2. **A sequence of them**: **Ήρθα, είδα, νίκησα.** — and that is Caesar in Greek, which is where the aorist shows what it is for.
3. **An action with a stated endpoint**: **Διάβασα το βιβλίο σε δύο μέρες.**
4. **Something that happened at a named time**: **Χθες πήγα στην αγορά.**

**Practice.** Give the aorist of these ten and say each in a sentence: **γράφω, διαβάζω, αγοράζω, ανοίγω, δουλεύω, κλείνω, μιλάω, ρωτάω, τηλεφωνώ, ακούω**. Then say five things you did yesterday, with the time word in front.
The augment, and where the stress goes:
A short lesson on the **ε-** at the front of some past forms, because knowing what it is for stops it being arbitrary.

**The rule: the past tense is stressed on the third syllable from the end** — and if the word has only two, an **ε-** is added to make a third.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **έγραψα** | 3 syllables, stress on the first — the augment supplies it |
| **γράψαμε** | already 3, no augment needed |
| **έγραψαν** | 3, with the augment |
| **διάβασα** | already 3 without help |
| **διαβάσαμε** | 4, stress third from end |

**So the augment appears in the four short forms** — I, you, he/she/it, they — and not in **we** and **you (pl.)**, which are a syllable longer.

**Why it exists at all.** In Ancient Greek the augment was a genuine marker of past time, on every past form. The modern language kept it only where the stress rule needs it, which is a tidy example of how Greek simplified: a grammatical marker became a phonological crutch.

**Where the augment is part of the word**, in a few verbs, and then it stays throughout:

- **έχω → είχα, είχες, είχε, είχαμε, είχατε, είχαν** — the stress is on **εί-** in all six
- **είμαι → ήμουν, ήσουν, ήταν, ήμασταν, ήσασταν, ήταν**
- **πηγαίνω → πήγα, πήγες, πήγε, πήγαμε, πήγατε, πήγαν**
- **λέω → είπα, είπες, είπε, είπαμε, είπατε, είπαν**
- **βλέπω → είδα, είδες, είδε, είδαμε, είδατε, είδαν**
- **βρίσκω → βρήκα, βρήκες, βρήκε, βρήκαμε, βρήκατε, βρήκαν**
- **τρώω → έφαγα, έφαγες, έφαγε, φάγαμε, φάγατε, έφαγαν**

**Those are the ones where the aorist looks nothing like the present**, and they are the next lesson.

**In compound verbs the augment goes inside**, after the prefix, in the formal register and before it in speech:

- **περιμένω → περίμενα** — the stress lands inside the word, no augment needed
- **καταλαβαίνω → κατάλαβα** — same
- **προσπαθώ → προσπάθησα** — same

**So compounds mostly need no augment at all**, because the prefix already gives them the syllables.

**One place the old augment survives as a real prefix**: the learned verbs in formal Greek, where you will see **εξετάσθηκε**, **εγκρίθηκε** and similar. That is register, and stage 9's subject.

**What to take from this lesson.** Not a rule to apply consciously — the augment comes out right if you put the stress third from the end and let the mouth add the vowel it needs. What matters is recognising **έ-**, **εί-** and **ή-** at the front of a verb as *this is a past tense*, which is one of the fastest reading cues in Greek.

**Practice.** Say these six aorists aloud and point to the stress in each: **έγραψα, γράψαμε, διάβασα, διαβάσαμε, κατάλαβα, τηλεφώνησα**. Then read a page of anything Greek and underline every verb beginning with **έ**, **εί** or **ή** — all of them are pasts.
The aorist of the irregular verbs:
The twenty aorists that are not derivable, and they belong to the twenty verbs you use most. This is a list to learn and there is no way round it.

| Present | Aorist | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **είμαι** | **ήμουν** | I was |
| **έχω** | **είχα** | I had |
| **λέω** | **είπα** | I said |
| **βλέπω** | **είδα** | I saw |
| **πηγαίνω / πάω** | **πήγα** | I went |
| **έρχομαι** | **ήρθα** | I came |
| **τρώω** | **έφαγα** | I ate |
| **πίνω** | **ήπια** | I drank |
| **δίνω** | **έδωσα** | I gave |
| **παίρνω** | **πήρα** | I took |
| **βρίσκω** | **βρήκα** | I found |
| **μπαίνω** | **μπήκα** | I went in |
| **βγαίνω** | **βγήκα** | I went out |
| **ανεβαίνω** | **ανέβηκα** | I went up |
| **κατεβαίνω** | **κατέβηκα** | I went down |
| **μένω** | **έμεινα** | I stayed |
| **φεύγω** | **έφυγα** | I left |
| **στέλνω** | **έστειλα** | I sent |
| **φέρνω** | **έφερα** | I brought |
| **μαθαίνω** | **έμαθα** | I learned |
| **καταλαβαίνω** | **κατάλαβα** | I understood |
| **θέλω** | **ήθελα** | I wanted — this is an imperfect doing aorist duty |

**θέλω is worth the footnote.** Its past is **ήθελα**, which is formally an imperfect, and it is used for both *I wanted* and *I was wanting*. There is a rare perfective **θέλησα** meaning *I decided to*. For everyday purposes **ήθελα** is the past of **θέλω**.

**The pattern inside the irregularity.** Most of these are built from the perfective stem you already learned, plus the augment:

- **δω → είδα** · **πω → είπα** · **πάω → πήγα** · **φάω → έφαγα** · **πιω → ήπια**
- **πάρω → πήρα** · **βρω → βρήκα** · **μπω → μπήκα** · **βγω → βγήκα**

**So if you know the pair, the aorist is nearly free** — which is the argument for learning verbs as pairs from the start, as the pairs lesson said.

**είχα and ήμουν are the exceptions to everything** and they are the two you will use most of all:

- **ήμουν, ήσουν, ήταν, ήμασταν, ήσασταν, ήταν**
- **είχα, είχες, είχε, είχαμε, είχατε, είχαν**

**They have their own lesson next**, because they are the backbone of any sentence about the past.

**How to drill this list.** Three columns — present, perfective, aorist — covered and rebuilt. Ten minutes a day for two weeks, then a weekly review. The deck carries each verb as a card with all three.

**Practice.** Say all twenty-two rows aloud as triples: **βλέπω — να δω — είδα**. Then cover the aorist column and produce it. Then say ten sentences about yesterday using ten different irregular aorists.
The imperfect:
The other past tense: the imperfective stem with the past endings. Used for description, background and habit.

**The recipe: imperfective stem + the past endings**, with the same augment rule.

**γράφω → έγραφα:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **έγραφα** | I was writing, I used to write |
| **έγραφες** | |
| **έγραφε** | |
| **γράφαμε** | |
| **γράφατε** | |
| **έγραφαν** | |

**The second conjugation takes -ούσα**, which is the thing to learn here:

| Present | Imperfect |
| --- | --- |
| αγαπάω | **αγαπούσα** |
| μιλάω | **μιλούσα** |
| ρωτάω | **ρωτούσα** |
| μπορώ | **μπορούσα** |
| τηλεφωνώ | **τηλεφωνούσα** |
| περπατάω | **περπατούσα** |

**And the stress is on the -ού-** throughout: **μιλούσα, μιλούσες, μιλούσε, μιλούσαμε, μιλούσατε, μιλούσαν**. No augment is needed because the word is long enough.

**μπορούσα is extremely useful**: *I could, I was able to*. **Δεν μπορούσα να έρθω** — I could not come.

**What the imperfect is for**, in its four uses:

**1. An action in progress in the past:**

- **Έγραφα όταν ήρθες.** — I was writing when you came.
- **Τι έκανες;** — What were you doing?

**2. A habit in the past:**

- **Πήγαινα στην εκκλησία κάθε Κυριακή.** — I used to go to church every Sunday.
- **Όταν ήμουν παιδί, έπαιζα ποδόσφαιρο.** — When I was a child I played football.

**3. Description and background:**

- **Έκανε ζέστη και ο ήλιος έλαμπε.** — It was hot and the sun was shining.
- **Ο παπάς ήταν μεγάλος και μιλούσε αργά.** — The priest was old and spoke slowly.

**4. Politeness and softening**, in a few verbs:

- **Ήθελα να σας ρωτήσω κάτι.** — I wanted to ask you something. (softer than θέλω)
- **Μπορούσατε να μου πείτε…** — Could you tell me…

**The one-sentence test**: if English would say *was ...-ing* or *used to*, Greek says the imperfect. If English would say the plain past, Greek usually says the aorist.

**With όταν — when — both are possible and they mean different things:**

- **Όταν έγραφα…** — while I was writing
- **Όταν έγραψα…** — once I had written

**Practice.** Give the imperfect of **γράφω, διαβάζω, μιλάω, μπορώ, πηγαίνω, είμαι**. Then say: *I was reading when you called · I used to live in London · it was raining · the priest was speaking slowly*. Then say three things you used to do as a child.
Aorist or imperfect:
The choosing lesson. One pair of tenses, one decision, and English mostly makes the same one — which is why this is easier than the future and the subjunctive.

**The rule: aorist for events, imperfect for background.**

**A story is a line of aorists with imperfect scenery around them:**

> **Χθες πήγα** στην εκκλησία. **Έκανε** κρύο και **έβρεχε**. Ο παπάς **μιλούσε** για την Κυριακή της Ορθοδοξίας. Μετά τη Λειτουργία **πήρα** αντίδωρο, **μίλησα** με τον Γιώργο και **πήγαμε** για καφέ. **Ήταν** πολύ ωραία.

**The aorists — πήγα, πήρα, μίλησα, πήγαμε — are what happened.** The imperfects — **έκανε, έβρεχε, μιλούσε, ήταν** — are what things were like. That paragraph is the whole lesson and it is worth reading aloud twice.

**The tests, when it is not obvious:**

| Use the imperfect if… | Use the aorist if… |
| --- | --- |
| English says *was ...-ing* | English says the plain past |
| English says *used to* | the action happened once |
| it is description or weather | it is an event in a sequence |
| it was going on when something else happened | it is the thing that happened |
| the sentence has **κάθε μέρα, συνήθως, πάντα, συνέχεια** | the sentence has **χθες, μια φορά, ξαφνικά, μετά** |

**The classic sentence shape**, with both:

- **Διάβαζα όταν χτύπησε το τηλέφωνο.** — I was reading when the phone rang.

**The imperfect is the frame, the aorist is the interruption.** That shape is in every story anyone tells.

**Two verbs where the choice changes the meaning noticeably:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ήξερα** | I knew (a state) — **έμαθα** is *I found out* |
| **είχα** | I had — **πήρα** is *I got* |
| **ήθελα** | I wanted — **θέλησα** is *I decided to* |
| **μπορούσα** | I was able — **μπόρεσα** is *I managed to* |

**That last pair is worth saying aloud**: **Δεν μπορούσα να έρθω** (I was not able to come — a state) against **Δεν μπόρεσα να έρθω** (I did not manage to come — an occasion). Both are good Greek and they say different things.

**Where English has no distinction and Greek does**: *I lived in London for ten years* — **έμενα** if you are describing that period of life, **έμεινα** if you are counting it off as a completed block. Both are heard.

**Practice.** Read the story paragraph aloud twice, then tell the same story about your own last Sunday, out loud, with at least three aorists and two imperfects. Then say five sentences of the shape *I was ...-ing when ...*.
ήμουν and είχα:
The past of **είμαι** and **έχω** — the two most useful past forms in the language, and both irregular.

**είμαι in the past:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ήμουν** | I was |
| **ήσουν** | you were |
| **ήταν** | he / she / it was |
| **ήμασταν** | we were |
| **ήσασταν** | you were |
| **ήταν** | they were |

**ήταν is both singular and plural**, exactly as **είναι** is in the present.

**You will also hear ήμουνα, ήσουνα, ήτανε** — colloquial longer forms, entirely standard in speech.

**έχω in the past:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **είχα** | I had |
| **είχες** | you had |
| **είχε** | he / she / it had |
| **είχαμε** | we had |
| **είχατε** | you had |
| **είχαν** | they had |

**Both are imperfects by form** — they describe a state rather than an event — and neither has a separate aorist in ordinary use. So there is no choice to make: the past of *be* is **ήμουν** and the past of *have* is **είχα**, and that is all.

**The sentences you will build with them:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ήμουν στην εκκλησία.** | I was at church. |
| **Ήταν πολύ ωραία.** | It was very nice. |
| **Όταν ήμουν παιδί…** | When I was a child… |
| **Δεν ήμουν εδώ.** | I was not here. |
| **Είχα δουλειά.** | I had work on. |
| **Δεν είχα χρόνο.** | I did not have time. |
| **Είχε πολύ κόσμο.** | There were a lot of people. (impersonal έχει in the past) |
| **Πόσων χρονών ήσουν;** | How old were you? |

**Όταν ήμουν παιδί is the opening of every reminiscence**, and it takes the imperfect after it for the same reason — habits and description.

**είχα also builds the pluperfect** — **είχα γράψει**, *I had written* — which is stage 6. For now it is simply *I had*.

**The impersonal uses carry over**: **ήταν κρύο** (it was cold), **έκανε ζέστη** (it was hot), **είχε βροχή** (there was rain), **υπήρχε** (there was — the past of υπάρχει).

**υπήρχε and υπήρχαν** complete the set: **Δεν υπήρχε πρόβλημα** — there was no problem.

**Practice.** Say both tables aloud, five times. Then say: **Ήμουν στην εκκλησία · Ήταν πολύ ωραία · Δεν είχα χρόνο · Όταν ήμουν παιδί έπαιζα ποδόσφαιρο · Είχε πολύ κόσμο**. Then describe last Sunday in five sentences, using **ήμουν**, **ήταν** and **είχα** at least once each.
The mediopassive: what it is:
A second set of endings, a second voice, and a group of verbs that only exist in it. This is the last structural piece of the Greek verb.

**Greek has two voices**: the **active**, which you have been using, and the **mediopassive**, which covers what English splits into passive, reflexive and middle.

**The three jobs it does:**

**1. Passive** — the subject has the action done to it:

- **Το γράμμα γράφτηκε.** — The letter was written.
- **Το σπίτι χτίστηκε το 1950.** — The house was built in 1950.

**2. Reflexive** — the subject does it to itself:

- **Πλένομαι.** — I wash (myself).
- **Ετοιμάζομαι.** — I am getting ready.
- **Ντύνομαι.** — I get dressed.

**3. Middle, which has no English equivalent** — the subject is involved in the action rather than performing it on something else:

- **Χαίρομαι.** — I am glad.
- **Θυμάμαι.** — I remember.
- **Φαίνεται.** — It seems.
- **Κάθομαι.** — I sit.

**And a large group of verbs are mediopassive and nothing else.** They have no active form at all, and their meaning is not passive in the least:

- **έρχομαι** — I come · **κάθομαι** — I sit · **γίνομαι** — I become
- **θυμάμαι** — I remember · **κοιμάμαι** — I sleep · **φοβάμαι** — I am afraid
- **σκέφτομαι** — I think · **χαίρομαι** — I am glad · **λυπάμαι** — I am sorry
- **βρίσκομαι** — I am located · **αισθάνομαι** — I feel · **εργάζομαι** — I work

**You have been using έρχομαι since stage 2** without knowing what shape it was. That is the point at which this lesson becomes necessary.

**The ending pattern is the giveaway**: a verb whose *I* form ends in **-μαι** is mediopassive. **έρχομαι, κάθομαι, θυμάμαι, φαίνομαι** — and, as the Spelling track noted, it is **-μαι** with **αι** and never **-με**.

**Why it matters for understanding rather than just speaking.** Formal and written Greek uses the passive constantly — notices, instructions, news — and recognising it is what makes those readable:

- **Απαγορεύεται** — it is forbidden
- **Ενοικιάζεται** — for rent (*it is being rented*)
- **Πωλείται** — for sale
- **Παρακαλείσθε** — you are requested

**Those four are on signs everywhere in Greece**, and all four are mediopassive.

**And in the Liturgy it is everywhere**, in the older forms of the same endings — **εὐλογημένος**, **ἀγαπῶμεν**, **πληρωθήτω**. That is the later curriculum's work, and the shape is recognisably this one.

**Practice.** Say these aloud and say which of the three jobs each is doing: **Το σπίτι χτίστηκε · Ετοιμάζομαι · Χαίρομαι · Έρχομαι · Απαγορεύεται · Φαίνεται**. Then list five **-μαι** verbs you already use.
The mediopassive present:
The forms, which are a second set of endings to learn — and the ten verbs you will use them with every day.

**The endings:**

| | Class A | Class B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | **-ομαι** | **-άμαι / -ούμαι** |
| you | **-εσαι** | **-άσαι / -είσαι** |
| he/she/it | **-εται** | **-άται / -είται** |
| we | **-όμαστε** | **-όμαστε / -ούμαστε** |
| you (pl.) | **-εστε / -όσαστε** | **-άστε / -είστε** |
| they | **-ονται** | **-ούνται** |

**έρχομαι — I come**, the one to know cold:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **έρχομαι** | I come |
| **έρχεσαι** | you come |
| **έρχεται** | he / she / it comes |
| **ερχόμαστε** | we come |
| **έρχεστε** | you come |
| **έρχονται** | they come |

**θυμάμαι — I remember**, which is the B pattern and irregular:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **θυμάμαι** | **θυμόμαστε** |
| **θυμάσαι** | **θυμάστε** |
| **θυμάται** | **θυμούνται** |

**κοιμάμαι** and **φοβάμαι** follow **θυμάμαι** exactly.

**The ten to have:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **έρχομαι** | I come | **κάθομαι** | I sit |
| **γίνομαι** | I become | **θυμάμαι** | I remember |
| **κοιμάμαι** | I sleep | **φοβάμαι** | I am afraid |
| **χαίρομαι** | I am glad | **λυπάμαι** | I am sorry |
| **σκέφτομαι** | I think | **φαίνομαι** | I seem |

**The sentences they make, which you will use constantly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Έρχομαι!** | I'm coming! |
| **Από πού έρχεσαι;** | Where are you coming from? |
| **Κάθισε / Καθίστε, παρακαλώ.** | Sit down, please. |
| **Δεν θυμάμαι.** | I do not remember. |
| **Θυμάσαι;** | Do you remember? |
| **Χαίρομαι πολύ.** | I am very glad. — and **Χάρηκα** for *pleased to meet you* |
| **Λυπάμαι πολύ.** | I am very sorry. |
| **Φοβάμαι ότι…** | I am afraid that… |
| **Μου φαίνεται ότι…** | It seems to me that… |
| **Τι γίνεται;** | What's going on? / How are things? |

**Τι γίνεται; is the everyday greeting** among friends, alongside **τι κάνεις** — and **γίνεται** is this conjugation.

**The perfective and past of these verbs** are stage 6's work, with one exception worth having now: **ήρθα** — *I came* — which you have already met in the irregular aorist list.

**Practice.** Say the **έρχομαι** and **θυμάμαι** tables aloud, five times. Then say the ten sentences. Then conjugate **κάθομαι** and **χαίρομαι** out loud, all six persons.
έρχομαι, πάω, λέω, τρώω:
Four verbs that break every pattern and appear in every conversation. Learn them as whole paradigms rather than as rules.

**πάω / πηγαίνω — I go.** Two presents, one meaning:

| | **πάω** | **πηγαίνω** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | πάω | πηγαίνω |
| you | πας | πηγαίνεις |
| he/she/it | πάει | πηγαίνει |
| we | πάμε | πηγαίνουμε |
| you (pl.) | πάτε | πηγαίνετε |
| they | πάνε | πηγαίνουν |

**πάω is the everyday one**; **πηγαίνω** is slightly fuller and is the one used for habitual going. **Perfective: να πάω. Aorist: πήγα. Imperative: πήγαινε / πηγαίνετε.**

**πάμε is *let's go*** and the single most used form of the verb.

**λέω — I say:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **λέω, λες, λέει, λέμε, λέτε, λένε** | |

**Perfective: να πω. Aorist: είπα. Imperative: πες / πείτε.**

- **Πώς το λένε;** — What is it called? (*how do they say it*)
- **Τι λες;** — What do you say? / What do you think?
- **Λέγεται ότι…** — It is said that… (mediopassive)
- **Πες μου.** — Tell me.

**τρώω — I eat:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **τρώω, τρως, τρώει, τρώμε, τρώτε, τρώνε** | |

**Perfective: να φάω. Aorist: έφαγα. Imperative: φάε / φάτε.**

**έρχομαι — I come**, from the last lesson, with its other forms:

**Perfective: να έρθω. Aorist: ήρθα. Imperative: έλα / ελάτε.**

**έλα is irregular and indispensable** — *come!*, *come on*, *oh come now* — and it is the imperative of a verb whose other forms look nothing like it.

**Two more that behave the same way:**

**πίνω — I drink**: πίνω, πίνεις… **Perfective να πιω. Aorist ήπια.**

**δίνω — I give**: δίνω, δίνεις… **Perfective να δώσω. Aorist έδωσα. Imperative δώσε / δώστε.**

**The pattern across all of them**: a regular-looking present, a short irregular perfective, an aorist built on the perfective with an augment, and an imperative that may be its own shape. Four forms per verb, and the deck stores all four.

**Why these four and not others.** Because *go, say, eat, come* are the verbs of ordinary life, and because all four are irregular in every language that has them. Spending a week on these four is worth more than a month on regular verbs.

**Practice.** Say all four paradigms aloud. Then say, for each: the present *I*, the **να** form, the aorist *I*, and the imperative. Then use each one in a sentence about today and one about yesterday.
Compound verbs and the prefixes:
Greek builds verbs by prefixing, and the prefixes are a small set with consistent meanings. Learning them multiplies your vocabulary without new memorisation.

**The commonest prefixes:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ξανα-** | again | **ξαναλέω** — I say again |
| **περι-** | around | **περιμένω** — I wait |
| **προ-** | before, forward | **προχωρώ** — I advance |
| **ανα- / ανε-** | up, again | **ανεβαίνω** — I go up |
| **κατα- / κατε-** | down, thoroughly | **κατεβαίνω** — I go down |
| **εισ-** | into | **εισάγω** — I import |
| **εξ- / εκ-** | out | **εξάγω** — I export |
| **συν- / συμ-** | with, together | **συμφωνώ** — I agree |
| **παρα-** | beside, too much | **παραγγέλνω** — I order |
| **δια-** | through | **διαβάζω** — I read |
| **επι-** | on, upon | **επιστρέφω** — I return |
| **υπο-** | under | **υπογράφω** — I sign (*write under*) |
| **αντι-** | against, instead | **αντιγράφω** — I copy |
| **μετα-** | change, after | **μεταφράζω** — I translate |
| **προσ-** | towards | **προσέχω** — I pay attention |
| **απο-** | away, off | **αποφασίζω** — I decide |

**ξανα- is the one you will use most actively**, because it is alive and productive: you can put it on almost any verb and be understood.

- **ξαναλέω** — say again · **ξαναπάω** — go again · **ξαναδιαβάζω** — reread · **ξαναγράφω** — rewrite
- **Ξαναπές το.** — Say it again.

**The others are mostly fossilised** — **διαβάζω** does not feel like *read through* to a Greek any more than *understand* feels like *stand under* to you. But recognising them helps in two ways: it makes long words parsable, and it connects Greek to the English words built from the same pieces — *diagram, synthesis, analysis, metaphor, hypothesis, epilogue*.

**How a compound behaves grammatically:**

1. **The stress and the augment go inside the word**: **περιμένω → περίμενα**, **καταλαβαίνω → κατάλαβα**.
2. **The perfective follows the simple verb's pattern**: **γράφω/γράψω**, so **υπογράφω/υπογράψω**, **αντιγράφω/αντιγράψω**.
3. **The weak pronouns still go in front of the whole thing**: **Το υπέγραψα.**

**That second point is a genuine multiplier.** Knowing **γράφω/γράψω/έγραψα** gives you **υπογράφω, αντιγράφω, περιγράφω, εγγράφω** and their full paradigms for free.

**Church vocabulary is dense with these**, and now readable: **προσεύχομαι** (I pray — *towards-wish*), **μεταλαμβάνω** (I receive communion — *take-with*), **εξομολογούμαι** (I confess — *out-speak-together*), **αναγιγνώσκω** (I read, liturgically).

**Practice.** Say five verbs with **ξανα-** out loud. Then take **γράφω** and name four compounds of it with their meanings. Then find three long Greek words in your reading, split them into prefix and stem, and say what each prefix contributes.
Verbs of motion:
Where you are going, where you are coming from, and the handful of verbs that carry all of it — with the prepositions they need.

**The core set:**

| | | Perfective | Aorist |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **πάω / πηγαίνω** | go | να πάω | πήγα |
| **έρχομαι** | come | να έρθω | ήρθα |
| **φεύγω** | leave, go away | να φύγω | έφυγα |
| **μπαίνω** | go in, enter | να μπω | μπήκα |
| **βγαίνω** | go out, come out | να βγω | βγήκα |
| **ανεβαίνω** | go up | να ανεβώ | ανέβηκα |
| **κατεβαίνω** | go down | να κατεβώ | κατέβηκα |
| **περνάω** | pass, drop by | να περάσω | πέρασα |
| **γυρίζω / επιστρέφω** | return | να γυρίσω | γύρισα |
| **φτάνω** | arrive | να φτάσω | έφτασα |
| **τρέχω** | run | να τρέξω | έτρεξα |
| **περπατάω** | walk | να περπατήσω | περπάτησα |
| **οδηγώ** | drive | να οδηγήσω | οδήγησα |
| **ταξιδεύω** | travel | να ταξιδέψω | ταξίδεψα |

**The prepositions they take:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **πάω σε** | go to — **πάω στην εκκλησία** |
| **έρχομαι από** | come from — **έρχομαι από τη δουλειά** |
| **φεύγω από** | leave from — **φεύγω από το σπίτι** |
| **μπαίνω σε** | go into — **μπαίνω στο σπίτι** |
| **βγαίνω από** | go out of — **βγαίνω από το σπίτι** |
| **περνάω από** | drop by, pass by — **πέρασε από το σπίτι** |
| **φτάνω σε** | arrive at — **φτάνω στην Αθήνα** |

**περνάω από is worth noticing**, because it is how Greeks say *drop in*: **Πέρασε από το σπίτι το βράδυ** — come round this evening. It is an invitation and it is said constantly.

**The transport words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **με το αυτοκίνητο** | by car |
| **με το λεωφορείο** | by bus |
| **με το τρένο** | by train |
| **με το αεροπλάνο** | by plane |
| **με το πλοίο** | by boat |
| **με τα πόδια** | on foot |
| **με το ποδήλατο** | by bicycle |

**με plus the accusative**, as always, and **με τα πόδια** is literally *with the feet*.

**The questions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πού πας;** | Where are you going? |
| **Από πού έρχεσαι;** | Where are you coming from? |
| **Πότε φεύγεις;** | When are you leaving? |
| **Πώς πας στη δουλειά;** | How do you get to work? |
| **Πόση ώρα κάνει;** | How long does it take? |
| **Πόσο μακριά είναι;** | How far is it? |

**And the answers you will need about Greece**: **Θα πάω στην Ελλάδα τον Αύγουστο. Θα μείνω δύο βδομάδες. Θα πάμε με το αεροπλάνο.**

**Practice.** Say the fourteen verbs with their perfectives and aorists. Then answer the six questions about your own day, out loud. Then say how you get to church, how long it takes, and when you leave.
Time words for the past:
The adverbs and phrases that place something in the past — and which of the two past tenses each one pulls.

**Pointing at a single past moment — aorist:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **χθες** | yesterday |
| **προχθές** | the day before yesterday |
| **την περασμένη βδομάδα** | last week |
| **τον περασμένο μήνα** | last month |
| **πέρυσι** | last year |
| **πριν από δύο μέρες** | two days ago |
| **μια φορά** | once |
| **ξαφνικά** | suddenly |
| **μετά** | then, afterwards |
| **τελικά** | in the end |
| **αμέσως** | immediately |
| **μόλις** | just now, as soon as |

**Describing a stretch of past time — imperfect:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **παλιά** | in the old days |
| **τότε** | then, at that time |
| **κάθε μέρα** | every day |
| **συνήθως** | usually |
| **πάντα** | always |
| **συνέχεια** | continuously |
| **όταν ήμουν παιδί** | when I was a child |
| **εκείνη την εποχή** | at that time |

**The two sequencing words to have cold:**

- **πρώτα** — first · **μετά** — then · **στο τέλος** — at the end
- **Πρώτα πήγα στην εκκλησία, μετά πήγα για καφέ, και στο τέλος γύρισα σπίτι.**

**That sentence is a narrative** and it is the shape of everything you will tell anyone about your week.

**πριν and μετά as prepositions and as conjunctions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **πριν από τη Λειτουργία** | before the Liturgy |
| **μετά τη Λειτουργία** | after the Liturgy |
| **πριν να φύγω** / **πριν φύγω** | before I left |
| **αφού έφυγα** | after I left |

**Note πριν takes να or nothing, and the verb after it is usually perfective.** **Αφού** is *after* with a clause.

**μόλις is useful twice over**: *just* (**Μόλις ήρθα** — I have just arrived) and *as soon as* (**Μόλις φτάσω, θα σου τηλεφωνήσω** — as soon as I arrive I will call you).

**ακόμα and πια, which are a pair:**

- **Δεν ήρθε ακόμα.** — He has not come yet.
- **Δεν μένει πια εδώ.** — He does not live here any more.

**And the two that mark how long ago:**

- **πριν από λίγο** — a little while ago
- **πριν από πολύ καιρό** — a long time ago

**Practice.** Say the twelve aorist words and the eight imperfect ones aloud. Then tell yesterday as a sequence with **πρώτα, μετά, στο τέλος**. Then say five sentences with **πριν** and **μετά**, out loud, and check the stem you used after each.
Asking about the past:
The questions that get a conversation going about what someone did — and the answers you will be giving.

**The question forms**, all of them the aorist with a question word:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι έκανες;** | What did you do? |
| **Πού πήγες;** | Where did you go? |
| **Πότε ήρθες;** | When did you come? |
| **Με ποιον πήγες;** | Who did you go with? |
| **Γιατί δεν ήρθες;** | Why did you not come? |
| **Πώς πέρασες;** | How was it? (*how did you pass*) |
| **Τι είπε;** | What did he say? |
| **Τι έγινε;** | What happened? |

**Πώς πέρασες; is the standard question after any event** — a trip, a weekend, a feast — and the answer is **Πέρασα πολύ ωραία** (I had a lovely time) or **Πέρασα καλά**.

**Τι έγινε; is the standard question about anything at all** that you have missed: *what happened*. And **Τι γίνεται;** in the present is *what's going on*.

**The answers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πήγα στην εκκλησία.** | I went to church. |
| **Δεν έκανα τίποτα.** | I did not do anything. |
| **Ήμουν στη δουλειά.** | I was at work. |
| **Πέρασα πολύ ωραία.** | I had a very nice time. |
| **Ήταν πολύ ωραία.** | It was lovely. |
| **Δεν μπόρεσα να έρθω.** | I was not able to come. |
| **Είχα δουλειά.** | I had things on. |
| **Ξέχασα!** | I forgot! |

**Δεν μπόρεσα να έρθω** is worth having exactly — it is the polite excuse, and the aorist **μπόρεσα** rather than **μπορούσα** makes it about that one occasion.

**The follow-up questions**, which is how a conversation continues rather than stopping:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Αλήθεια;** | Really? |
| **Και μετά;** | And then? |
| **Τι έκανες μετά;** | What did you do afterwards? |
| **Πόση ώρα έμεινες;** | How long did you stay? |
| **Ποιος ήταν εκεί;** | Who was there? |
| **Σου άρεσε;** | Did you like it? |
| **Τι ωραία!** | How lovely! |
| **Κρίμα.** | What a shame. |

**Those eight are worth more than any amount of vocabulary**, because they keep a conversation alive while you think. A learner who can say **Αλήθεια; Και μετά;** will be talked to for an hour; one who can only answer questions will be asked three and left alone.

**At church, specifically**, the questions you will be asked after the Liturgy:

- **Σου άρεσε;** — Did you like it? · **Κατάλαβες;** — Did you understand?
- **Ήταν ωραία η Λειτουργία.** — The Liturgy was lovely.
- **Κατάλαβα λίγο.** — I understood a little.
- **Ο ψάλτης ήταν πολύ καλός.** — The chanter was very good.

**Practice.** Say the eight questions and the eight answers aloud. Then have both halves of a conversation about your last Sunday, out loud, using at least four follow-up questions. Then prepare your answer to **Πώς πέρασες;** for this coming week.
The past of the mediopassive verbs:
The mediopassive in the past, which you need as soon as you tell a story — because *I came*, *I sat*, *I remembered* and *I was glad* are all in this voice.

**The aorist: a -θ- appears.** Most mediopassive verbs form their aorist with **-θηκ-** and the ordinary past endings:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **θυμήθηκα** | I remembered |
| **κοιμήθηκα** | I slept |
| **φοβήθηκα** | I was afraid |
| **σκέφτηκα** | I thought |
| **λυπήθηκα** | I was sorry |
| **χάρηκα** | I was glad |
| **ετοιμάστηκα** | I got ready |
| **σηκώθηκα** | I got up |
| **βρέθηκα** | I found myself, I was found |
| **γράφτηκε** | it was written |

**The full set of endings:** **-θηκα, -θηκες, -θηκε, -θήκαμε, -θήκατε, -θηκαν**.

- **θυμήθηκα, θυμήθηκες, θυμήθηκε, θυμηθήκαμε, θυμηθήκατε, θυμήθηκαν**

**The irregular ones, which are the common ones:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **έρχομαι → ήρθα** | I came |
| **γίνομαι → έγινα** | I became, it happened |
| **κάθομαι → κάθισα** | I sat |
| **χαίρομαι → χάρηκα** | I was glad |
| **φαίνομαι → φάνηκα** | I seemed |

**έγινα is the one you will hear most**, in the impersonal: **Τι έγινε;** — what happened. And **Έγινε!** on its own means *done*, *consider it done* — the single most useful one-word reply in Greek.

**Χάρηκα** you already know as *pleased to meet you*, and now you can see what it is: the aorist of *I am glad* — *I was glad*, said at the moment of meeting.

**The imperfect: -όμουν.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ερχόμουν** | I was coming, I used to come |
| **καθόμουν** | I was sitting |
| **θυμόμουν** | I remembered, I used to remember |
| **φοβόμουν** | I was afraid |

**The endings: -όμουν, -όσουν, -όταν, -όμασταν, -όσασταν, -ονταν.**

- **ερχόμουν, ερχόσουν, ερχόταν, ερχόμασταν, ερχόσασταν, έρχονταν**

**The aspect choice works exactly as in the active:**

- **Καθόμουν όταν ήρθε.** — I was sitting when he came.
- **Κάθισα και περίμενα.** — I sat down and waited.
- **Δεν θυμόμουν το όνομά του.** — I could not remember his name. (a state)
- **Ξαφνικά θυμήθηκα.** — Suddenly I remembered. (an event)

**That last pair is the aspect distinction at its clearest** and it is worth saying aloud a few times.

**The passive in the past**, which is what you will read rather than say:

- **Το σπίτι χτίστηκε το 1950.** — The house was built in 1950.
- **Η εκκλησία ανακαινίστηκε.** — The church was renovated.
- **Γεννήθηκα στη Νότια Αφρική.** — I was born in South Africa.

**Γεννήθηκα is worth noting**: *I was born* is a passive in Greek as in English, and it is one of the first sentences you will need about yourself.

**Practice.** Say the ten aorists and the four imperfects aloud. Then say: **Χάρηκα · Τι έγινε; · Έγινε! · Γεννήθηκα στη… · Θυμήθηκα · Δεν θυμόμουν**. Then tell three things that happened to you yesterday using a mediopassive aorist each time.
Telling a story in the past:
A production lesson. Everything in stage 4, used for the thing the past tenses exist for: telling someone what happened.

**The shape of a Greek narrative**, which is the shape of any narrative: aorists carry the events, imperfects set the scene, and the sequencing words hold it together.

**A worked example, to read aloud twice:**

> **Την Κυριακή ξύπνησα** στις οχτώ. **Έκανε** κρύο και **έβρεχε**, αλλά **πήγα** στην εκκλησία με τα πόδια. **Ήταν** πολύ κόσμος. Ο πατέρας Γιώργος **μιλούσε** για τον Άγιο Δημήτριο και **κατάλαβα** σχεδόν τα μισά. **Μετά** τη Λειτουργία **πήρα** αντίδωρο και **μίλησα** με τη κυρία Ελένη. **Με ρώτησε** για τα παιδιά και **της είπα** ότι είναι καλά. **Ύστερα πήγαμε** για καφέ και **έμεινα** μια ώρα. **Γύρισα** σπίτι στη μία και **έφαγα** με την οικογένειά μου. **Ήταν** μια πολύ ωραία μέρα.

**Count what is in it**: fourteen aorists, four imperfects, four sequencing words, two reported speech constructions with **ότι**, and one **να**-free sentence. That is a complete piece of spoken Greek built entirely from this stage.

**The sequencing kit:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **πρώτα** | first |
| **μετά / ύστερα** | then |
| **έπειτα** | next |
| **στο τέλος / τελικά** | in the end |
| **ξαφνικά** | suddenly |
| **αμέσως** | immediately |
| **ενώ** | while |
| **όταν** | when |
| **αφού** | after |
| **γιατί** | because |
| **αλλά** | but |
| **και** | and |

**Reporting what someone said: ότι.**

- **Μου είπε ότι θα έρθει.** — He told me he would come.
- **Είπα ότι δεν μπορώ.** — I said I could not.

**Greek does not shift the tense the way English does.** English moves *will* to *would*; Greek keeps the original: **Μου είπε ότι θα έρθει** — literally *he told me that he will come*. That is simpler and it takes some unlearning.

**The three habits of a good story in a foreign language:**

1. **Short sentences.** A chain of **και** and **μετά** is better Greek than one long clause you cannot finish.
2. **One tense at a time.** If the story is in the aorist, stay there until you need scenery.
3. **Keep going.** A wrong ending in a flowing story costs nothing; stopping to fix it loses your listener.

**Practice.** Tell last Sunday aloud, in at least ten sentences, with the shape above: wake, weather, go, who was there, what the priest spoke about, what you understood, who you spoke to, where you went after, when you got home, how it was. Then write it down and check every verb's stem and ending.
At church: talking about the service aft:
The specific conversation this curriculum exists for, built out of stage 4's grammar.

**What you will be asked**, and the answers in order of usefulness:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Σου άρεσε;** | Did you like it? — **Μου άρεσε πολύ.** |
| **Κατάλαβες;** | Did you understand? — **Κατάλαβα λίγο.** / **Κατάλαβα μερικές λέξεις.** |
| **Πόσο καιρό μαθαίνεις ελληνικά;** | — **Μαθαίνω έναν χρόνο.** |
| **Έρχεσαι κάθε Κυριακή;** | — **Προσπαθώ να έρχομαι κάθε Κυριακή.** |
| **Είσαι Ορθόδοξος;** | — and whatever your answer is |
| **Θα έρθεις την άλλη Κυριακή;** | — **Θα έρθω, αν μπορέσω.** |

**What you can say about the service**, which is where the vocabulary from stage 2 meets this stage's verbs:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ήταν πολύ ωραία η Λειτουργία.** | The Liturgy was lovely. |
| **Ο ψάλτης ήταν πολύ καλός.** | The chanter was very good. |
| **Δεν κατάλαβα το κήρυγμα.** | I did not understand the sermon. |
| **Κατάλαβα όταν μιλούσε αργά.** | I understood when he spoke slowly. |
| **Άκουσα τη λέξη «αγάπη».** | I heard the word *agapi*. |
| **Πήρα αντίδωρο.** | I took the antidoron. |
| **Άναψα ένα κερί.** | I lit a candle. |
| **Προσκύνησα την εικόνα.** | I venerated the icon. |
| **Σήμερα ήταν η εορτή του Αγίου…** | Today was the feast of St… |

**The questions you can ask**, which is the half that makes you a participant rather than a spectacle:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι εορτάζουμε σήμερα;** | What are we celebrating today? |
| **Ποιος άγιος είναι σήμερα;** | Which saint is it today? |
| **Τι σημαίνει αυτή η λέξη;** | What does this word mean? |
| **Πώς το λένε αυτό;** | What is this called? |
| **Τι ώρα είναι η Λειτουργία την άλλη Κυριακή;** | What time is the Liturgy next Sunday? |
| **Μπορείτε να μου εξηγήσετε;** | Could you explain it to me? |
| **Ποιο βιβλίο να διαβάσω;** | Which book should I read? |

**Τι σημαίνει αυτή η λέξη; is the single most productive question** you can ask in a parish hall. It gets you a word, a conversation, and usually a cup of coffee.

**The three things worth being able to say about your own position**, honestly and in advance:

- **Μαθαίνω ελληνικά για να μιλάω με τους ανθρώπους στην εκκλησία.**
- **Θέλω να καταλάβω τη Λειτουργία, αλλά ξέρω ότι είναι άλλη γλώσσα.**
- **Διαβάζω και μαθαίνω σιγά σιγά.** — *slowly, little by little*, and **σιγά σιγά** is a phrase Greeks will say back to you approvingly.

**σιγά σιγά is worth adopting.** It is the standard Greek encouragement for anything long and difficult, and it is the right description of this curriculum.

**Practice.** Say the six answers and the seven questions aloud. Then have the whole conversation with yourself, both parts, out loud. Then pick one question to actually ask this Sunday — **Τι εορτάζουμε σήμερα;** is a good one — and ask it.
How to store a verb:
A short, practical lesson on what a verb card has to contain — because a verb stored wrongly is a verb you cannot use.

**The four forms a Greek verb needs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The present** | γράφω — the imperfective, and the dictionary form |
| **The dependent** | να γράψω — the perfective |
| **The aorist** | έγραψα — the past perfective |
| **The imperative** | γράψε / γράψτε — if it has one in use |

**Those four give you everything else.** From **γράφω** you get the whole present and the imperfect; from **να γράψω** you get the future and the subjunctive; from **έγραψα** you get the whole aorist. Three stems, four forms, and the rest is endings.

**So the card looks like this:**

> **γράφω** · **να γράψω** · **έγραψα** — to write
>
> *Class A. Imperative γράψε / γράψτε.*

**For a mediopassive verb**, add the voice and its aorist:

> **θυμάμαι** · **να θυμηθώ** · **θυμήθηκα** — to remember
>
> *Mediopassive, B pattern. Imperfect θυμόμουν.*

**What to leave off.** Everything else. The full paradigm belongs in the Forms track, not on a card; a card that tries to carry twenty forms is a card you will not review.

**The reverse card is the important one.** Given the English, produce all four Greek forms aloud. That is the test that matters, because it is what speaking requires.

**The three mistakes to avoid when storing verbs:**

1. **Storing only the present.** Half a verb, and the half you need least in conversation about anything that already happened.
2. **Storing the aorist without the dependent.** You will be able to say what you did and not what you will do.
3. **Storing without the stress mark.** **γραψε** and **γράψε** are not the same word, and the accent is part of the spelling.

**How many a week.** Ten verbs a week, properly stored and reviewed, is a hundred verbs in ten weeks — which is most of the verbs in ordinary conversation. More than that and the review load grows past what you will actually do.

**Where to get the forms**: the Triantafyllidis dictionary gives the full conjugation of any verb; Lexiscope takes any form and gives the rest. Both are free and both take seconds.

**And the sentence card, which is worth as much as the verb card.** Store one real sentence per verb — **Του έγραψα ένα γράμμα** — because a verb in a sentence is a verb you can use, and a verb in isolation is a word you can recognise.

**Practice.** Take the twenty irregular pairs from earlier in this stage and store them properly, four forms each, in the deck. Then for five of them write a sentence card too. Then test yourself in the reverse direction: English to all four forms, aloud.
The aspect drill:
A dedicated practice lesson, because aspect is the one thing in Greek that genuinely needs drilling rather than understanding.

**The drill, and it takes ten minutes:**

**1. The pair drill.** Take ten verbs. For each, say both stems aloud: **γράφω — να γράψω**. Then both aorists where they differ: **έγραφα — έγραψα**. Thirty seconds a verb.

**2. The two-sentence drill.** For each verb, make two sentences — one of each aspect — and say what each means:

- **Θα γράφω κάθε βδομάδα.** — I will write every week.
- **Θα γράψω απόψε.** — I will write tonight.

**3. The translation drill, English to Greek**, which is where the choice is forced on you:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| I want to read this book | **Θέλω να διαβάσω αυτό το βιβλίο.** |
| I want to read more | **Θέλω να διαβάζω πιο πολύ.** |
| Call me tomorrow | **Να μου τηλεφωνήσεις αύριο.** |
| Call me every day | **Να μου τηλεφωνείς κάθε μέρα.** |
| I was eating when he came | **Έτρωγα όταν ήρθε.** |
| I ate and left | **Έφαγα και έφυγα.** |
| Do not smoke (ever) | **Μην καπνίζεις.** |
| Do not smoke (that one) | **Μην καπνίσεις.** |

**4. The story drill.** Tell something in the past, deliberately mixing: three aorists for events and two imperfects for scenery. Out loud, in under a minute.

**5. The listening drill.** Take an Easy Greek clip and count the verbs after **θα** and **να**, noting which stem each is. You will not catch all of them, and noticing even half is training.

**What to drill it on.** The twenty irregular pairs first, because they are the common verbs and their stems look different enough to be unmistakable. Then the regular ones, which are easier to form and harder to hear.

**How long this takes to stick.** Expect the pair knowledge in a fortnight, the correct choice in simple sentences within a couple of months, and the automatic choice at speaking speed over a year or more. That is the normal curve and it is not a sign of doing it wrong.

**The one shortcut worth having.** If you cannot decide mid-sentence, use the perfective. It is the commoner choice and the error is smaller.

**And the one thing not to do**: avoid the construction. A learner who avoids **θα** and **να** to dodge the choice ends up unable to talk about the future or to use any of the modal verbs — which is most of a conversation.

**Practice.** Do all five drills today, on ten verbs. Then do drill 3 again tomorrow with the book closed. Then keep drill 1 as a daily ten-minute habit for the rest of this stage.
