How often: the frequency words:
A small vocabulary lesson that pairs with aspect, because these words are what tell you which stem to use.

**The scale, from always to never:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **πάντα** | always |
| **συνήθως** | usually |
| **συχνά** | often |
| **μερικές φορές** | sometimes |
| **καμιά φορά** | sometimes, now and then |
| **σπάνια** | rarely |
| **ποτέ** | never — with **δεν** |

- **Δεν πάω ποτέ.** — I never go. · **Πάντα πηγαίνω την Κυριακή.** — I always go on Sunday.

**The counting phrases:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **μία φορά** | once |
| **δύο φορές** | twice |
| **πολλές φορές** | many times |
| **κάθε μέρα / βδομάδα / μήνα / χρόνο** | every day / week / month / year |
| **μία φορά τη βδομάδα** | once a week |
| **δύο φορές τον μήνα** | twice a month |
| **κάθε δεύτερη Κυριακή** | every other Sunday |

**Note the accusative with no preposition** in **μία φορά τη βδομάδα** — *once a week* — the same time-phrase accusative as **την Κυριακή**.

**The ones about duration and continuation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **συνέχεια** | continuously, all the time |
| **ακόμα** | still, yet |
| **πια** | any more, by now |
| **πλέον** | any more (formal) |
| **ήδη** | already |
| **μόλις** | just |
| **ξανά / πάλι** | again |
| **για λίγο** | for a while |
| **για πάντα** | forever |

- **Δεν μένω πια εδώ.** — I do not live here any more.
- **Είναι ακόμα εδώ.** — He is still here.
- **Ήρθα μόλις τώρα.** — I have only just arrived.

**And the aspect connection**, which is why this lesson is here: each of these words pulls one stem.

| Pulls the imperfective | Pulls the perfective |
| --- | --- |
| πάντα, συνήθως, συχνά | μία φορά, ξαφνικά |
| κάθε μέρα, συνέχεια | απόψε, αύριο, τώρα |
| ακόμα, για πάντα | ήδη, μόλις, τελικά |
| σπάνια, μερικές φορές | αμέσως |

**So the adverb is often a decision already made for you**, which is the practical shortcut this lesson offers: hear or say **κάθε μέρα** and the verb after it is imperfective; hear **ξαφνικά** and it is perfective.

**Where they go in the sentence.** Usually after the verb, sometimes at the front for emphasis: **Πάω πάντα την Κυριακή** or **Πάντα πάω την Κυριακή**. Both are fine.

**Practice.** Say the seven frequency words aloud, then describe your week with five of them — out loud, choosing the stem each requires. Then say five sentences with **ακόμα**, **πια**, **ήδη** and **μόλις**.
Reading: the narrative past:
What to read now that you have the past tenses, which is the point at which Greek stories open up.

**Why this is a step change.** Until now you could read descriptions and dialogue. Narrative — anything that tells what happened — is built on the aorist and the imperfect, so the whole of children's literature, folk tale and history has been closed and now is not.

**What to read:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ανθολόγιο Β΄–Γ΄ Δημοτικού** | the school readers, free at ebooks.edu.gr — folk tales and stories |
| **Greek folk tales** (παραμύθια) | short, formulaic, repetitive — ideal |
| **Αίσωπος — the fables** | twenty lines each, a moral at the end, and in modern Greek versions free online |
| **Children's picture books** in Greek | if the parish or a friend has any |
| **Simple saints' lives** (βίοι αγίων) | written for children, narrative past throughout, and exactly your subject matter |
| **News in brief** | the first paragraph of a news item, which is all aorists |

**The saints' lives deserve the emphasis.** They are narrative, they are short, they exist at every reading level including children's, they are about something you care about, and the vocabulary overlaps heavily with what you hear at church. For your purposes they are the best reading material available.

**What to expect, and it will be the main difficulty:** the past tenses of verbs whose present you know but whose aorist you have not met. **Είδε, είπε, πήρε, βρήκε, έφυγε** — all third person, all irregular, all extremely common. The twenty-verb list from earlier in this stage covers most of them; the rest you look up once.

**The technique for a narrative page:**

1. **Read it aloud once**, without stopping, for the shape.
2. **Mark every verb.** Aorist or imperfect?
3. **Read it again** and notice that the aorists are the plot and the imperfects are the scenery.
4. **Look up two or three verbs**, no more.
5. **Reread it a third time**, which is where the comprehension actually arrives.

**That verb-marking exercise is the intensive reading** for this stage, and one page a week of it is enough. The rest should be extensive — read, enjoy, move on.

**Where to find the free material**: ebooks.edu.gr for the school books; the Greek Wikisource (el.wikisource.org) for fables and folk tales; the various parish and monastery sites for saints' lives, which are usually written simply on purpose.

**One target for the end of this stage**: read one whole Aesop fable aloud, understand it without a dictionary, and be able to retell it in three sentences. That is a real and achievable milestone and it is the first time Greek will feel like a language you can use rather than study.

**Practice.** Find an Aesop fable in modern Greek. Read it aloud, mark its verbs, look up two, read it again. Then retell it in three sentences of your own, out loud.
Listening: following a story:
The listening habit at the point where you can follow a narrative — which is a different skill from following a conversation and an easier one.

**Why stories are easier than conversation.** One voice, no overlap, a predictable shape, and a listener who is expected to be following. Conversation has two voices, interruptions, and no one making allowances. So narrative listening is where to build.

**What to listen to:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Helinika's story series** | comprehensible-input narratives, free |
| **Greek children's audiobooks** | παραμύθια read aloud, on YouTube, free |
| **The Easy Greek beginner podcast** | two speakers, slow, and with transcripts |
| **Greek cartoons** | dubbed children's series, which are narrative and repetitive |
| **The sermon at church** | the single most useful thing on this list, and the hardest |
| **Greek music** | still, and still worth it |

**The sermon deserves its own note.** A κήρυγμα is a monologue, in modern Greek rather than in liturgical Greek, on a subject you can often guess from the day's feast, delivered slowly and clearly to a congregation. It is in every way the ideal listening exercise for you — and at this stage you will catch perhaps a tenth of it. Catch that tenth deliberately: the feast, the saint's name, the repeated words, one whole sentence.

**The three-pass method from stage 3 still applies**, and at this level add a fourth:

1. **Listen once** without help.
2. **Listen with the transcript or subtitles.**
3. **Listen again without.**
4. **Retell what happened**, out loud, in three sentences.

**That fourth step is the new one** and it is the one that converts listening into speaking. A story you can retell is a story you understood; one you can only recognise is one you followed.

**What to listen for specifically at this stage:**

- **The aorists**, which carry the events. They usually begin with **έ-**, **εί-** or **ή-**, which is an audible cue.
- **The sequencing words** — **μετά, ύστερα, τότε, ξαφνικά** — which tell you where you are in the story.
- **ότι**, which flags reported speech.
- **θα** and **να**, and which stem follows each.

**A realistic expectation**: you follow a children's story told slowly; you follow about half of an Easy Greek clip; you catch the subject and some sentences of a sermon; you do not follow two Greeks talking quickly to each other. The last of those arrives in stages 6 to 8 and it arrives suddenly, after a long period of apparently no progress.

**Practice.** Take one Helinika story or one Greek children's audiobook. Do the four-pass method on it, including the retelling. Then at church, listen to the sermon with the single aim of catching one complete sentence, and write it down afterwards.
Writing: a paragraph in the past:
The writing habit, raised from sentences to a paragraph — which is where the sequencing and the tense choices start to interact.

**The new requirement: one paragraph a day, in the past, about yesterday.** Five to eight sentences, with at least two imperfects in it.

**The shape to follow**, which is the narrative shape from earlier in this stage:

1. **When and where** — the frame, often with **ήταν** or **έκανε**.
2. **Three or four things that happened** — aorists, in order, with **μετά** and **ύστερα**.
3. **Something that was going on** — an imperfect.
4. **How it was** — **ήταν ωραία**, **πέρασα καλά**.

**A worked example at the right level:**

> **Χθες ήταν Κυριακή. Ξύπνησα στις οχτώ και πήγα στην εκκλησία. Έβρεχε, αλλά δεν είχε πολύ κόσμο. Ο πατέρας Γιώργος μιλούσε για τον Άγιο Δημήτριο και κατάλαβα λίγο. Μετά τη Λειτουργία πήρα αντίδωρο και μίλησα με δύο ανθρώπους. Γύρισα σπίτι στη μία και έφαγα με την οικογένειά μου. Πέρασα πολύ ωραία.**

**Then the check, which is the exercise.** For every verb:

1. **Aorist or imperfect — and is that the right choice?**
2. **Is the stem right?** The perfective for aorists, the imperfective for imperfects.
3. **Is the ending right?** **-α, -ες, -ε, -αμε, -ατε, -αν**.
4. **Is the augment where the stress needs it?**
5. **Is the accent written?**

**And for everything else:** gender, case, agreement, spelling — the five questions from stage 3's writing lesson, which do not go away.

**Then one harder sentence a week:**

- A sentence with **ότι** reporting what someone said.
- A sentence of the shape *I was ...-ing when ...* — imperfect plus aorist.
- A sentence with **πριν** or **αφού** and a clause.

**Where to get it checked.** The same three places: the dictionary for forms, Lexiscope for any verb form at all, and your own five-question pass. There is no teacher here; the check is the substitute and it is a good one if you actually do it.

**What this habit is worth.** Writing is where the aspect choice is made consciously and slowly, which is exactly what it needs while it is being learned. Speaking is too fast to think about it; writing is where the thinking happens, and the speaking improves afterwards.

**Keep them, as before.** A paragraph a day for three months is ninety paragraphs, and reading the first one next to the ninetieth is the clearest evidence of progress you will have.

**Practice.** Write yesterday's paragraph now, following the four-part shape. Then run the five-verb checks on it. Then write one of the three harder sentences and verify it.
Where you should be: Pimsleur, Language:
A checkpoint lesson. Four stages in, this is what the three running resources should have given you, and what to do if any of them has stalled.

**Pimsleur.** Thirty lessons of Level 1, ideally finished, and into Level 2. If you have been doing half an hour most days since stage 1 you are there or close.

- **What it gives**: pronunciation, the rhythm of question and answer, and about three hundred words so deeply embedded that they come out without thought.
- **What it does not give**: grammar you can extend, reading, or anything about aspect.
- **If it has stalled**: restart at the lesson you last did properly rather than at the beginning. Pimsleur is cumulative but forgiving.

**Language Transfer — Complete Greek.** Forty to sixty of the hundred and twenty lessons by now, which is roughly where its explanation of the verb system sits.

- **What it gives**: the reasoning behind the grammar, and specifically a very good treatment of the two stems and of **να** — the subject of this whole stage, explained in a completely different way from these lessons.
- **Worth doing deliberately now**: find its lessons on the subjunctive and the aorist and listen to them even if you are behind. Two explanations of aspect are better than one.

**The deck.** By the end of stage 4 you should have roughly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Vocabulary** | six to eight hundred words, each with its gender or its verb forms |
| **Verbs** | a hundred, stored as three or four forms each |
| **Phrases** | fifty or so, whole |
| **Spelling cards** | whatever the Spelling track has thrown up |
| **Daily** | ten new, the rest review — which is twenty to thirty minutes |

**If the deck has got away from you** — and it will, at least once — the fix is to stop adding new cards for a week and clear the backlog. A deck with four hundred cards due is a deck you will abandon; a deck with forty due is one you will do.

**FSI**, the demoted resource: if you have been using its drills, you are probably in Volume 1 around unit 10 to 15. If you have not touched it, that is fine — it is there for pattern practice when a structure refuses to stick, not as a spine.

**The honest self-assessment for the end of stage 4.** You should be able to:

- Say what you did yesterday, in several sentences, in the past.
- Say what you will do tomorrow.
- Ask someone to do something, and tell them not to.
- Use **θέλω να, μπορώ να, πρέπει να** freely.
- Follow a slow story.
- Read a children's story aloud and understand it.
- Hold a five-minute conversation about yourself, your family and your parish.

**That is approximately A2**, and it is the level at which a language stops being a subject and starts being usable. If two or three of those are shaky, the thing to do is not to move on faster — it is to spend a fortnight talking out loud to yourself about yesterday.

**Practice.** Go through the seven abilities above and test each one out loud. Then clear whatever backlog the deck has. Then decide which of the three resources has slipped most, and restart that one this week.
Review: stage 4:
The end of the hinge stage. What should be true, and what stage 5 does.

**What should now be true:**

- **Aspect**: that every verb has two stems, and what each one means.
- The three sound rules for forming the perfective — labial **ψ**, velar **ξ**, dental **σ** — and **-ήσω** for the second conjugation.
- The twenty irregular pairs, learned as pairs: **βλέπω/δω, λέω/πω, τρώω/φάω, παίρνω/πάρω**.
- That the perfective stem cannot stand alone, and the list of particles it depends on.
- That Greek has no infinitive, and **να** plus a conjugated verb does the job — including **θέλω να πας**, which English cannot do so neatly.
- **να** in all its uses, including the blessings and wishes that are much of the warmth of the language.
- The subjunctive in both aspects, and the decision procedure between them.
- **θέλω να, μπορώ να, πρέπει να**, and the family around them.
- The future with **θα**, in both aspects.
- The imperative in both aspects, with **μην** for the negative and **ας** for *let's*.
- The aorist: its formation, its endings, the augment as a stress device, and the irregulars.
- The imperfect, including **-ούσα** for the second conjugation.
- Choosing between them: the aorist tells the story, the imperfect paints the scene.
- **ήμουν** and **είχα** cold.
- The mediopassive: what it is, the present endings, the **-θηκα** aorists, and the dozen deponent verbs you use daily.
- **πάω, λέω, τρώω, έρχομαι** as whole paradigms.
- The prefixes, and that one known verb gives you its whole compound family.
- The verbs of motion with their prepositions, and **περνάω από** as an invitation.
- The time and frequency words, and which stem each pulls.
- You can tell a story in the past, ask about someone else's, and talk about the service afterwards.
- A verb is stored in the deck as four forms, never one.

**What stage 4 deliberately did not do.** The perfect tenses (**έχω γράψει**), the pluperfect, the conditional (**θα πήγαινα**), the passive in every tense, and the participles. All of those are built from what you now have, and they are stage 6.

**What stage 5 does.** Everyday Greek — the A2 vocabulary and situations, used hard: the house, the shops, food, the doctor, travel, work, the telephone, money, the body, clothes, appointments, and a great deal of parish life. It is the stage with the least new grammar and the most new words, and it is where the grammar from stages 2 to 4 becomes fluent through use rather than through study.

**It is also the stage where speaking should overtake studying.** By the end of it you should be having real conversations, badly and continuously.

**Practice.** Go down the list. Then tell the story of your last week out loud, in the past, for two minutes without stopping — and notice that you could not have done that four stages ago.
What stage 5 is: use, not study:
The stage with the least new grammar and the most new words — and the one where Greek should stop being a subject.

**What changes.** Stages 2 to 4 built the machinery: the noun system, the verb system, aspect. This stage uses it. There is almost no new grammar in the next forty lessons; there are several hundred words, two dozen situations, and a running instruction to talk.

**Why that is the right shape now.** A learner with the grammar of stage 4 and the vocabulary of stage 4 can construct almost any sentence and has nothing to put in it. The constraint has moved from structure to words, and the cure for that is subject matter rather than explanation.

**The three rules for this stage:**

1. **Learn the vocabulary in situations, not in lists.** The bakery, the doctor, the parish hall. A word learned in a situation comes back in that situation; a word learned in a list comes back in a test.
2. **Say every lesson's sentences out loud.** This stage is almost entirely phrases, and a phrase you have not said is a phrase you do not have.
3. **Use what you can and work round what you cannot.** By now you have enough grammar to paraphrase anything: **δεν ξέρω τη λέξη, αλλά είναι σαν…** — I do not know the word, but it is like…

**The vocabulary load, honestly.** About forty new words a lesson, which is sixteen hundred over the stage — too many to memorise deliberately. So:

- **Card the ones you will use**, which is perhaps a third.
- **Recognise the rest**, which happens through the reading and listening.
- **Do not try to card everything.** A deck of two thousand cards you cannot keep up with is worse than a deck of eight hundred you review.

**Where the grammar does appear**, and it is small: a few more prepositions, the comparative in use, the impersonal verbs, and a great deal of practice with aspect in real sentences. The Spelling and Forms tracks continue and this is a good stage to catch up on either.

**What "use" means in practice this stage:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Out loud, alone** | narrate your own day as you do it, in Greek, badly |
| **At church** | one real conversation a week, however short |
| **In writing** | the paragraph a day, now about situations rather than yourself |
| **Reading** | menus, notices, messages, signs — the real world's Greek |
| **Listening** | shop exchanges and the parish hall, deliberately |

**The honest expectation at the end of it.** Not fluency — the ability to handle an ordinary day in Greek: shop, order, ask the way, make an appointment, describe a problem, accept an invitation, and talk for ten minutes about family, work and the weather. That is A2 going on B1, and it is the level at which people stop switching to English.

**Practice.** Read the next lesson and start the vocabulary habit: ten words a day into the deck, chosen because you will use them. Then narrate your morning out loud in Greek before you look at any of it.
The house and the rooms:
The place you spend most of your life, and the words for describing it — which is one of the first conversations anyone has.

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το σπίτι** | house, home | **το διαμέρισμα** | flat |
| **η πολυκατοικία** | block of flats | **ο όροφος** | floor, storey |
| **το ισόγειο** | ground floor | **το υπόγειο** | basement |
| **η αυλή** | yard, courtyard | **ο κήπος** | garden |
| **το μπαλκόνι** | balcony | **η ταράτσα** | roof terrace |
| **η σκάλα** | stairs | **το ασανσέρ** | lift |
| **η πόρτα** | door | **το παράθυρο** | window |
| **ο τοίχος** | wall | **το πάτωμα** | floor |
| **η οροφή / το ταβάνι** | ceiling | **η στέγη** | roof |

**The rooms:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το σαλόνι** | sitting room | **η κουζίνα** | kitchen |
| **η τραπεζαρία** | dining room | **το υπνοδωμάτιο** | bedroom |
| **η κρεβατοκάμαρα** | bedroom (everyday) | **το μπάνιο** | bathroom |
| **η τουαλέτα** | toilet | **ο διάδρομος** | hall, corridor |
| **το γραφείο** | study, office | **η αποθήκη** | storeroom |

**The sentences:**

- **Μένω σε ένα διαμέρισμα στον δεύτερο όροφο.** — I live in a flat on the second floor.
- **Το σπίτι έχει τρία υπνοδωμάτια.** — The house has three bedrooms.
- **Έχουμε μπαλκόνι και μικρό κήπο.** — We have a balcony and a small garden.
- **Η κουζίνα είναι μεγάλη.** — The kitchen is big.
- **Το μπάνιο είναι στο τέλος του διαδρόμου.** — The bathroom is at the end of the hall.

**The questions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πού μένεις;** | Where do you live? |
| **Μένεις σε σπίτι ή σε διαμέρισμα;** | Do you live in a house or a flat? |
| **Πόσα δωμάτια έχει;** | How many rooms does it have? |
| **Έχεις κήπο;** | Do you have a garden? |
| **Πόσο καιρό μένεις εκεί;** | How long have you lived there? |

**The Greek housing facts worth knowing**, because they come up in conversation: most Greeks in cities live in a **πολυκατοικία**, often one their family built or bought floor by floor; a **ταράτσα** is a social space, not just a roof; and asking what floor someone lives on is ordinary small talk rather than nosiness.

**The verb for living somewhere is μένω** — which also means *stay*, so **μένω στην Αθήνα** is *I live in Athens* and **θα μείνω δύο μέρες** is *I will stay two days*. Context does the work.

**Practice.** Describe your own home in six sentences, out loud. Then answer the five questions. Then card ten of the words above — the ten about your own house.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ανοίγω / κλείνω** | open / close — a door, a window, the light |

**Practice.** Name twenty things in the room you are in, out loud, with their articles. Then say what you did in the house yesterday using five of the verbs, in the aorist. Then report one thing that is broken.
The day: morning to night:
Your own routine, which is the most useful paragraph you can own — and which uses the mediopassive verbs from stage 4 constantly.

**The sequence:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ξυπνάω** | I wake up |
| **σηκώνομαι** | I get up |
| **πλένομαι** | I wash |
| **πλένω τα δόντια μου** | I brush my teeth |
| **κάνω ντους** | I have a shower |
| **ξυρίζομαι** | I shave |
| **ντύνομαι** | I get dressed |
| **παίρνω πρωινό** | I have breakfast |
| **φεύγω για τη δουλειά** | I leave for work |
| **δουλεύω** | I work |
| **τρώω μεσημεριανό** | I have lunch |
| **γυρίζω σπίτι** | I come home |
| **ξεκουράζομαι** | I rest |
| **μαγειρεύω** | I cook |
| **τρώω βραδινό** | I have dinner |
| **βλέπω τηλεόραση** | I watch television |
| **διαβάζω** | I read |
| **προσεύχομαι** | I pray |
| **πάω για ύπνο** | I go to bed |
| **κοιμάμαι** | I sleep |

**Notice how many are mediopassive**: σηκώνομαι, πλένομαι, ξυρίζομαι, ντύνομαι, ξεκουράζομαι, κοιμάμαι, προσεύχομαι. The reflexive half of the day is in that voice, which is exactly what stage 4's lesson said it was for.

**The meals:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το πρωινό** | breakfast |
| **το μεσημεριανό** | lunch — the main meal, eaten mid-afternoon |
| **το βραδινό** | dinner, eaten late |
| **ο καφές** | the coffee, which is a social event rather than a meal |

**The Greek day is shifted later than the English one.** Lunch at two or three, dinner at nine or ten, and the afternoon rest — **το μεσημέρι** — between. Saying **θα φάμε στις εφτά** to a Greek will get you a puzzled look.

**The time phrases:**

- **κάθε μέρα** — every day · **το πρωί** — in the morning · **το βράδυ** — in the evening
- **στις εφτά** — at seven · **μετά τη δουλειά** — after work · **πριν κοιμηθώ** — before I sleep

**A model paragraph, in the present:**

> **Ξυπνάω στις εφτά. Σηκώνομαι, πλένομαι και ντύνομαι. Παίρνω πρωινό και φεύγω για τη δουλειά στις οχτώ. Δουλεύω μέχρι τις πέντε. Μετά γυρίζω σπίτι, τρώμε με την οικογένεια και βλέπω λίγη τηλεόραση. Διαβάζω λίγα ελληνικά πριν κοιμηθώ. Πάω για ύπνο στις έντεκα.**

**Then the same in the aorist, about yesterday**, which is the stage 4 exercise applied to something you know cold.

**Practice.** Say your routine in the present, out loud, in ten sentences. Then say it again in the aorist, about yesterday. Then say it in the future, about tomorrow. Three tenses, one paragraph — and that is most of what conversation about ordinary life consists of.

The two shops where the vocabulary is specific and the transaction is quick — and where you will be understood on your first attempt.

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| **το φραντζολάκι** | small loaf | **η φραντζόλα** | long loaf |

| **η σπανακόπιτα** | spinach pie | **το κρουασάν** | croissant |
| **τα κουλουράκια** | little biscuit rings | **το παξιμάδι** | rusk |
| **η πίτα** | flatbread, pie | **το προζύμι** | sourdough |
| **η τσουρέκι** | the Easter bread — **το** τσουρέκι | **η βασιλόπιτα** | the New Year cake |

**φρέσκο and της ημέρας** — fresh, and *of the day* — are what you ask for.

**The transaction:**

— **Καλημέρα! Τι θα πάρετε;**
— **Ένα χωριάτικο, παρακαλώ. Είναι φρέσκο;**
— **Από το πρωί. Κάτι άλλο;**
— **Δύο τυρόπιτες και ένα κουλούρι.**
— **Αμέσως. Εφτά ευρώ και είκοσι.**
— **Ευχαριστώ πολύ.**
— **Να 'στε καλά. Καλή σας μέρα!**

**Να 'στε καλά** — *be well* — is the shopkeeper's farewell and one of the warmest things anyone says to you in a day.

**At the butcher — το κρεοπωλείο, or in speech ο χασάπης** (the butcher himself):

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ένα κιλό** | a kilo | **μισό κιλό** | half a kilo |
| **ο κιμάς** | mince | **οι μπριζόλες** | chops |
| **το φιλέτο** | fillet | **το σουβλάκι** | the skewer |
| **τα παϊδάκια** | lamb chops | **το κοτόπουλο** | chicken |
| **το στήθος** | breast | **το μπούτι** | leg, thigh |
| **καθαρισμένο** | cleaned, trimmed | **κομμένο** | cut |

**Note παϊδάκια with its diaeresis** — from the Spelling track, and now in a shop.

- **Ένα κιλό κιμά, παρακαλώ.** — A kilo of mince, please.
- **Μπορείτε να το κόψετε;** — Can you cut it?
- **Τι μου προτείνετε;** — What do you recommend?
- **Πόσο κάνει το κιλό;** — How much a kilo?

**The small-shop convention worth knowing**: in a bakery or a butcher's, you are served in order, you are often addressed as **κυρία** or **κύριε**, and small talk is normal. The queue is informal and the question **Ποιος είναι πρώτος;** — who is first? — sorts it out.

**Practice.** Read both exchanges aloud, both parts. Then order from each shop out loud, five things in total, with quantities. Then ask **Τι μου προτείνετε;** and invent the answer.

**Buying them:**

- **Ένα κιλό ντομάτες, παρακαλώ.** — A kilo of tomatoes, please.
- **Είναι ώριμα;** — Are they ripe?
- **Αυτά είναι της εποχής;** — Are these in season?
- **Μισό κιλό φασολάκια.** — Half a kilo of green beans.
- **Τι έχετε φρέσκο σήμερα;** — What is fresh today?

**Της εποχής — *of the season* — is the key question** at a Greek greengrocer or market, and the answer tells you what to cook.

**Practice.** Name everything in your fruit bowl and your fridge, out loud, with articles. Then buy five things from a market stall out loud, with quantities. Then ask **Τι έχετε φρέσκο σήμερα;** and answer it.
At the taverna: the menu:
Reading a Greek menu, which is one of the most immediately rewarding things this curriculum gives you.

**The sections:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ορεκτικά** | starters | **σαλάτες** | salads |
| **μεζέδες** | small plates to share | **κυρίως πιάτα** | main courses |
| **της ώρας** | grilled to order | **μαγειρευτά** | cooked dishes, ready |
| **θαλασσινά** | seafood | **ζυμαρικά** | pasta |
| **γαρνιτούρες / συνοδευτικά** | side dishes | **γλυκά** | desserts |
| **ποτά** | drinks | **κρασί χύμα** | house wine, by the jug |

**της ώρας against μαγειρευτά is the real division** in a Greek taverna: *of the hour* means meat grilled when you order it, **μαγειρευτά** means the day's pots — slow-cooked dishes that are ready and are often better. Asking **Τι μαγειρευτά έχετε σήμερα;** marks you as someone who knows how to order.

**The starters you will meet constantly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **τζατζίκι** | yoghurt, cucumber, garlic |
| **ταραμοσαλάτα** | fish-roe dip |
| **μελιτζανοσαλάτα** | aubergine dip |
| **τυροκαυτερή** | spicy cheese dip |
| **ντολμαδάκια** | stuffed vine leaves |
| **σαγανάκι** | fried cheese |
| **κολοκυθοκεφτέδες** | courgette fritters |
| **φάβα** | yellow split-pea purée |
| **γίγαντες** | baked butter beans |

**The salads:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **χωριάτικη** | the village salad — tomato, cucumber, onion, feta, olives |
| **μαρούλι** | lettuce, dressed |
| **ντάκος** | rusk, tomato, cheese — Cretan |
| **χόρτα** | boiled wild greens |
| **παντζάρια** | beetroot |

**The mains:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **σουβλάκι** | skewer — and the wrap if it is **σε πίτα** |
| **γύρος** | the carved meat |
| **μπιφτέκι** | burger-shaped mince |
| **παϊδάκια** | lamb chops |
| **κοντοσούβλι** | large skewered chunks |
| **μουσακάς** | aubergine and mince, béchamel |
| **παστίτσιο** | baked pasta and mince |
| **γεμιστά** | stuffed tomatoes and peppers |
| **μπριάμ** | baked vegetables |
| **κοκκινιστό** | cooked in tomato |
| **λεμονάτο** | cooked with lemon |
| **στιφάδο** | with onions, in sauce |

**The menu abbreviations and notes** you will see: **Κ/Ψ** (κατεψυγμένο — frozen, which the law requires them to declare), **τιμή κατά βάρος** (price by weight), **περιλαμβάνεται** (included), **ΦΠΑ** (VAT).

**Κ/Ψ beside a fish means frozen**, and knowing that one abbreviation is worth more than most of the menu.

**The drinks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **χύμα κρασί** | house wine from the barrel — ordered by the **κιλό** or the καράφα |
| **λευκό / κόκκινο / ροζέ** | white / red / rosé |
| **ρετσίνα** | the resinated wine |
| **τσίπουρο / ούζο** | the spirits, ordered with μεζέδες |
| **μπύρα** | beer — ask for **μικρή** or **μεγάλη** |

**Practice.** Find a Greek menu online — any taverna's — and read it aloud, section by section. Name five things you would order. Then say **Τι μαγειρευτά έχετε σήμερα;** and **Είναι νηστίσιμο;** aloud.
Ordering a meal, in full:
The whole transaction, from sitting down to paying, as a script to learn and then vary.

**Arriving:**

— **Καλησπέρα! Για πόσους;** — *For how many?*
— **Για τέσσερις, παρακαλώ.**
— **Ορίστε, καθίστε εδώ.** — *Here you are, sit here.*

**Ορίστε is the word of a thousand uses**: *here you are*, *go ahead*, *pardon?*, *can I help you?*, and *yes?* when answering the phone. Learn it now and you will hear it ten times a day.

**Ordering:**

— **Τι θα πάρετε;**
— **Θα πάρουμε μια χωριάτικη, τζατζίκι και ψωμί. Και τι μαγειρευτά έχετε σήμερα;**
— **Έχουμε γεμιστά, μπριάμ και κοκκινιστό.**
— **Δύο γεμιστά και ένα μπριάμ. Και παϊδάκια.**
— **Τι θα πιείτε;**
— **Μισό κιλό χύμα κόκκινο και ένα μεγάλο νερό.**
— **Αμέσως.**

**During:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλή όρεξη!** | enjoy your meal |
| **Είναι πολύ νόστιμο.** | it is very tasty |
| **Μπορείτε να μας φέρετε λίγο ψωμί;** | could you bring us some bread? |
| **Ένα πιάτο ακόμα, παρακαλώ.** | another plate, please |
| **Λείπει ένα πιρούνι.** | a fork is missing |
| **Αυτό δεν το παραγγείλαμε.** | we did not order this |
| **Δεν μπορώ άλλο!** | I cannot manage any more |

**Paying:**

— **Τον λογαριασμό, παρακαλώ.**
— **Αμέσως. Σαράντα δύο ευρώ.**
— **Μπορώ με κάρτα;**
— **Βεβαίως.**
— **Ευχαριστούμε πολύ, ήταν πολύ ωραία.**
— **Να 'στε καλά. Καλή συνέχεια!**

**Καλή συνέχεια** — *a good continuation* — is what you are wished on leaving anywhere in the middle of the day.

**The things that will happen that a phrasebook will not tell you:**

1. **You will be brought something you did not order** — a small plate, a dessert, a shot of tsipouro — **κερασμένο**, on the house. The correct response is **Ευχαριστούμε πολύ!** and to accept it.
2. **The bill is not itemised** in small tavernas, and nobody checks it.
3. **Splitting the bill is unusual.** One person pays, and the roles rotate over time. Insisting on your share can be mildly rude.
4. **Ordering is collective.** Dishes arrive in the middle and everyone eats from them. Ordering your own main course and guarding it is the foreign behaviour.
5. **Bread and water appear automatically** and are charged, which is normal.

**κερασμένο is worth knowing as a word**: *treated, on the house*. **Σας το κεράσαμε** — *it's on us*.

**Practice.** Read the whole script aloud, both parts, twice. Then order a meal for four out loud without looking. Then say the seven during-the-meal phrases five times each.
Greek food: what the dishes actually are:
A cultural lesson with vocabulary in it, because knowing what things are is half of being able to talk about them — and food is what Greeks talk about.

**The dishes you will be given at a Greek table:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **μουσακάς** | layers of aubergine, mince and béchamel, baked |
| **παστίτσιο** | tubular pasta, mince, béchamel |
| **γεμιστά** | tomatoes and peppers stuffed with rice and herbs |
| **μπριάμ** | potatoes, courgettes and tomato baked in oil |
| **φασολάκια λαδερά** | green beans in oil and tomato |
| **σπανακόρίζο** | spinach and rice |
| **γίγαντες** | butter beans baked in tomato |
| **κοκκινιστό** | meat braised in tomato |
| **λεμονάτο** | meat braised with lemon |
| **στιφάδο** | beef or rabbit with small onions |
| **γιουβέτσι** | meat baked with orzo pasta |
| **παϊδάκια** | lamb chops, grilled, with lemon and oregano |
| **κοντοσούβλι** | chunks of pork on a skewer |
| **κοκορέτσι** | offal wrapped in intestine, spit-roasted — the Easter dish |
| **μαγειρίτσα** | the soup eaten after the Resurrection service |
| **αρνί στον φούρνο** | roast lamb — Easter Sunday |

**The last three are feast food**, and they matter: **μαγειρίτσα** after midnight on Holy Saturday, **αρνί** and **κοκορέτσι** on Pascha itself. Being able to name them, and to say you have eaten them, places you in the year.

**The fasting dishes — τα λαδερά:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **φασολάδα** | bean soup |
| **φακές** | lentils |
| **ρεβίθια** | chickpeas |
| **χόρτα** | boiled wild greens |
| **γίγαντες** | the butter beans again |
| **καλαμαράκια** | squid — allowed on some fast days |
| **χαλβάς** | the sesame sweet, which is fasting food |
| **λαγάνα** | the flatbread of Clean Monday |

**Κούλουμα and Καθαρά Δευτέρα** — Clean Monday, the start of Lent, eaten outdoors with **λαγάνα**, **ταραμοσαλάτα** and **χαλβάς**, and kites flown. It is one of the most distinctive days in the Greek year.

**The sweets:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **μπακλαβάς** | filo, nuts, syrup |
| **γαλακτομπούρεκο** | filo, custard, syrup |
| **κανταΐφι** | shredded pastry, nuts, syrup |
| **λουκουμάδες** | fried dough balls in honey |
| **ρυζόγαλο** | rice pudding |
| **καρυδόπιτα** | walnut cake |
| **μελομακάρονα** | the honey biscuits of Christmas |
| **κουραμπιέδες** | the icing-sugar biscuits of Christmas |
| **τσουρέκι** | the sweet bread of Easter |
| **βασιλόπιτα** | the New Year cake with a coin in it |

**The feast-day sweets are a calendar**: μελομακάρονα and κουραμπιέδες in December, βασιλόπιτα on the first of January, τσουρέκι at Easter. Someone will hand you each of them in turn, and **Χρόνια πολλά** is the right thing to say.

**And the one piece of table etiquette that matters**: refusing food twice is expected and refusing it three times is accepted. **Φτάνει, ευχαριστώ** said once will be ignored, which is not rudeness — it is the form.

**Practice.** Name ten of these dishes aloud and say whether each is νηστίσιμο. Then say which three you have eaten and what you thought: **Έχω φάει μουσακά. Ήταν πολύ νόστιμος.** Then learn the four feast sweets with their seasons.
The kafeneio, properly:
Coffee in Greek life, which is an institution rather than a drink — and the vocabulary of the place where most of your parish conversations will happen.

**The places:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το καφενείο** | the traditional café: Greek coffee, tsipouro, backgammon, older men, no hurry |
| **η καφετέρια** | the modern one: freddo, laptops, younger people |
| **το ζαχαροπλαστείο** | the patisserie — sweets, and coffee |
| **το μπαρ** | the bar, evening |
| **το ουζερί / το τσιπουράδικο** | spirits with small plates |

**The coffees, in full:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ελληνικός** | Greek coffee, boiled in a briki, served with the grounds |
| **σκέτος / μέτριος / γλυκός** | no sugar / a little / sweet — the three ways |
| **φραπέ** | instant, shaken cold with ice |
| **φρέντο εσπρέσο** | cold espresso, shaken |
| **φρέντο καπουτσίνο** | the same, with cold milk foam |
| **εσπρέσο / καπουτσίνο** | hot, as elsewhere |
| **νες** | instant, hot |
| **διπλός** | double |
| **με λίγο γάλα** | with a little milk |

**φρέντο is what Greece actually drinks** — a cold espresso or cappuccino, shaken, year round — and ordering a **φρέντο καπουτσίνο μέτριο** is the most ordinary thing you can do in a Greek café.

**The social rules, which are the real content of this lesson:**

1. **A coffee is an hour.** Nobody drinks it and leaves. Sitting with one coffee for ninety minutes is normal and expected.
2. **Someone will pay for everyone.** The turn rotates; arguing about it is part of it, and insisting on paying your share every time marks you as foreign.
3. **Πάμε για καφέ** is an invitation to talk, and declining it needs a reason.
4. **Water comes with it**, free, always.
5. **You order, and then you order again.** Nobody is rushed and nobody rushes you.

**The phrases:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πάμε για καφέ;** | Shall we go for a coffee? |
| **Έλα να πιούμε έναν καφέ.** | Come and have a coffee. |
| **Εγώ κερνάω.** | My treat. |
| **Όχι, εγώ!** | No, me! — and you will have this argument |
| **Τι θα πάρεις;** | What will you have? |
| **Το ίδιο κι εγώ.** | The same for me. |
| **Ένα νερό ακόμα, παρακαλώ.** | Another water, please. |
| **Ήταν ωραία. Να το ξανακάνουμε.** | That was nice. Let's do it again. |

**Εγώ κερνάω — my treat — is worth having ready**, and offering it once in a while is how you take your turn without making a performance of it.

**The things people do there**: τάβλι (backgammon), cards, arguing about politics and football, and talking. A **καφενείο** in a village is the social centre, and in a parish the hall after the Liturgy works the same way.

**Practice.** Order three different coffees out loud. Then say the eight phrases five times each. Then invite someone for a coffee — in Greek, this week, for real.
Clothes:
What you wear, which comes up in shops, in conversation about the weather, and in the one Greek context where it matters more than in England: church.

**The clothes:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το πουκάμισο** | shirt | **το παντελόνι** | trousers |
| **η μπλούζα** | top, blouse | **το φόρεμα** | dress |
| **η φούστα** | skirt | **το κοστούμι** | suit |
| **το σακάκι** | jacket | **το παλτό** | overcoat |
| **το μπουφάν** | jacket, casual | **το πουλόβερ** | jumper |
| **η ζακέτα** | cardigan | **το μπλουζάκι** | t-shirt |
| **τα παπούτσια** | shoes | **οι κάλτσες** | socks |
| **τα εσώρουχα** | underwear | **η γραβάτα** | tie |
| **η ζώνη** | belt | **το καπέλο** | hat |
| **το μαντήλι** | handkerchief, headscarf | **τα γυαλιά** | glasses |
| **το ρολόι** | watch | **η τσάντα** | bag |
| **η ομπρέλα** | umbrella | **το μαγιό** | swimming costume |

**The verbs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **φοράω** | I wear — **Τι φοράς;** |
| **ντύνομαι** | I get dressed |
| **βγάζω** | I take off |
| **βάζω** | I put on |
| **αλλάζω** | I change |
| **μου πάει** | it suits me |
| **μου κάνει** | it fits me |
| **δοκιμάζω** | I try on |

**μου πάει and μου κάνει are the two to know**, and they are both in the stage 2 pattern of **μου αρέσει**: *it suits me*, *it fits me*, with the person in the genitive.

- **Μου πάει αυτό το χρώμα;** — Does this colour suit me?
- **Δεν μου κάνει.** — It does not fit me.

**Church dress, which is a real thing and worth asking about rather than guessing:** in a Greek parish, men wear trousers and a shirt with sleeves; women generally cover shoulders, and in monasteries skirts are expected and often provided at the door. Practice varies between a city parish and a monastery, and between Greece and the diaspora — and nobody will mind you asking.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι πρέπει να φορέσω;** | What should I wear? |
| **Είναι εντάξει αυτό;** | Is this all right? |
| **Χρειάζομαι σακάκι;** | Do I need a jacket? |
| **Στο μοναστήρι;** | At the monastery? |

**The weather connection**, since this is what you will mostly use these words for:

- **Κάνει κρύο, πάρε παλτό.** — It is cold, take a coat.
- **Βρέχει, πάρε ομπρέλα.** — It is raining, take an umbrella.
- **Κάνει ζέστη, μη βάλεις σακάκι.** — It is hot, do not put a jacket on.

**Practice.** Say what you are wearing, out loud, in four sentences. Then say what you will wear on Sunday. Then ask **Τι πρέπει να φορέσω;** about a monastery visit and answer it.
Shopping for clothes:
Sizes, trying things on, and the exchange — which uses the comparatives from stage 3 constantly.

**The shop words:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το μέγεθος** | size | **το νούμερο** | size (shoes), number |
| **το δοκιμαστήριο** | fitting room | **η ταμειακή** | the till |
| **η απόδειξη** | receipt | **η αλλαγή** | exchange |
| **η επιστροφή** | return | **η έκπτωση** | discount |
| **οι εκπτώσεις** | the sales | **η προσφορά** | offer |
| **το χρώμα** | colour | **το ύφασμα** | fabric |
| **βαμβακερό** | cotton | **μάλλινο** | woollen |
| **δερμάτινο** | leather | **μεταξωτό** | silk |

**The sizes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **μικρό, μέτριο, μεγάλο** | small, medium, large |
| **σαράντα, σαράντα δύο** | the number sizes — European |
| **πιο μεγάλο / πιο μικρό** | bigger / smaller |
| **Τι νούμερο φοράτε;** | What size do you take? |

**The exchange:**

— **Καλημέρα, μπορώ να βοηθήσω;**
— **Ψάχνω ένα πουκάμισο.**
— **Τι νούμερο φοράτε;**
— **Σαράντα δύο. Έχετε σε μπλε;**
— **Ορίστε. Θέλετε να το δοκιμάσετε;**
— **Ναι. Πού είναι το δοκιμαστήριο;**
— **Εκεί δεξιά.**

**Afterwards:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μου κάνει.** | It fits. |
| **Είναι λίγο μικρό.** | It is a bit small. |
| **Έχετε πιο μεγάλο;** | Do you have a bigger one? |
| **Έχετε άλλο χρώμα;** | Do you have another colour? |
| **Πόσο κάνει;** | How much is it? |
| **Είναι ακριβό.** | It is expensive. |
| **Θα το πάρω.** | I will take it. |
| **Θα το σκεφτώ.** | I will think about it. |
| **Μπορώ να το αλλάξω;** | Can I exchange it? |
| **Κρατάω την απόδειξη.** | I will keep the receipt. |

**Θα το σκεφτώ is the polite exit** — *I will think about it* — and it is understood exactly as in English.

**The grammar in use here**, which is the point of the lesson: **πιο μεγάλο** and **πιο μικρό** are stage 3's comparatives; **μου κάνει** is the **μου αρέσει** pattern; **θα το πάρω** and **θα το σκεφτώ** are stage 4's future with the pronoun in front. Nothing new, all of it working.

**The Greek shopping facts**: the sales — **οι εκπτώσεις** — are fixed by law to two periods a year, winter and summer; small shops close in the afternoon; and bargaining is not done in shops but is normal at a market stall or for something large.

**Practice.** Do the whole exchange aloud, both parts. Then try on five imaginary things, each with a different problem — too small, wrong colour, too expensive. Then say **Θα το σκεφτώ** and leave.
The body:
The parts of the body, which you need for the doctor, for the pharmacy, and for the enormous number of Greek idioms built on them.

**The head and face:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το κεφάλι** | head | **τα μαλλιά** | hair |
| **το πρόσωπο** | face | **το μάτι / τα μάτια** | eye / eyes |
| **η μύτη** | nose | **το στόμα** | mouth |
| **το αυτί / τα αυτιά** | ear / ears | **το δόντι / τα δόντια** | tooth / teeth |
| **η γλώσσα** | tongue — and *language* | **ο λαιμός** | throat, neck |
| **το μέτωπο** | forehead | **το πιγούνι** | chin |

**The body:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το σώμα** | body | **ο ώμος** | shoulder |
| **το χέρι / τα χέρια** | hand, arm | **το δάχτυλο** | finger, toe |
| **η πλάτη** | back | **το στήθος** | chest |
| **η κοιλιά** | stomach, belly | **το στομάχι** | stomach (organ) |
| **το πόδι / τα πόδια** | foot, leg | **το γόνατο** | knee |
| **ο αγκώνας** | elbow | **ο καρπός** | wrist |
| **η καρδιά** | heart | **το αίμα** | blood |
| **το κόκαλο** | bone | **ο μυς** | muscle |
| **το δέρμα** | skin | **ο εγκέφαλος** | brain |

**Note that χέρι covers hand and arm, and πόδι covers foot and leg** — Greek does not split them the way English does, and **το χέρι μου** is whichever part is relevant.

**η γλώσσα means both tongue and language**, which is why **τα ελληνικά** is also **η ελληνική γλώσσα**.

**Saying what hurts** — and the construction is the **μου αρέσει** pattern again:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Με πονάει το κεφάλι.** | My head hurts. |
| **Μου πονάει το στομάχι.** | My stomach hurts. |
| **Πονάω.** | I am in pain. |
| **Πού σε πονάει;** | Where does it hurt? |
| **Έχω πονοκέφαλο.** | I have a headache. |
| **Έχω πυρετό.** | I have a temperature. |
| **Έχω βήχα.** | I have a cough. |
| **Είμαι κρυωμένος.** | I have a cold. |

**Both με πονάει and μου πονάει are heard**, with the accusative slightly more common in the south and the genitive in the north. Either is understood everywhere.

**The idioms, which are everywhere in speech:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μου έφαγε το κεφάλι.** | He drove me mad. (*ate my head*) |
| **Έχει μάτια πίσω του.** | He has eyes behind him. |
| **Με όλη μου την καρδιά.** | With all my heart. |
| **Βάζω το χέρι μου στο φωτιά.** | I would swear to it. |
| **Από το στόμα σου και στον Θεό.** | From your mouth to God's ear. |
| **Καλή σου καρδιά.** | Bless your kind heart. |

**That last pair are church-adjacent and said constantly**, and both are worth having.

**Practice.** Name twenty parts of the body aloud, with articles. Then say five things that hurt, using both constructions. Then learn **Από το στόμα σου και στον Θεό** and use it the next time someone wishes you something good.
At the doctor:
The conversation you hope not to have and should be able to have. It is also one of the most formulaic in the language, which makes it learnable in advance.

**Getting seen:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Θέλω να δω έναν γιατρό.** | I want to see a doctor. |
| **Μπορώ να κλείσω ραντεβού;** | Can I make an appointment? |
| **Είναι επείγον.** | It is urgent. |
| **Πού είναι το νοσοκομείο;** | Where is the hospital? |
| **Τα επείγοντα** | A&E, the emergency department |
| **Καλέστε ασθενοφόρο!** | Call an ambulance! |

**The symptoms:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν αισθάνομαι καλά.** | I do not feel well. |
| **Με πονάει εδώ.** | It hurts here. |
| **Έχω πυρετό.** | I have a fever. |
| **Έχω ζαλάδα.** | I feel dizzy. |
| **Έχω ναυτία.** | I feel sick. |
| **Δεν μπορώ να κοιμηθώ.** | I cannot sleep. |
| **Έχω αλλεργία στο…** | I am allergic to… |
| **Παίρνω φάρμακα για…** | I take medication for… |
| **Έσπασα το χέρι μου.** | I have broken my arm. |
| **Έπεσα.** | I fell. |
| **Εδώ και τρεις μέρες.** | For three days now. |

**Εδώ και τρεις μέρες** is the standard way to say *for three days now* — literally *here and three days* — and it is what the doctor is asking for.

**What the doctor says:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πού σας πονάει;** | Where does it hurt? |
| **Από πότε;** | Since when? |
| **Ανοίξτε το στόμα σας.** | Open your mouth. |
| **Πάρτε βαθιά ανάσα.** | Take a deep breath. |
| **Ξαπλώστε εδώ.** | Lie down here. |
| **Έχετε πυρετό;** | Do you have a temperature? |
| **Θα σας γράψω αντιβίωση.** | I will prescribe you antibiotics. |
| **Πάρτε ένα χάπι τρεις φορές την ημέρα.** | Take one tablet three times a day. |
| **Να ξεκουραστείτε.** | Rest. |
| **Θα περάσει.** | It will pass. |

**Those are all in the polite plural**, which is what a doctor uses — and recognising the imperative plural (**ανοίξτε, πάρτε, ξαπλώστε**) is stage 4's grammar in a real setting.

**The vocabulary of treatment:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το φάρμακο** | medicine | **το χάπι** | tablet |
| **η συνταγή** | prescription | **η αντιβίωση** | antibiotics |
| **η ένεση** | injection | **η εξέταση** | test, examination |
| **η αιματολογική** | blood test | **η ακτινογραφία** | X-ray |
| **ο γιατρός** | doctor | **η νοσοκόμα** | nurse |
| **ο οδοντίατρος** | dentist | **το ασθενοφόρο** | ambulance |
| **η ασφάλεια** | insurance | **το ΑΜΚΑ** | the Greek social-security number |

**The practical note for a visitor**: EU and UK visitors use the appropriate health card at state facilities; private doctors are paid cash and give a receipt; and pharmacies handle a great deal that would need an appointment elsewhere — which is the next lesson.

**Practice.** Say the eleven symptom sentences aloud. Then play both parts of a consultation: you have had a sore throat and a temperature for three days. Then learn **Θα περάσει** and say it to yourself.
At the pharmacy:
The Greek pharmacy does far more than the English one, which makes this a short lesson with a high return.

**Why it matters.** A Greek **φαρμακείο** will advise on symptoms, dispense a great many things without a prescription, take your blood pressure, and tell you whether you need a doctor at all. For minor problems it is the first stop rather than the last.

**The words:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το φαρμακείο** | pharmacy | **ο φαρμακοποιός** | pharmacist |
| **το φάρμακο** | medicine | **η συνταγή** | prescription |
| **το χάπι** | tablet | **το σιρόπι** | syrup |
| **η αλοιφή** | ointment | **οι σταγόνες** | drops |
| **το σπρέι** | spray | **ο επίδεσμος** | bandage |
| **το τσιρότο** | plaster | **το αντισηπτικό** | antiseptic |
| **οι βιταμίνες** | vitamins | **το αντιηλιακό** | sun cream |
| **το παυσίπονο** | painkiller | **το αντιπυρετικό** | something for fever |

**The asking:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Έχετε κάτι για τον πονοκέφαλο;** | Do you have something for a headache? |
| **Έχετε κάτι για τον βήχα;** | …for a cough? |
| **Έχετε κάτι για το στομάχι;** | …for an upset stomach? |
| **Χρειάζομαι συνταγή;** | Do I need a prescription? |
| **Είμαι αλλεργικός στην πενικιλίνη.** | I am allergic to penicillin. |
| **Πόσα χάπια την ημέρα;** | How many tablets a day? |
| **Πριν ή μετά το φαγητό;** | Before or after food? |
| **Έχει παρενέργειες;** | Does it have side effects? |

**Έχετε κάτι για…; is the whole lesson** — one sentence, with the complaint on the end, and it gets you served anywhere.

**What the pharmacist says:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πάρτε ένα το πρωί και ένα το βράδυ.** | Take one in the morning and one at night. |
| **Μετά το φαγητό.** | After food. |
| **Για πέντε μέρες.** | For five days. |
| **Αν δεν περάσει, πηγαίνετε σε γιατρό.** | If it does not pass, go to a doctor. |
| **Χωρίς συνταγή δεν μπορώ.** | Without a prescription I cannot. |

**The practical details**: pharmacies close in the afternoon and at weekends, but there is always a **διανυκτερεύον φαρμακείο** — a duty pharmacy open overnight — and the rota is posted on every pharmacy door and online. The word is worth recognising on a notice.

**The green cross** is the sign, and **ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΙΟ** in capitals is one of the first words you learned to read, back in stage 1.

**Practice.** Say the eight questions aloud. Then do the exchange for a cough, a headache and a stomach upset, both parts. Then read the duty-pharmacy notice on any Greek pharmacy's website and find the word **διανυκτερεύον**.
Money and the bank:
Paying, withdrawing, and the handful of sentences that get you through a bank or a cash machine.

**The words:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **τα λεφτά / τα χρήματα** | money | **τα μετρητά** | cash |
| **η κάρτα** | card | **το ΑΤΜ** | cash machine |
| **η τράπεζα** | bank | **ο λογαριασμός** | account — and *the bill* |
| **η κατάθεση** | deposit | **η ανάληψη** | withdrawal |
| **το επιτόκιο** | interest rate | **η χρέωση** | charge |
| **το νόμισμα** | coin, currency | **το χαρτονόμισμα** | banknote |
| **τα ψιλά** | small change | **η ισοτιμία** | exchange rate |
| **η απόδειξη** | receipt | **ο κωδικός / το PIN** | code, PIN |

**λογαριασμός is both a bank account and a restaurant bill**, which is worth not confusing: **τον λογαριασμό, παρακαλώ** in a taverna, **ο λογαριασμός μου** at the bank.

**Paying:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Με κάρτα ή με μετρητά;** | Card or cash? |
| **Μπορώ με κάρτα;** | Can I pay by card? |
| **Δεν έχω ψιλά.** | I do not have change. |
| **Έχετε να μου χαλάσετε πενήντα;** | Can you break a fifty for me? |
| **Κρατήστε τα ρέστα.** | Keep the change. |
| **Μου δίνετε απόδειξη;** | Could you give me a receipt? |

**At the bank:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Θέλω να κάνω ανάληψη.** | I want to make a withdrawal. |
| **Θέλω να ανοίξω λογαριασμό.** | I want to open an account. |
| **Ποια είναι η ισοτιμία;** | What is the exchange rate? |
| **Υπάρχει χρέωση;** | Is there a charge? |
| **Το ΑΤΜ δεν δουλεύει.** | The cash machine is not working. |
| **Πόσο είναι η προμήθεια;** | How much is the commission? |

**At the cash machine**, which is reading practice:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Εισάγετε την κάρτα σας** | insert your card |
| **Πληκτρολογήστε τον κωδικό σας** | enter your PIN |
| **Ανάληψη / Κατάθεση / Υπόλοιπο** | withdrawal / deposit / balance |
| **Επιλέξτε ποσό** | select an amount |
| **Θέλετε απόδειξη;** | do you want a receipt? |
| **Παρακαλώ περιμένετε** | please wait |
| **Πάρτε την κάρτα σας** | take your card |

**All of those are imperative plurals** — stage 4's grammar, in the most practical possible setting.

**The money facts**: Greece uses the euro; cash is still common for small amounts and in villages; card is universal in cities; and receipts matter, because tax inspection is a real thing and a shop will press one on you.

**Practice.** Say the six paying sentences and the six bank sentences aloud. Then read the seven cash-machine instructions and say what each one is telling you to do. Then say **Δεν έχω ψιλά** and **Κρατήστε τα ρέστα** until both are automatic.
The post office and deliveries:
Sending and receiving things, which turns up more often than you expect — and the vocabulary of forms, which is useful well beyond the post office.

**The places:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **τα ΕΛΤΑ** | the Greek post office |
| **το ταχυδρομείο** | the post office (the word) |
| **η κούριερ** | the courier company |
| **το γραμματοκιβώτιο** | letterbox |
| **το πρακτορείο** | the agency, depot |

**The things:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το γράμμα** | letter | **ο φάκελος** | envelope |
| **το γραμματόσημο** | stamp | **το πακέτο** | parcel |
| **το κουτί** | box | **η κάρτα** | postcard |
| **το βάρος** | weight | **η διεύθυνση** | address |
| **ο ταχυδρομικός κώδικας** | postcode | **ο παραλήπτης** | recipient |
| **ο αποστολέας** | sender | **η παράδοση** | delivery |
| **συστημένο** | registered | **εξπρές** | express |

**The sentences:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Θέλω να στείλω ένα γράμμα στην Αγγλία.** | I want to send a letter to England. |
| **Πόσο κάνει;** | How much is it? |
| **Πόσες μέρες κάνει;** | How many days does it take? |
| **Θέλω συστημένο.** | I want it registered. |
| **Έχετε γραμματόσημα;** | Do you have stamps? |
| **Περιμένω ένα πακέτο.** | I am expecting a parcel. |
| **Δεν ήρθε ακόμα.** | It has not arrived yet. |
| **Πού μπορώ να το παραλάβω;** | Where can I collect it? |

**Filling in a form**, which is the transferable part of this lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Όνομα** | first name |
| **Επώνυμο** | surname |
| **Πατρώνυμο** | father's name — asked for constantly in Greece |
| **Διεύθυνση** | address |
| **Οδός / Αριθμός** | street / number |
| **Τηλέφωνο** | telephone |
| **Ημερομηνία** | date |
| **Υπογραφή** | signature |
| **Συμπληρώστε** | fill in |
| **Με κεφαλαία** | in capitals |

**Πατρώνυμο is the one that surprises people**: Greek official forms ask for your father's name as a matter of course, because it is part of how a person is identified in the registry.

**Υπογραφή — signature — is literally *under-writing***, from **υπογράφω**, which stage 4's prefix lesson built.

**Practice.** Say the eight post-office sentences aloud. Then fill in an imaginary form out loud, naming each field. Then send a parcel to England and ask how long it takes, both parts.
The telephone:
Calling, answering and messaging — the hardest everyday Greek, because there is no face and no context.

**Answering:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ναι;** | Yes? — the commonest answer |
| **Παρακαλώ;** | Hello? |
| **Ορίστε;** | Hello? / Yes? |
| **Λέγετε.** | Speak. — slightly formal |
| **Εμπρός;** | Hello? — older |

**Παρακαλώ and Ορίστε as phone answers** are the two to recognise; **Ναι;** is what you will mostly hear.

**Calling:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γεια σας, είμαι ο…** | Hello, this is… |
| **Μπορώ να μιλήσω με τον κύριο…;** | May I speak to Mr…? |
| **Είναι εκεί ο Γιώργος;** | Is George there? |
| **Σας ενοχλώ;** | Am I disturbing you? |
| **Σας παίρνω για…** | I am calling about… |
| **Θα σε πάρω αργότερα.** | I will call you later. |
| **Σε παίρνω εγώ.** | I'll call you. |

**παίρνω τηλέφωνο** — literally *I take telephone* — is the everyday verb for calling, alongside **τηλεφωνώ**.

**When it goes wrong**, which on the phone it will:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν σας ακούω καλά.** | I cannot hear you well. |
| **Μπορείτε να μιλάτε πιο αργά;** | Could you speak more slowly? |
| **Μπορείτε να το επαναλάβετε;** | Could you repeat that? |
| **Κόπηκε η γραμμή.** | The line was cut off. |
| **Έχω κακό σήμα.** | I have a bad signal. |
| **Λάθος αριθμός.** | Wrong number. |
| **Θα σας ξαναπάρω.** | I will call you back. |

**Ending:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ευχαριστώ, γεια σας.** | Thank you, goodbye. |
| **Τα λέμε.** | See you / talk soon. |
| **Καλή συνέχεια.** | Have a good rest of the day. |
| **Φιλιά.** | Kisses — to family and close friends |
| **Να 'σαι καλά.** | Be well. |

**Τα λέμε** is the standard sign-off between friends — *we'll talk* — and it is as common as *bye*.

**Messaging**, which is where you will read the most Greek:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το μήνυμα** | message |
| **Θα σου στείλω μήνυμα.** | I will text you. |
| **Πήρες το μήνυμά μου;** | Did you get my message? |
| **ΟΚ / Εντάξει** | okay |
| **Τπτ** | τίποτα — nothing |
| **Τι κανς;** | τι κάνεις — abbreviated |
| **Καλημ** | καλημέρα |

**And Greeklish**, from stage 1's typing lesson: **kalimera, ti kaneis, tha se paro** — Latin letters for Greek words, used constantly in messages. You should read it and should not write the curriculum's exercises in it.

**The phone is the hardest listening there is** and the best practice: no lips, no gestures, compressed audio. Expect to understand less on the phone than in person for a long time, and say **Δεν σας ακούω καλά** without embarrassment.

**Practice.** Say the five answers and the seven calling phrases aloud. Then do a whole call, both parts: you ring the church to ask what time the Liturgy is on Sunday. Then say **Τα λέμε** and **Να 'σαι καλά**.
Making an appointment:
Fixing a time with someone, which needs the future, the days and the times — all of which you have — and a handful of set phrases.

**Asking:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μπορώ να κλείσω ραντεβού;** | Can I make an appointment? |
| **Πότε μπορείτε;** | When can you? |
| **Τι ώρα σας βολεύει;** | What time suits you? |
| **Είστε ελεύθερος την Τρίτη;** | Are you free on Tuesday? |
| **Σας βολεύει στις πέντε;** | Does five suit you? |
| **Μπορούμε να το κάνουμε αύριο;** | Can we do it tomorrow? |

**βολεύει is the useful verb**: *it suits, it is convenient*, in the **μου αρέσει** pattern — **Μου βολεύει**, **Δεν μου βολεύει**.

**Answering:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ναι, βεβαίως.** | Yes, certainly. |
| **Μου βολεύει.** | That suits me. |
| **Δεν μπορώ τότε.** | I cannot then. |
| **Έχω κάτι άλλο.** | I have something else on. |
| **Λίγο αργότερα;** | A bit later? |
| **Ας το κάνουμε Πέμπτη.** | Let's make it Thursday. |
| **Εντάξει, κανονίστηκε.** | All right, it is settled. |
| **Τα κανονίζουμε.** | We will sort it out. |

**κανονίζω** — to arrange — and **κανονίστηκε** — *it's arranged* — are the words for the whole business. **Τα κανονίζουμε** is the vaguer, very Greek version: *we'll work it out*, said when nothing has been fixed.

**Changing and cancelling:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μπορούμε να το αλλάξουμε;** | Can we change it? |
| **Θα αργήσω λίγο.** | I will be a bit late. |
| **Συγγνώμη, δεν μπορώ να έρθω.** | Sorry, I cannot come. |
| **Ας το αναβάλουμε.** | Let's postpone it. |
| **Την άλλη βδομάδα;** | Next week? |

**Θα αργήσω is worth having ready**, because you will need it — and the Greek attitude to time is more elastic than the English one, so a text saying it is normal rather than apologetic.

**The time-and-day kit, from stage 2 and 3:**

- **την Τρίτη στις πέντε** — on Tuesday at five
- **αύριο το πρωί** — tomorrow morning
- **μεθαύριο** — the day after tomorrow
- **την άλλη βδομάδα** — next week
- **στις 14 του μηνός** — on the 14th
- **το απόγευμα** — in the afternoon

**And the Greek timekeeping facts, honestly**: social arrangements are approximate, professional ones are kept, and **θα τα πούμε** or **τα κανονίζουμε** means *no date has been set* even when it sounds like a plan. If a time matters, fix it and confirm it by message.

**Practice.** Say the six asking and eight answering phrases aloud. Then arrange a coffee for next week, both parts, including one change of day. Then send yourself a message saying **Θα αργήσω δέκα λεπτά**.
Travel: buses, trains and boats:
Getting around Greece, which is mostly buses and boats — and the vocabulary of timetables, which is reading practice.

**The transport:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το λεωφορείο** | bus | **το ΚΤΕΛ** | the intercity bus network |
| **το τρένο** | train | **το μετρό** | metro |
| **το τραμ** | tram | **το τρόλεϊ** | trolleybus |
| **το ταξί** | taxi | **το πλοίο** | ship, ferry |
| **το δελφίνι / το ταχύπλοο** | hydrofoil, fast boat | **το αεροπλάνο** | plane |
| **το αυτοκίνητο** | car | **η μοτοσικλέτα** | motorbike |

**The places and things:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ο σταθμός** | station | **η στάση** | stop |
| **η αφετηρία** | terminus, departure point | **το λιμάνι** | port |
| **το εισιτήριο** | ticket | **το εκδοτήριο** | ticket office |
| **η αποσκευή / οι βαλίτσες** | luggage / suitcases | **η θέση** | seat |
| **η αναχώρηση** | departure | **η άφιξη** | arrival |
| **η καθυστέρηση** | delay | **το δρομολόγιο** | route, timetable |
| **με επιστροφή** | return | **απλή μετάβαση** | one way |

**αναχωρήσεις and αφίξεις are the two words on every board** — departures and arrivals — and both are plurals of nouns you can now parse.

**Buying and asking:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ένα εισιτήριο για τη Θεσσαλονίκη, παρακαλώ.** | One ticket to Thessaloniki, please. |
| **Με επιστροφή.** | Return. |
| **Τι ώρα φεύγει το επόμενο;** | What time does the next one leave? |
| **Από πού φεύγει;** | Where does it leave from? |
| **Πόση ώρα κάνει;** | How long does it take? |
| **Σταματάει στο…;** | Does it stop at…? |
| **Έχει καθυστέρηση;** | Is it delayed? |
| **Πού είναι η στάση;** | Where is the stop? |
| **Μου λέτε πού να κατεβώ;** | Could you tell me where to get off? |

**Μου λέτε πού να κατεβώ; is the sentence to have** on a bus in a place you do not know, and people will not only tell you, they will remind you when you get there.

**In a taxi:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Στο κέντρο, παρακαλώ.** | To the centre, please. |
| **Στη διεύθυνση αυτή.** | To this address. |
| **Πόσο θα κάνει περίπου;** | Roughly how much will it be? |
| **Βάλτε το ταξίμετρο, παρακαλώ.** | Put the meter on, please. |
| **Εδώ είναι καλά.** | Here is fine. |
| **Κρατήστε τα ρέστα.** | Keep the change. |

**The boat vocabulary, for the islands:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το κατάστρωμα** | deck |
| **η καμπίνα** | cabin |
| **αεροπορικό κάθισμα** | airline-type seat |
| **το γκαράζ** | the car deck |
| **απαγορεύεται λόγω καιρού** | cancelled because of the weather |

**That last one is a real and frequent announcement** — **απαγορεύτηκε ο απόπλους** — the sailing is prohibited because of wind. Any island plan in Greece has that contingency in it.

**Practice.** Say the nine travel sentences aloud. Then buy a return ticket to Thessaloniki and ask three questions about the journey, both parts. Then read a Greek bus or ferry timetable online and find **αναχώρηση**, **άφιξη** and **καθυστέρηση**.
At the airport:
A short lesson, because airports are signposted in English too — but the words are worth having, and the announcements are good listening practice.

**The signs:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **αναχωρήσεις** | departures | **αφίξεις** | arrivals |
| **έλεγχος εισιτηρίων** | check-in | **παραλαβή αποσκευών** | baggage reclaim |
| **έλεγχος ασφαλείας** | security | **έλεγχος διαβατηρίων** | passport control |
| **πύλη** | gate | **επιβίβαση** | boarding |
| **καθυστέρηση** | delay | **ακυρώθηκε** | cancelled |
| **εσωτερικού / εξωτερικού** | domestic / international | **τελωνείο** | customs |
| **έξοδος** | exit | **αφορολόγητα** | duty-free |

**εσωτερικού and εξωτερικού are genitives** — *of the interior*, *of the exterior* — which is stage 3's case in a departure hall.

**The sentences:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πού είναι ο έλεγχος εισιτηρίων για την Αθήνα;** | Where is check-in for Athens? |
| **Έχω μία βαλίτσα για παράδοση.** | I have one bag to check in. |
| **Μόνο χειραποσκευή.** | Only hand luggage. |
| **Από ποια πύλη;** | From which gate? |
| **Τι ώρα είναι η επιβίβαση;** | What time is boarding? |
| **Η πτήση έχει καθυστέρηση;** | Is the flight delayed? |
| **Χάθηκε η βαλίτσα μου.** | My suitcase is lost. |
| **Πού είναι το ταξί;** | Where are the taxis? |

**The announcements**, which are worth deliberately listening to because they are slow, repeated and formulaic:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Οι επιβάτες της πτήσης… παρακαλούνται να…** | Passengers on flight… are requested to… |
| **…να προσέλθουν στην πύλη…** | …to proceed to gate… |
| **Τελευταία κλήση** | final call |
| **Η πτήση… αναχωρεί από την πύλη…** | flight… departs from gate… |

**παρακαλούνται is a mediopassive** — *they are requested* — and **να προσέλθουν** is **να** with a perfective. The whole announcement is stage 4's grammar, delivered slowly over a loudspeaker, which makes it the easiest formal Greek you will ever hear.

**At passport control:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Το διαβατήριό σας.** | Your passport. |
| **Για πόσες μέρες;** | For how many days? |
| **Για διακοπές ή για δουλειά;** | Holiday or business? |
| **Πού θα μείνετε;** | Where will you stay? |
| **Καλή διαμονή.** | Enjoy your stay. |

**Practice.** Read the fourteen signs aloud. Then say the eight sentences. Then find a recording of a Greek airport announcement — they are on YouTube — and listen for **παρακαλούνται** and **πύλη**.
Booking a room:
Staying somewhere, which is a short script and one you will use on any trip to Greece — including the one you will eventually make for a feast.

**The places:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το ξενοδοχείο** | hotel |
| **το δωμάτιο** | room |
| **τα ενοικιαζόμενα δωμάτια** | rooms to rent — the cheap, common option |
| **το διαμέρισμα** | apartment |
| **ο ξενώνας** | guesthouse |
| **ο ξενώνας μονής** | monastery guesthouse — and relevant to you |

**The words:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **μονόκλινο** | single room | **δίκλινο** | double |
| **τρίκλινο** | triple | **με διπλό κρεβάτι** | with a double bed |
| **με μπάνιο** | with a bathroom | **με πρωινό** | with breakfast |
| **με θέα** | with a view | **η κλιματιστικό** | air conditioning — **το** κλιματιστικό |
| **η υποδοχή / η ρεσεψιόν** | reception | **το κλειδί** | key |
| **η κράτηση** | booking | **η διαμονή** | stay |

**μονόκλινο, δίκλινο, τρίκλινο are built from the numbers** — *one-bed*, *two-bed*, *three-bed* — which is stage 3's numerals making vocabulary.

**The script:**

— **Καλησπέρα. Έχετε δωμάτια;**
— **Για πόσες νύχτες;**
— **Για τρεις. Ένα δίκλινο, παρακαλώ.**
— **Με πρωινό;**
— **Ναι. Πόσο κάνει τη βραδιά;**
— **Εξήντα ευρώ.**
— **Εντάξει, θα το πάρω. Έχω κάνει κράτηση στο όνομα…**

**The questions once you are in:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι ώρα είναι το πρωινό;** | What time is breakfast? |
| **Υπάρχει wi-fi;** | Is there wi-fi? |
| **Ποιος είναι ο κωδικός;** | What is the password? |
| **Μπορώ να αφήσω τις βαλίτσες;** | Can I leave my bags? |
| **Τι ώρα πρέπει να φύγουμε;** | What time is checkout? |
| **Δεν δουλεύει το κλιματιστικό.** | The air conditioning is not working. |
| **Έχετε άλλο δωμάτιο;** | Do you have another room? |
| **Πού είναι η πλησιέστερη εκκλησία;** | Where is the nearest church? |

**That last question is worth having** and it will be answered with enthusiasm and directions.

**Monastery guesthouses** are a particular case and worth knowing about: many monasteries offer **φιλοξενία** — hospitality — for a night or two, free or for a donation, with the expectation that you attend the services. The words to know: **φιλοξενία** (hospitality), **ο αρχοντάρης** (the guestmaster), **το κελί** (the cell, i.e. room), and **Έχετε θέση για ένα βράδυ;** — do you have room for a night?

**φιλοξενία is one of the great Greek words** — *stranger-loving* — and the concept is taken seriously enough that it will be extended to you repeatedly.

**Practice.** Do the booking script aloud, both parts. Then ask the eight in-room questions. Then say **Έχετε θέση για ένα βράδυ;** and **Πού είναι η πλησιέστερη εκκλησία;**
Directions, in full:
Asking the way and understanding the answer — and the second half is the hard part, because Greeks give directions fast and with their hands.

**Asking:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Συγγνώμη, πού είναι…;** | Excuse me, where is…? |
| **Πώς πάω στο…;** | How do I get to…? |
| **Είναι μακριά;** | Is it far? |
| **Μπορείτε να μου δείξετε στον χάρτη;** | Could you show me on the map? |
| **Είμαι χαμένος.** | I am lost. |
| **Ψάχνω την οδό…** | I am looking for … Street. |
| **Είναι εδώ κοντά;** | Is it near here? |
| **Πόσο θέλει με τα πόδια;** | How long does it take on foot? |

**Συγγνώμη first, always** — it is the opener for stopping a stranger, and it does the work of *excuse me*, *sorry* and *pardon*.

**The answers, which is what to practise understanding:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ευθεία.** | Straight on. |
| **Πηγαίνετε ευθεία και μετά δεξιά.** | Go straight on and then right. |
| **Στρίψτε αριστερά.** | Turn left. |
| **Στο πρώτο στενό.** | At the first side street. |
| **Στα φανάρια.** | At the traffic lights. |
| **Μετά την πλατεία.** | After the square. |
| **Απέναντι από την εκκλησία.** | Opposite the church. |
| **Δίπλα στο φαρμακείο.** | Next to the pharmacy. |
| **Στη γωνία.** | On the corner. |
| **Δύο δρόμους πιο κάτω.** | Two streets further down. |
| **Θα το δείτε.** | You will see it. |
| **Είναι πέντε λεπτά.** | It is five minutes. |
| **Πάρτε το λεωφορείο νούμερο…** | Take the number … bus. |

**Θα το δείτε is the standard Greek ending** to a set of directions and means *you cannot miss it*, which is sometimes true.

**The landmarks Greeks use:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **η εκκλησία** | the church | **η πλατεία** | the square |
| **τα φανάρια** | the lights | **το περίπτερο** | the kiosk |
| **η στάση** | the bus stop | **το φαρμακείο** | the pharmacy |
| **η τράπεζα** | the bank | **το σχολείο** | the school |
| **η παραλία** | the seafront | **ο πλατανός** | the plane tree — in a village, genuinely |

**The church is the commonest landmark in Greece**, and in a village it is the one everybody knows — which happens to be convenient for you.

**The survival moves when you lose the answer**, which you will:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πιο αργά, παρακαλώ.** | More slowly, please. |
| **Αριστερά ή δεξιά;** | Left or right? |
| **Μπορείτε να μου το δείξετε;** | Can you show me? |
| **Ευχαριστώ πολύ!** | Thank you very much! |

**And the cultural note**: a Greek asked for directions will often walk you there, or at least to the corner, and will certainly keep talking. Letting that happen is the fastest listening practice available.

**Practice.** Ask the way to five places out loud. Then give the thirteen answers aloud until you can follow them at speed. Then get someone to give you directions in Greek — or play a recording — and draw the route.
The city and its services:
The places you need to name, and the offices you may have to deal with — which is also the vocabulary of every local notice.

**Around town:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το κέντρο** | the centre | **η πλατεία** | square |
| **η αγορά** | market | **η λαϊκή** | the weekly street market |
| **το περίπτερο** | kiosk | **το φαρμακείο** | pharmacy |
| **η τράπεζα** | bank | **το ταχυδρομείο** | post office |
| **το νοσοκομείο** | hospital | **το κέντρο υγείας** | health centre |
| **η αστυνομία** | police | **η πυροσβεστική** | fire brigade |
| **το δημαρχείο** | town hall | **η βιβλιοθήκη** | library |
| **το μουσείο** | museum | **το θέατρο** | theatre |
| **το γυμναστήριο** | gym | **το γήπεδο** | stadium, pitch |
| **το σχολείο** | school | **το πανεπιστήμιο** | university |
| **η εκκλησία** | church | **το κοιμητήριο** | cemetery |
| **το μοναστήρι** | monastery | **το παρεκκλήσι** | chapel |

**η λαϊκή is the weekly market** — *the people's* — and it is where Greeks buy fruit and vegetables. Every neighbourhood has a day, and going is both shopping and listening practice.

**The offices and their words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **η ΔΟΥ / η εφορία** | the tax office |
| **το ΚΕΠ** | the citizens' service centre — where paperwork happens |
| **το ΙΚΑ / ο ΕΦΚΑ** | social insurance |
| **η άδεια** | permit, licence — and *leave* |
| **το πιστοποιητικό** | certificate |
| **η βεβαίωση** | confirmation, attestation |
| **η αίτηση** | application |
| **η ταυτότητα** | identity card |
| **ο ΑΦΜ** | tax number |
| **το ΑΜΚΑ** | social security number |

**ΚΕΠ, ΑΦΜ and ΑΜΚΑ are the three acronyms** anyone dealing with Greek officialdom learns first. They are also good examples of why reading capitals matters.

**Bureaucratic sentences, which are formulaic:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι χαρτιά χρειάζομαι;** | What papers do I need? |
| **Πού πρέπει να πάω;** | Where do I have to go? |
| **Μπορώ να το κάνω online;** | Can I do it online? |
| **Πόσο θα πάρει;** | How long will it take? |
| **Υπάρχει ουρά;** | Is there a queue? |
| **Είναι ανοιχτά το απόγευμα;** | Are they open in the afternoon? |

**τα χαρτιά** — *the papers* — is the word for documents in general, and **Θέλει χαρτιά** is the standard Greek summary of any official process.

**The opening hours fact**: public offices work mornings, shops close in the afternoon and reopen in the evening on some days, and everything closes on Sunday. The useful question is **Τι ώρες είστε ανοιχτά;**

**Practice.** Name fifteen places in your own town, in Greek, out loud. Then say the six bureaucratic sentences. Then look up a Greek **ΚΕΠ** page online and read three lines of it aloud.
Work and jobs:
What you do, which is the third question anyone asks after where you are from and whether you have children.

**The jobs:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ο δάσκαλος / η δασκάλα** | primary teacher | **ο καθηγητής** | teacher, professor |
| **ο γιατρός** | doctor | **η νοσοκόμα** | nurse |
| **ο δικηγόρος** | lawyer | **ο μηχανικός** | engineer |
| **ο προγραμματιστής** | programmer | **ο λογιστής** | accountant |
| **ο υπάλληλος** | employee, clerk | **ο οδηγός** | driver |
| **ο μάγειρας** | cook | **ο σερβιτόρος** | waiter |
| **ο ηλεκτρολόγος** | electrician | **ο υδραυλικός** | plumber |
| **ο αγρότης** | farmer | **ο ψαράς** | fisherman |
| **ο επιχειρηματίας** | businessman | **ο συνταξιούχος** | pensioner |
| **ο φοιτητής** | university student | **ο άνεργος** | unemployed |
| **ο ιερέας** | priest | **ο στρατιωτικός** | soldier |

**The feminine forms vary**: **η δασκάλα, η γιατρός** (unchanged, or **η γιατρίνα** informally), **η δικηγόρος**, **η καθηγήτρια**, **η μάγειρας → η μαγείρισσα**. Modern usage is in flux and the masculine form with a feminine article — **η γιατρός** — is standard and safe.

**The sentences:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι δουλειά κάνεις;** | What work do you do? |
| **Είμαι δάσκαλος.** | I am a teacher. — no article, as stage 2 said |
| **Δουλεύω σε μια εταιρεία.** | I work for a company. |
| **Δουλεύω από το σπίτι.** | I work from home. |
| **Δουλεύω με υπολογιστές.** | I work with computers. |
| **Έχω τη δική μου επιχείρηση.** | I have my own business. |
| **Είμαι συνταξιούχος.** | I am retired. |
| **Ψάχνω δουλειά.** | I am looking for work. |

**The workplace words:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **η δουλειά** | work, job | **το γραφείο** | office, desk |
| **η εταιρεία** | company | **το αφεντικό** | the boss |
| **ο συνάδελφος** | colleague | **ο μισθός** | salary |
| **η σύμβαση** | contract | **οι ώρες** | hours |
| **η άδεια** | leave, holiday | **η υπερωρία** | overtime |
| **η συνάντηση** | meeting | **η βάρδια** | shift |
| **η απεργία** | strike | **η σύνταξη** | pension |

**η απεργία is a word you will need in Greece** — strikes are frequent and they affect transport, and **Έχει απεργία** is a normal sentence.

**Talking about it:**

- **Δουλεύω οχτώ ώρες τη μέρα.** — I work eight hours a day.
- **Δουλεύω από τις εννιά μέχρι τις πέντε.** — I work from nine to five.
- **Μου αρέσει η δουλειά μου.** — I like my job.
- **Είναι κουραστικό αλλά ενδιαφέρον.** — It is tiring but interesting.
- **Έχω πολλή δουλειά αυτή τη βδομάδα.** — I have a lot of work on this week.

**Practice.** Answer **Τι δουλειά κάνεις;** in four sentences, out loud. Then say your hours, what you like and what is hard about it. Then name ten jobs of people you know, with the right article.
School and studies:
The education words, which you need for talking about children, about your own learning, and for reading anything about the Greek school system — including the readers you are reading.

**The stages of school:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο παιδικός σταθμός** | nursery |
| **το νηπιαγωγείο** | kindergarten |
| **το δημοτικό** | primary school — six years, Α΄ to ΣΤ΄ |
| **το γυμνάσιο** | lower secondary — three years |
| **το λύκειο** | upper secondary — three years |
| **το πανεπιστήμιο** | university |
| **το μεταπτυχιακό** | master's degree |
| **το φροντιστήριο** | the private cramming school — a Greek institution |

**το φροντιστήριο deserves the note**: Greek children attend private after-school tuition for exams and for languages on a scale that has no English equivalent, and **πάω φροντιστήριο** is an ordinary sentence for a teenager.

**Α΄ Δημοτικού, Β΄ Γυμνασίου** — the alphabetic numerals from stage 1, used to name the year. This is where that lesson pays off, and it is how the free school books you read are labelled.

**The words:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ο μαθητής / η μαθήτρια** | pupil | **ο φοιτητής / η φοιτήτρια** | student |
| **ο δάσκαλος** | primary teacher | **ο καθηγητής** | secondary teacher |
