- **Θέλω να μάθω.** · **Μου είπε να περιμένω.** · **Ήρθα για να σε δω.**

**So there are three connectors** and the choice is by meaning:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ότι / πως** | a fact — *that he is here* |
| **να** | something not yet real — a wish, a command, a purpose |
| **αν** | a question or a condition |

**The commonest mistake** is **ότι** where **να** belongs: **Θέλω ότι έρθεις** is wrong; **Θέλω να έρθεις** is right. **Ότι** reports what is; **να** points at what is wanted.

**The other embedding words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **γιατί / επειδή** | because |
| **αφού** | since, after |
| **ενώ** | while, whereas |
| **όταν** | when |
| **μόλις** | as soon as |
| **παρόλο που** | although |
| **αν και** | although |
| **εκτός αν** | unless |
| **έτσι που / ώστε** | so that, with the result that |
| **για να** | in order to |
| **πριν / μέχρι να** | before / until |

**παρόλο που and αν και both mean *although***, and both take an ordinary clause: **Παρόλο που έβρεχε, πήγαμε.**

**One register note**: **διότι** is the formal *because*, **εφόσον** the formal *since*, **καθώς** *as*, and **προκειμένου να** the formal *in order to*. All four are reading vocabulary.

**Practice.** Embed five questions — two yes/no and three with question words. Then say five sentences with **ότι** and five with **να**, and say why each takes what it takes. Then join ten short sentences with ten different connectors from the list.
The verb, consolidated:
Every form of one verb, in one place. This is the page to come back to, and the Forms track has it again as reference.

**γράφω — active:**

| | Imperfective | Perfective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Present** | γράφω | — |
| **Imperfect / aorist** | έγραφα | έγραψα |
| **Dependent** | να γράφω | να γράψω |
| **Future** | θα γράφω | θα γράψω |
| **Perfect** | — | έχω γράψει |
| **Pluperfect** | — | είχα γράψει |
| **Future perfect** | — | θα έχω γράψει |
| **Conditional** | θα έγραφα | — |
| **Past conditional** | — | θα είχα γράψει |
| **Imperative** | γράφε / γράφετε | γράψε / γράψτε |
| **Participle** | γράφοντας | γραμμένος |

**γράφομαι — mediopassive:**

| | Imperfective | Perfective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Present** | γράφομαι | — |
| **Imperfect / aorist** | γραφόμουν | γράφτηκα |
| **Dependent** | να γράφομαι | να γραφτώ |
| **Future** | θα γράφομαι | θα γραφτώ |
| **Perfect** | — | έχω γραφτεί |
| **Pluperfect** | — | είχα γραφτεί |
| **Imperative** | — | γράψου / γραφτείτε |
| **Participle** | — | γραμμένος |

**What generates all of it: three stems and four particles.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **γράφ-** | the imperfective stem |
| **γράψ-** | the perfective stem |
| **γραφτ-** | the passive perfective stem |
| **θα, να, έχω, είχα** | the four assemblers |

**So a verb is learned as three stems**, and every cell above follows. That is why the deck stores **γράφω · να γράψω · έγραψα** — those three give you the stems, and the passive one follows the sound rules.

**The order to drill the table in**, which is how it becomes usable rather than impressive:

1. **Present, aorist, future, dependent** — the four from stage 4, which carry 90 per cent of speech.
2. **Perfect and pluperfect**, which are **έχω** and **είχα** plus one shape.
3. **The conditional**, which is **θα** plus the imperfect.
4. **The passive aorist**, from which the rest of the passive comes.
5. **The participles**, which are two words.

**What Greek does not have**, and it is worth knowing what you are not missing: no infinitive, no gerund as a noun, no continuous aspect marked separately from the imperfective, no perfect progressive, and no sequence-of-tenses rule in reported speech. The system is smaller than the table makes it look.

**Practice.** Fill in both tables for **διαβάζω** from memory. Then do it for **παίρνω**, whose perfective is irregular. Then say which cells you have never used, and use three of them today.
Written Greek: what it uses that speech:
The register difference, which is the real reason stage 6's grammar matters — and the point at which reading becomes possible.

**What written Greek uses more:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The passive** | **ανακοινώθηκε, εγκρίθηκε, διαπιστώθηκε** |
| **The perfect and pluperfect** | where speech would use the aorist |
| **ο οποίος** | where speech uses **που** |
| **Participles** | **έχοντας, εργαζόμενος, δεδομένου ότι** |
| **The genitive**, including plurals | where speech restructures |
| **Formal connectives** | **επομένως, ωστόσο, εντούτοις, παρ' όλα αυτά** |
| **Learned vocabulary** | the Greek of the educated register |
| **Long sentences** | with two or three subordinate clauses |

**The formal connectives, which are the practical half of this lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **επομένως / άρα** | therefore |
| **ωστόσο / όμως** | however |
| **εντούτοις** | nevertheless — formal |
| **παρ' όλα αυτά** | in spite of all that |
| **αφ' ενός… αφ' ετέρου** | on the one hand… on the other |
| **εν τω μεταξύ** | meanwhile |
| **εν ολίγοις** | in short |
| **δηλαδή** | that is, I mean |
| **πράγματι** | indeed |
| **σύμφωνα με** | according to |
| **όσον αφορά** | as regards |
| **λόγω** | because of — **λόγω της βροχής** |
| **προκειμένου να** | in order to |
| **εφόσον** | provided that, since |

**Several of those are frozen learned forms.** **Αφ' ενός**, **εν τω μεταξύ**, **εν ολίγοις** and **λόγω** are datives and genitives from an older grammar — the register this curriculum deliberately skipped — and they survive as fixed phrases. You read them and use the common ones; the grammar behind them is the later curriculum's.

**λόγω plus the genitive is the one to adopt**, because it is everywhere: **λόγω καιρού** (because of the weather), **λόγω έργων** (because of works), **λόγω απεργίας** (because of a strike).

**What written Greek looks like, in one sentence**, built out of this stage:

> **Σύμφωνα με ανακοίνωση του Υπουργείου, τα σχολεία θα παραμείνουν κλειστά λόγω της κακοκαιρίας, ενώ αναμένεται να ανοίξουν την Τρίτη.**

**Take it apart**: **σύμφωνα με** (according to), a genitive (**του Υπουργείου**), a future (**θα παραμείνουν**), a passive participle used adjectivally (**κλειστά**), **λόγω** plus a genitive, **ενώ** (while), and a passive (**αναμένεται**) with **να**. Every piece of that is in stages 3 to 6.

**That sentence is a newspaper's whole method**, and being able to dismantle it is what this stage was for.

**What to do about the vocabulary gap**, which is the remaining obstacle: read the same kind of thing repeatedly. News uses a closed set of a few hundred words — **κυβέρνηση, υπουργείο, δήλωση, απόφαση, αύξηση, μείωση, εκλογές, συνάντηση** — and a fortnight of headlines teaches most of it.

**Practice.** Read the sample sentence aloud and name every construction in it. Then find one Greek news sentence and do the same. Then learn the fourteen connectives — they are the scaffolding of everything written.
Nominalisation: verbs as nouns:
How Greek turns a verb into a noun, which is how written Greek compresses and which multiplies your vocabulary.

**The four patterns:**

**1. -σιμο — the act, neuter.** From the perfective stem:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **γράφω → το γράψιμο** | writing |
| **διαβάζω → το διάβασμα** | reading |
| **πλένω → το πλύσιμο** | washing |
| **μαγειρεύω → το μαγείρεμα** | cooking |
| **τρώω → το φαγητό** | food, the eating |

**2. -ση / -ξη / -ψη — the action or its result, feminine.** The group whose plural is **-εις**, from stage 2:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **κινώ → η κίνηση** | movement, traffic |
| **αποφασίζω → η απόφαση** | decision |
| **σκέφτομαι → η σκέψη** | thought |
| **λύνω → η λύση** | solution |
| **γράφω → η γραφή** | writing, script |
| **πράττω → η πράξη** | act, action |
| **αυξάνω → η αύξηση** | increase |
| **μειώνω → η μείωση** | decrease |

**Those last two are news vocabulary**, and the pattern means that knowing a verb gives you the noun: **αυξάνω / αύξηση**, **μειώνω / μείωση**, **ανακοινώνω / ανακοίνωση**, **συναντώ / συνάντηση**, **αποφασίζω / απόφαση**.

**3. -τής / -τρια, -ας — the doer, masculine and feminine:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **μαθαίνω → ο μαθητής** | pupil |
| **διαβάζω → ο αναγνώστης** | reader |
| **εργάζομαι → ο εργάτης** | worker |
| **παίζω → ο παίκτης** | player |
| **οδηγώ → ο οδηγός** | driver |
| **ψάλλω → ο ψάλτης** | chanter |

**4. -μένος as an adjective**, which is the passive participle from earlier: **γραμμένος, κουρασμένος, παντρεμένος**.

**Why this matters.** Written Greek prefers nouns where speech prefers verbs:

| Speech | Writing |
| --- | --- |
| **Αποφάσισαν να αυξήσουν τους φόρους.** | **Η απόφαση για αύξηση των φόρων…** |
| **Έκλεισαν τα σχολεία.** | **Το κλείσιμο των σχολείων…** |
| **Συναντήθηκαν.** | **Η συνάντηση…** |

**So the same content comes in two registers**, and recognising the noun version is most of what makes a headline readable. A Greek headline is often a string of nouns in the genitive: **Αύξηση των τιμών λόγω της κρίσης** — *increase of prices because of the crisis*.

**The genitive chains from stage 3 are what hold those together**, which is why that stage mattered more than it looked.

**Practice.** Give the noun for ten verbs you know, using the four patterns. Then take three spoken sentences and rewrite each as a noun phrase. Then read three Greek headlines and count the nouns and the genitives in each.
The verbs of church life:
The verbs for what happens at and around a service — which are mostly mediopassive, mostly compounds, and all of them now parsable.

| Present | Dependent | Aorist | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **προσεύχομαι** | να προσευχηθώ | προσευχήθηκα | pray |
| **εκκλησιάζομαι** | να εκκλησιαστώ | εκκλησιάστηκα | attend church |
| **νηστεύω** | να νηστέψω | νήστεψα | fast |
| **εξομολογούμαι** | να εξομολογηθώ | εξομολογήθηκα | confess |
| **κοινωνώ** | να κοινωνήσω | κοινώνησα | receive communion |
| **μεταλαμβάνω** | να μεταλάβω | μετάλαβα | receive communion — the older verb |
| **προσκυνώ** | να προσκυνήσω | προσκύνησα | venerate, bow before |
| **ανάβω** | να ανάψω | άναψα | light — a candle |
| **σταυροκοπιέμαι** | να σταυροκοπηθώ | σταυροκοπήθηκα | cross oneself |
| **βαφτίζω** | να βαφτίσω | βάφτισα | baptise |
| **βαφτίζομαι** | να βαφτιστώ | βαφτίστηκα | be baptised |
| **στεφανώνω** | να στεφανώσω | στεφάνωσα | crown, i.e. marry (as sponsor) |
| **παντρεύομαι** | να παντρευτώ | παντρεύτηκα | marry |
| **κηδεύω** | να κηδέψω | κήδεψα | bury |
| **μνημονεύω** | να μνημονεύσω | μνημόνευσα | commemorate |
| **ευλογώ** | να ευλογήσω | ευλόγησα | bless |
| **ψάλλω** | να ψάλω | έψαλα | chant |
| **διαβάζω** | να διαβάσω | διάβασα | read — and *to read prayers over* someone |
| **λειτουργώ** | να λειτουργήσω | λειτούργησα | celebrate the Liturgy — and *to function* |
| **εορτάζω / γιορτάζω** | να γιορτάσω | γιόρτασα | celebrate a feast or a name day |

**Several of these are two words in one.** **Μεταλαμβάνω** is *take-with*; **προσκυνώ** is *towards-kiss*; **εξομολογούμαι** is *out-speak-together*; **σταυροκοπιέμαι** is *cross-strike oneself*. Stage 4's prefix lesson is what makes them readable.

**λειτουργώ is worth the note**: it means both *to celebrate the Liturgy* and *to function, to work* — of a machine or a shop. **Το ασανσέρ δεν λειτουργεί** is *the lift is out of order*, and the same verb is what a priest does on Sunday. Both come from **λειτουργία** — *public work*.

**The sentences you will use:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πάω στην εκκλησία κάθε Κυριακή.** | I go to church every Sunday. |
| **Άναψα ένα κερί για την οικογένειά μου.** | I lit a candle for my family. |
| **Προσκύνησα την εικόνα.** | I venerated the icon. |
| **Νηστεύω τη Σαρακοστή.** | I fast during Lent. |
| **Εξομολογήθηκα πριν τα Χριστούγεννα.** | I confessed before Christmas. |
| **Κοινώνησα την Κυριακή.** | I received communion on Sunday. |
| **Γιορτάζει του Αγίου Γεωργίου.** | His name day is St George's. |
| **Θα γίνει μνημόσυνο το Σάββατο.** | There will be a memorial service on Saturday. |
| **Ποιος λειτουργεί σήμερα;** | Who is celebrating today? |

**And the things said to you:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλή Λειτουργία.** | — said as you arrive |
| **Ο Θεός να σε ευλογεί.** | God bless you. |
| **Με υγεία.** | with health — on receiving something |
| **Να 'ναι ευλογημένο.** | may it be blessed |
| **Δι' ευχών.** | through prayers — the monastic farewell |

**Δι' ευχών is an old dative** and a monastery phrase; it is the sort of thing you will hear and should recognise rather than analyse.

**Practice.** Say all four forms of ten of these verbs. Then say the nine sentences aloud. Then describe your last Sunday using five church verbs in the aorist.
At church: death, memory and the words a:
A hard lesson and a necessary one: what is said at a death, a funeral and a memorial — because you will be present at one and the wrong silence is worse than imperfect Greek.

**The words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο θάνατος** | death |
| **πέθανε** | he / she died — from **πεθαίνω** |
| **εκοιμήθη** | he fell asleep — the church's word, a learned passive |
| **ο κεκοιμημένος** | the departed |
| **η κηδεία** | the funeral |
| **το μνημόσυνο** | the memorial service |
| **τα κόλλυβα** | the boiled wheat eaten at a memorial |
| **το κοιμητήριο** | the cemetery — *the sleeping place* |
| **ο τάφος** | the grave |
| **το μακαρίτης / η μακαρίτισσα** | the late… |
| **τα συλλυπητήρια** | condolences |
| **το σαράντα** | the fortieth day, and its memorial |
| **το τρισάγιο** | the short prayer service for the dead |

**εκοιμήθη is the one to recognise.** It is Koine — *he fell asleep* — and it is what a death notice and a priest will say. **Πέθανε** is the everyday word and it is not wrong, but at church the softer one is used.

**What to say to the bereaved:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Συλλυπητήρια.** | My condolences. — the standard, and sufficient |
| **Τα θερμά μου συλλυπητήρια.** | My warm condolences. |
| **Ζωή σε λόγου σας.** | Life to you — the traditional response, meaning *may you live* |
| **Να ζήσετε να τον θυμάστε.** | May you live to remember him. |
| **Καλό Παράδεισο.** | May he rest in paradise. |
| **Αιωνία του η μνήμη.** | May his memory be eternal. |
| **Ο Θεός να τον αναπαύσει.** | God rest him. |
| **Κουράγιο.** | Courage. — said with a hand on the arm |

**Ζωή σε λόγου σας is the formula** and it is specifically a reply to a death being mentioned: you say **συλλυπητήρια**, they say **ζωή σε λόγου σας**, or the other way about. It has no English equivalent and using it correctly matters.

**Αιωνία η μνήμη** is sung at the end of the service and said as a formula. It is a learned form — an old adjective and a genitive — and you say it without parsing it.

**At the memorial — το μνημόσυνο:**

- It is held on the third, ninth and fortieth days, at six months, at a year, and annually.
- **Τα κόλλυβα** — boiled wheat with sugar and nuts, symbolising the resurrection — are blessed and handed out.
- You take some, you eat it, and you say **Θεός σχωρέσ' τον** — *God forgive him* — or **Αιωνία του η μνήμη**.

**Θεός σχωρέσ' τον is the phrase handed round with the κόλλυβα**, and it is the one most people say.

**The notice board again:** a death notice will read **Κηδεία: Σάββατο 3 μ.μ.** or **Θα τελεσθεί μνημόσυνο υπέρ αναπαύσεως της ψυχής του…** — and now you can read both the modern half and recognise the learned half.

**What to do, as well as say.** Go. Stand. Take the **κόλλυβα**. Say **συλλυπητήρια** to the family, and **Αιωνία του η μνήμη** at the end. That is all that is required of you, and it is all noticed.

**Practice.** Say the eight condolence phrases aloud until **Συλλυπητήρια** and **Αιωνία του η μνήμη** are automatic. Then learn **Ζωή σε λόγου σας** and what it answers. Then read a Greek death notice online and find **εκοιμήθη**.
Reading: the news paragraph:
The first paragraph of a news item, which is where stage 6's grammar lives — and which is the most learnable piece of hard Greek there is.

**Why the first paragraph.** News writing front-loads: the first sentence or two carries who, what, where and when, in a fixed register, with a closed vocabulary. The rest of the article is detail. So reading only the opening of many articles is far better practice than struggling through one.

**The grammar it uses, all from this stage:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The passive** | ανακοινώθηκε, εγκρίθηκε, συνελήφθη |
| **The perfect** | έχει ξεκινήσει, έχουν αυξηθεί |
| **ότι clauses** | δήλωσε ότι, ανέφερε ότι |
| **Nominalisations** | η αύξηση, η απόφαση, η συνάντηση |
| **Genitive chains** | η απόφαση της κυβέρνησης για την αύξηση των τιμών |
| **λόγω, σύμφωνα με, όσον αφορά** | the formal connectives |
| **Participles** | εργαζόμενοι, δεδομένου ότι |

**The closed vocabulary — learn these forty and most headlines open:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **η κυβέρνηση** | government | **το υπουργείο** | ministry |
| **ο πρωθυπουργός** | prime minister | **ο υπουργός** | minister |
| **η βουλή** | parliament | **οι εκλογές** | elections |
| **η απόφαση** | decision | **η δήλωση** | statement |
| **η ανακοίνωση** | announcement | **η συνάντηση** | meeting |
| **η αύξηση / η μείωση** | increase / decrease |  **οι τιμές** | prices |
| **η οικονομία** | economy | **ο πληθωρισμός** | inflation |
| **η απεργία** | strike | **οι εργαζόμενοι** | workers |
| **το νομοσχέδιο** | bill, draft law | **ο νόμος** | law |
| **η αστυνομία** | police | **ο θάνατος** | death |
| **το δυστύχημα** | accident | **η πυρκαγιά** | fire |
| **ο σεισμός** | earthquake | **η κακοκαιρία** | bad weather |
| **το νοσοκομείο** | hospital | **η υγεία** | health |
| **η Εκκλησία** | the Church | **ο Αρχιεπίσκοπος** | the Archbishop |
| **η Σύνοδος** | the Synod | **η ενορία** | the parish |
| **ο δήμος** | municipality | **η περιφέρεια** | region |
| **τα σχολεία** | schools | **οι μαθητές** | pupils |
| **η έρευνα** | investigation, research | **τα στοιχεία** | data, figures |
| **αυξήθηκε / μειώθηκε** | rose / fell | **αναμένεται** | it is expected |
| **ξεκίνησε** | began | **ολοκληρώθηκε** | was completed |

**Where to read.** The state broadcaster **ΕΡΤ** (ert.gr) writes plainly; **Καθημερινή** (kathimerini.gr) is the broadsheet; **in.gr** and **newsbeast** are tabloid and easier. The Church's own news — **romfea.gr**, **orthodoxianewsagency.gr** — is in exactly the register you want and about subjects you know, which makes it the best place to start.

**romfea.gr deserves the recommendation**: it is church news in modern Greek, with the names, feasts and places you already know from the parish, and it uses the learned register sparingly.

**The method, ten minutes a day:**

1. **Read the headline.** Name the nouns and the genitives.
2. **Read the first paragraph aloud.**
3. **Find the main verb** and say whether it is active or passive, and what tense.
4. **Say in English what happened.** One sentence.
5. **Look up no more than three words.**
6. **Move to the next article.**

**Five articles a day in ten minutes** is better than one article in thirty.

**Practice.** Open romfea.gr or ert.gr. Do the six-step method on five items. Then write down the three words you looked up and card the ones that recur.
Listening: the news and the sermon:
Two kinds of formal spoken Greek, both slower and clearer than conversation — which makes them the easiest listening at this level and the best bridge to native speed.

**The news bulletin.** A newsreader speaks slowly, in complete sentences, with no overlap and standard pronunciation, about subjects whose vocabulary you have just learned.

**Where**: ΕΡΤ's bulletins are on YouTube and on ertflix; ERT's radio news is on the hour; and most channels put their bulletins up daily.

**The method:**

1. **Read the headlines first**, on the website. Knowing the content is not cheating — it is how a human listens to news in their own language.
2. **Listen to the first three items**, once, with no text.
3. **Listen again and write down every word you catch.**
4. **Read the corresponding written article.**
5. **Listen a third time.** It will be dramatically clearer.

**Ten minutes, three items, three passes.** The third pass is where the learning is.

**What to listen for, specifically:** the names of countries and people, the numbers, the verbs of saying (**δήλωσε, ανακοίνωσε, ανέφερε**), and the passive forms. Those four categories carry the shape of the item.

**The sermon — το κήρυγμα.** This is the one that matters to you and it is harder, because the subject matter is abstract and the register is mixed.

**What is in a sermon, linguistically**: modern Greek grammar, with liturgical quotations in the older language, and a vocabulary of theological words that are mostly recognisable because English borrowed them.

**The strategy**, which is different from the news:

1. **Know the day before you go.** The feast and the Gospel reading are on the notice board or online; reading the passage in English on Saturday means you arrive knowing the subject.
2. **Listen for the Gospel's key words**, which will be repeated: **αγάπη, πίστη, έλεος, μετάνοια, σταυρός, ανάσταση, ταπείνωση, υπομονή**.
3. **Catch one whole sentence.** Write it down afterwards and look it up during the week. One sentence a week is fifty sentences a year.
4. **Expect the quotations to be opaque.** When the priest quotes the Gospel in Koine, that is not your Greek failing.

**The theological vocabulary that recurs**, and almost all of it is in English somewhere:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **η αγάπη** | love | **η πίστη** | faith |
| **η ελπίδα** | hope | **το έλεος** | mercy |
| **η μετάνοια** | repentance | **η ταπείνωση** | humility |
| **η υπομονή** | patience | **η χάρη** | grace |
| **η ψυχή** | soul | **το πνεύμα** | spirit |
| **η σωτηρία** | salvation | **η αμαρτία** | sin |
| **ο σταυρός** | cross | **η ανάσταση** | resurrection |
| **η θυσία** | sacrifice | **η προσευχή** | prayer |
| **η νηστεία** | fasting | **η ευχαριστία** | thanksgiving |
| **ο λόγος** | word | **η αλήθεια** | truth |

**Those twenty words are most of a sermon's content words**, and knowing them means you catch the subject even when the sentences escape you.

**Practice.** This week: three news items with the five-step method, and one sermon with the four-step strategy — including reading the Gospel passage in English the day before. Then write down the one sentence you caught.
Writing: letters and emails:
Written Greek that you produce rather than read, which needs the register conventions as much as the grammar.

**The informal message or email:**

> **Γεια σου Γιώργο,**
>
> **Τι κάνεις; Ελπίζω να είσαι καλά. Σου γράφω για να σου πω ότι θα έρθω στην Αθήνα τον Μάιο. Θα ήθελα πολύ να σε δω. Θα είμαι εκεί από τις 10 μέχρι τις 17.**
>
> **Πες μου αν σου βολεύει. Χαιρετισμούς στην οικογένεια.**
>
> **Φιλικά,**
> **[name]**

**The sign-offs, by closeness:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Φιλιά** | kisses — family and close friends |
| **Με αγάπη** | with love |
| **Φιλικά** | kind regards |
| **Με εκτίμηση** | with respect — formal |
| **Με σεβασμό** | with respect — more formal |
| **Ευχαριστώ εκ των προτέρων** | thank you in advance |

**The formal letter or email:**

> **Αξιότιμε κύριε / Αξιότιμη κυρία,**
>
> **Σας γράφω σχετικά με… **
>
> **Θα ήθελα να σας ρωτήσω αν…**
>
> **Σας ευχαριστώ εκ των προτέρων για τον χρόνο σας.**
>
> **Με εκτίμηση,**
> **[full name]**

**The formal openers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Αξιότιμε κύριε / κυρία** | Dear Sir / Madam |
| **Αγαπητέ κύριε Παπαδόπουλε** | Dear Mr Papadopoulos |
| **Προς: …** | To: — on an official letter |
| **Θέμα: …** | Subject: |
| **Σας γράφω σχετικά με…** | I am writing regarding… |
| **Σε συνέχεια της επικοινωνίας μας…** | Following our correspondence… |
| **Παρακαλώ να με ενημερώσετε…** | Please inform me… |
| **Αναμένω την απάντησή σας.** | I await your reply. |

**Writing to a priest**, which you may need:

> **Σεβαστέ πάτερ,** / **Πάτερ Γιώργο,**
>
> … the body in the polite plural …
>
> **Με σεβασμό / Ευλογείτε,**
> **[name]**

**Ευλογείτε** — *bless* — is the traditional greeting and sign-off to a priest or monk, and the reply is **Ο Κύριος**. Both are formulas and using them correctly is noticed.

**The conventions worth knowing:**

1. **Polite plural throughout** a formal letter, with **εσείς** and plural verbs.
2. **No comma after the opening** in Greek practice; a comma is increasingly used under English influence.
3. **The date goes top right**, as **Αθήνα, 14 Οκτωβρίου 2026**.
4. **Full name at the end**, with the surname — and if it is a form, in capitals.
5. **Accents are written**, even in email. Unaccented Greek reads as careless.

**What to write this stage.** One email a week in Greek, to a real person if you have one — a Greek friend, a parish, a monastery guesthouse, a shop. Real correspondence is worth ten exercises.

**Practice.** Write the informal email above, in your own words, about a real plan. Then write a formal one: ask a parish what time the Liturgy is on a feast day. Then write **Ευλογείτε** and know what it answers.
Speaking: narrating and explaining:
The speaking skill for this stage, which is longer turns: telling a story with depth and explaining why something is so.

**What stage 5's speaking lesson got you**: exchanges, answers, short turns. **What this stage adds**: the ability to hold the floor for a minute or two, which is what a real conversation requires.

**Narrating with depth**, using the tenses of this stage:

> **Την Κυριακή πήγα στην εκκλησία. Είχα πάει και το Σάββατο στον εσπερινό, γιατί ήταν η γιορτή του Αγίου Δημητρίου. Όταν έφτασα, η Λειτουργία είχε αρχίσει και η εκκλησία ήταν γεμάτη. Ο ψάλτης, που είναι από την Κύπρο, έψαλλε πολύ ωραία. Μετά, στην αίθουσα, μίλησα με μια κυρία που με ρώτησε γιατί μαθαίνω ελληνικά, και της εξήγησα. Μου είπε ότι θα με βοηθήσει. Αν δεν είχα πάει, δεν θα την είχα γνωρίσει.**

**Count what is in it**: aorists for the events, a pluperfect for what came before, an imperfect for description, a relative clause with **που**, reported speech with **ότι**, and an unreal past conditional at the end. That is stage 6 in one paragraph, and it is a minute of speech.

**The structure of a narrative turn:**

1. **Set the scene** — when, where, imperfect.
2. **What had happened before**, if it matters — pluperfect.
3. **The events** — aorists, with **μετά, ύστερα, τότε**.
4. **What someone said** — **ότι** or **να**.
5. **How it was, or what it meant** — imperfect or a comment.

**Explaining**, which is the other long turn:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γιατί…** | because |
| **Επειδή…** | because — fuller, and can start a sentence |
| **Γι' αυτό…** | that is why |
| **Έτσι…** | so |
| **Δηλαδή…** | that is to say |
| **Για παράδειγμα…** | for example |
| **Από τη μια… από την άλλη…** | on the one hand… on the other |
| **Το θέμα είναι ότι…** | the thing is that |
| **Αυτό που θέλω να πω είναι ότι…** | what I want to say is that |
| **Τελικά…** | in the end |

**Δηλαδή is the most useful of them** and it is what you say when your first attempt at a sentence failed: **δηλαδή…** and then a simpler version. It buys time and sounds fluent.

**The three habits for a longer turn:**

1. **Signpost.** Say how many things you are about to say: **δύο πράγματα**, **πρώτα απ' όλα**.
2. **Do not stop to correct.** Finish the sentence, then rephrase with **δηλαδή** if you must.
3. **Finish with a comment**, not with a trailing off: **Ήταν πολύ ωραία**, **Αυτό ήθελα να πω**.

**And the exercise that builds this, which is free**: narrate your week out loud to nobody, once a week, for two minutes, using the five-part structure. Then do the same thing to a person.

**Practice.** Narrate last Sunday in a one-minute turn with the five-part structure, out loud. Then explain in a minute why you are learning Greek, using five of the ten connectives. Then do both again, and notice the second attempt is better.
The verbs that carry everything: κάνω, β:
Four verbs that combine with nouns to make hundreds of expressions — the Greek equivalent of English's *get*, *take*, *put* and *make*, and the fastest vocabulary multiplier at this level.

**κάνω — do, make:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **κάνει ζέστη / κρύο** | it is hot / cold |
| **κάνω μπάνιο / ντους** | I have a bath / shower |
| **κάνω παρέα** | I keep company |
| **κάνω λάθος** | I make a mistake |
| **κάνω υπομονή** | I am patient |
| **κάνω ησυχία** | I keep quiet |
| **κάνω τον σταυρό μου** | I cross myself |
| **κάνω κέφι** | I am in the mood |
| **δεν κάνει** | it is not done, it is not right |
| **τι κάνεις;** | how are you? |
| **πόσο κάνει;** | how much is it? |
| **κάνει δουλειά** | it will do, it serves |

**βάζω — put:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **βάζω μπροστά** | I start (an engine), I get going |
| **βάζω τα δυνατά μου** | I do my utmost |
| **βάζω στοίχημα** | I bet |
| **βάζω φωτιά** | I set fire |
| **βάζω με το νου μου** | I imagine |
| **τα βάζω με κάποιον** | I pick a fight with someone |
| **βάλε μου λίγο** | pour me a little |

**παίρνω — take, get:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **παίρνω τηλέφωνο** | I phone |
| **παίρνω μέρος** | I take part |
| **παίρνω φωτιά** | I catch fire — and *I lose my temper* |
| **παίρνω σειρά** | I take my turn |
| **με παίρνει ο ύπνος** | I fall asleep |
| **παίρνει καιρό** | it takes time |
| **τα παίρνω** | I take offence |
| **πάρε κι άλλο** | have some more |

**πάω — go:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **πάει καλά** | it is going well |
| **πώς πάει;** | how is it going? |
| **πάει ο καιρός** | how time passes |
| **μου πάει** | it suits me |
| **πάει να πει** | it means, that is to say |
| **δεν πάει άλλο** | it cannot go on |
| **πάμε** | let's go |
| **πού πάει το μυαλό σου;** | what are you thinking? |

**Why these four matter so much.** Greek, like English, builds a great deal of ordinary speech by pairing a very common verb with a noun. Learning **κάνω υπομονή** is one item; working it out from **κάνω** and **υπομονή** is not possible, because the combination is the vocabulary.

**Two more worth adding: έχω and λέω.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **έχω δίκιο / άδικο** | I am right / wrong |
| **έχει πλάκα** | it is funny |
| **δεν έχει σημασία** | it does not matter |
| **τι έχεις;** | what is wrong? |
| **τα λέμε** | see you, we'll talk |
| **πώς το λένε;** | what is it called? |
| **λέει κάτι;** | does that mean anything? |
| **ό,τι πεις** | whatever you say |
| **δεν λέει** | it is no good, it does not do |

**The learning method**: card the whole expression, never the parts. **κάνω υπομονή** is one card; **υπομονή** alone is another word entirely.

**Practice.** Say all forty expressions aloud. Then use ten of them in sentences about today. Then card the fifteen you would actually say.
Knowing, thinking and understanding:
Four or five verbs whose meanings overlap and whose aspect behaviour is distinctive — and getting them right is a large part of sounding fluent.

**ξέρω — know, as a state.** No perfective stem, so no aspect choice: **ξέρω, ήξερα**.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ξέρω ελληνικά.** | I know Greek. |
| **Ξέρεις πού είναι;** | Do you know where it is? |
| **Δεν ξέρω.** | I do not know. |
| **Ξέρω να μαγειρεύω.** | I know how to cook. |
| **Ποιος ξέρει;** | Who knows? |
| **Ξέρω κι εγώ;** | How should I know? — idiomatic |

**γνωρίζω — know, meet, be acquainted with.** Has a perfective: **να γνωρίσω, γνώρισα** — which means *to meet*.

- **Γνωρίζω τον πατέρα Γιώργο.** — I know Father George.
- **Γνώρισα τον πατέρα Γιώργο πέρυσι.** — I met him last year.
- **Χάρηκα που σας γνώρισα.** — Pleased to have met you.

**That pair is the aspect distinction doing semantic work**: the imperfective is a state (*I know him*), the perfective an event (*I met him*). Same verb, two English words.

**μαθαίνω — learn, and also find out.**

- **Μαθαίνω ελληνικά.** — I am learning Greek.
- **Έμαθα ότι παντρεύτηκε.** — I heard / found out that he got married.
- **Πού το έμαθες;** — Where did you hear that?

**Again the aspect splits the meaning**: imperfective is *learning*, perfective is *finding out*.

**καταλαβαίνω — understand.**

- **Δεν καταλαβαίνω.** — I do not understand. (now, generally)
- **Δεν κατάλαβα.** — I did not catch that. (that one thing)
- **Κατάλαβα!** — I see! / Got it!

**Κατάλαβα as a one-word reply is extremely common** and it is the aorist: *I have grasped it*.

**νομίζω and πιστεύω — think and believe:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Νομίζω ότι…** | I think that… |
| **Δεν νομίζω.** | I do not think so. |
| **Πιστεύω ότι…** | I believe that… |
| **Πιστεύω στον Θεό.** | I believe in God. |
| **Έτσι νομίζω.** | I think so. |

**πιστεύω σε plus the accusative is *believe in***, and **πιστεύω ότι** is *think that*. The Creed begins **Πιστεύω εις ένα Θεόν** — the same verb, in the older form of the same construction.

**σκέφτομαι — think, in the sense of reflect or consider:**

- **Σκέφτομαι.** — I am thinking.
- **Το σκέφτομαι.** — I am considering it.
- **Σκέφτηκα κάτι.** — I have had an idea.
- **Τι σκέφτεσαι;** — What are you thinking about?

**νομίζω is opinion, σκέφτομαι is the activity of thinking.** *I am thinking that* is **σκέφτομαι ότι** only when you mean the process; for an opinion it is **νομίζω**.

**And θυμάμαι, ξεχνάω, θυμίζω:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **θυμάμαι** | I remember |
| **θυμήθηκα** | I remembered — it came to me |
| **ξεχνάω / ξέχασα** | I forget / I forgot |
| **μου θυμίζει** | it reminds me of |

**Practice.** Say the contrast pairs aloud: **γνωρίζω / γνώρισα**, **μαθαίνω / έμαθα**, **καταλαβαίνω / κατάλαβα**. Then give the English of each. Then use all six verbs in sentences about learning Greek.
Politeness, in full:
The whole politeness system, now that you have the conditional — because Greek politeness is grammatical as well as lexical.

**The four levels of a request**, from blunt to very polite:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δώσε μου το αλάτι.** | Pass the salt. — imperative, familiar |
| **Μου δίνεις το αλάτι;** | Will you pass the salt? — present as a question |
| **Μπορείς να μου δώσεις το αλάτι;** | Can you pass me the salt? |
| **Θα μπορούσατε να μου δώσετε το αλάτι;** | Could you pass me the salt? — conditional and plural |

**The conditional plus the plural is the full polite form**, and it is what you use with a stranger, an official or the priest.

**The politeness toolkit:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **παρακαλώ** | please |
| **σε / σας παρακαλώ** | I beg you — stronger |
| **συγγνώμη** | excuse me, sorry |
| **με συγχωρείτε** | forgive me — fuller |
| **ευχαριστώ / ευχαριστώ πολύ** | thank you / thank you very much |
| **ευχαριστώ θερμά** | warm thanks — formal |
| **τίποτα / παρακαλώ** | not at all, you're welcome |
| **αν δεν σας πειράζει** | if you do not mind |
| **αν γίνεται** | if possible |
| **μήπως…;** | might you…? — a softener |
| **θα ήθελα** | I would like |
| **θα μπορούσατε** | could you |
| **μου επιτρέπετε;** | may I? |

**μήπως is worth adopting**: it turns a question into a tentative one — **Μήπως ξέρετε πού είναι…;** (*Might you know where … is?*) — and it is the standard way to approach a stranger.

**Apologising:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Συγγνώμη.** | Sorry. |
| **Με συγχωρείς / Με συγχωρείτε.** | Forgive me. |
| **Λυπάμαι πολύ.** | I am very sorry. |
| **Δεν το ήθελα.** | I did not mean to. |
| **Ζητώ συγγνώμη.** | I apologise. — formal |
| **Δεν πειράζει.** | Never mind. — the reply |
| **Τίποτα.** | It is nothing. — the reply |

**Thanking and the reply**, which is a short ritual:

— **Ευχαριστώ πολύ!**
— **Τίποτα. / Παρακαλώ. / Να 'σαι καλά.**

**Να 'σαι καλά as a reply to thanks** is warmer than **παρακαλώ** and very common.

**What is *not* impolite in Greek**, which English speakers over-correct:

1. **The imperative.** **Πες μου**, **Έλα**, **Κάθισε** are perfectly normal between people who know each other.
2. **Directness.** **Δεν μου αρέσει** is not rude.
3. **Interrupting.** In a lively conversation it is participation.
4. **Asking personal questions.** Age, salary, marital status and why you have no children are ordinary small talk, and you may decline to answer without offence.

**And what is impolite:**

1. **Using the singular to someone much older**, unless invited.
2. **Refusing hospitality outright**, rather than with a reason and a counter-offer.
3. **Being brisk about money** between friends.
4. **Not greeting** on entering a small shop or a room. **Καλημέρα** on entering is expected.

**That last one is the easiest and most noticed**: say **Καλημέρα** when you walk into a shop, a waiting room or a hall, and **Γεια σας** when you leave.

**Practice.** Say one request at all four levels of politeness. Then say the thirteen toolkit phrases aloud. Then practise entering a room: **Καλημέρα!** — and leaving it: **Γεια σας, καλή συνέχεια.**
What English speakers get wrong:
A diagnostic lesson. The dozen errors that mark an English speaker's Greek, with the correction for each — and most of them are things you have been taught and will still do.

**1. Using the subject pronoun.** **Εγώ πάω, εγώ θέλω, εγώ είμαι** in every sentence. The verb ending already says who; **εγώ** means *I, as opposed to someone else*.

**2. The wrong aspect.** **Θέλω να τρώω** for *I want to eat*. One meal is perfective: **θέλω να φάω**.

**3. Avoiding the genitive.** Saying **το σπίτι από τον πατέρα μου** instead of **το σπίτι του πατέρα μου**. The genitive is not optional.

**4. Over-using the perfect.** **Έχω φάει** where a Greek says **Έφαγα**. The aorist does most of what English does with *have*.

**5. The present for *how long*.** This is the reverse error: English speakers say **έχω μένει εδώ δέκα χρόνια**. It is **μένω εδώ δέκα χρόνια**.

**6. Forgetting the article.** With names (**ο Γιώργος**), with possessives (**ο φίλος μου**), with countries (**η Ελλάδα**), and after **αυτός** (**αυτό το παιδί**).

**7. Putting the weak pronoun after the verb.** **Ξέρω το** instead of **Το ξέρω**. Before the verb in a statement, after it only in a command.

**8. The wrong case after a preposition.** **Για του φίλου μου** instead of **για τον φίλο μου**. Prepositions take the accusative, always.

**9. Reducing unstressed vowels.** Saying *thálasa* with an English schwa in the middle. Every Greek vowel is fully pronounced.

**10. The English r.** It is a single tap, and an English **ρ** is the most audible foreign sound you can make.

**11. Shifting the tense in reported speech.** **Μου είπε ότι θα ερχόταν** for *he said he would come*. Greek keeps the original: **ότι θα έρθει**.

**12. Using ότι where να belongs.** **Θέλω ότι έρθεις**. Wanting, asking and intending take **να**.

**13. The politeness mismatch.** Using **εσύ** to someone much older, or the full conditional with a friend. Both are small and both are noticed.

**14. Translating English idiom.** **Είμαι κρύος** for *I am cold* — which means *I am a cold person*. It is **κρυώνω** or **μου κρυώνει**.

**15. Saying συγγνώμη for everything.** It is *excuse me* and *sorry*; for *sorry* in the sense of sympathy, it is **λυπάμαι**.

**The three to fix first**, because they occur in nearly every sentence: the subject pronoun, the weak pronoun's position, and the vowel reduction. Fix those and your Greek sounds markedly better without any new grammar.

**How to fix them.** Not by thinking about them while speaking — that makes everything worse — but by drilling each one deliberately for a week: a day of sentences with no subject pronouns, a day of pronoun-first sentences, a day of reading aloud with every vowel full.

**Practice.** Go through the fifteen and mark the ones you know you do. Then take the three worst and write ten correct sentences for each. Then read a paragraph aloud with no reduced vowels and one tap on every ρ.
The deck at this level:
How to keep the deck working when it has over a thousand cards, which is where you now are — and what to do when it gets away from you.

**Where it should be by the end of stage 6:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Vocabulary** | fifteen hundred to two thousand words |
| **Verbs** | a hundred and fifty, as three or four forms each |
| **Phrases and sentences** | two or three hundred |
| **Spelling cards** | whatever the Spelling track has produced |
| **Grammar cards** | the paradigms worth recalling cold |
| **Daily load** | ten new, and thirty to sixty review — twenty to forty minutes |

**The three things that break a deck of this size:**

**1. Adding faster than you review.** Ten new cards a day means roughly a hundred reviews a day at steady state. If you add thirty a day for a week because a stage was vocabulary-heavy, the backlog arrives a fortnight later and the deck dies.

**The fix**: stop adding for a week, clear the backlog, then resume at ten.

**2. Cards that cannot be answered.** A card asking for a word with no context, or a sentence so long you skip it. Those become permanent leeches.

**The fix**: delete them. A card you have failed six times is not teaching you anything; the word will come back through reading, and the card is costing you the review slot of something that works.

**3. Reviewing in one place only.** A deck done at a desk gets skipped on a busy day.

**The fix**: it is on the site, so it is on the phone. Ten minutes in a queue is a session.

**What to card at this level, and what not to:**

| Card it | Do not card it |
| --- | --- |
| A word you have met three times and still do not know | Every word in a lesson |
| A whole expression — **κάνω υπομονή** | Its parts separately |
| A verb as three forms | A verb as a present only |
| A noun with its article and plural | A noun bare |
| A sentence you want to be able to say | A sentence you only want to understand |
| A spelling you have got wrong in writing | Every spelling |

**The sentence card is the one to add more of now.** At this level, whole sentences are worth more than words: they carry the grammar, the collocation and the rhythm together, and they come out of your mouth as units.

**Where the cards should come from:**

1. **Your own errors** — from the writing, which is why the paragraph a day matters.
2. **Words met three times in reading** and still unknown.
3. **Phrases heard at church** that you wrote down afterwards.
4. **The stage's lessons**, selectively.

**Not from word lists.** A frequency list is a tempting shortcut and the words come without context, which is exactly what makes them hard to retain.

**And the honest note about review**: at a thousand cards, review is twenty to forty minutes a day, every day, and it is the least interesting part of this curriculum. It is also the part that makes the rest work. The only two acceptable settings are *doing it* and *doing less of it* — not *stopping*.

**Practice.** Count what is in your deck. If there is a backlog, stop adding and clear it this week. Then delete the five worst leeches. Then add five sentence cards from your own writing.
Where you should be at the end of stage:
A checkpoint. Six stages and roughly a year to eighteen months in, this is what should be true — and what to do about whatever is not.

**The grammar. You should be able to:**

- Use both aspects correctly most of the time, in the future, the subjunctive, the imperative and the past.
- Form and use the perfect, the pluperfect and the conditional.
- Build all three kinds of conditional sentence.
- Form the passive in any tense and recognise it everywhere.
- Use both participles.
- Report what someone said, without shifting the tense.
- Handle the modal verbs and the politeness forms.
- Decline any noun and adjective, in all four cases.
- Use the pronouns, strong and weak, in the right positions.

**The four skills, honestly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Speaking** | you can hold a conversation about ordinary subjects, narrate, explain and argue a little, with errors and hesitation |
| **Listening** | you follow a clear conversation addressed to you, a news bulletin after a second pass, and the subject of a sermon |
| **Reading** | you read a news paragraph, a notice, a menu and a children's book without a dictionary at your elbow |
| **Writing** | you write a paragraph or an email, with the accents and the endings mostly right |

**That is B1**, going on B2 in reading. If you sat the Ellinomatheia B1 paper now you would probably pass it, which is not the point but is a useful calibration.

**The habits that should be running:**

- Ten minutes of ear training or focused listening, most days.
- Ten minutes of reading, daily.
- A paragraph of writing, most days.
- The deck, daily.
- One real conversation a week, minimum.
- The Spelling and Forms tracks, one lesson every three or four route lessons.

**What to do about the gaps**, and there will be gaps:

| If this is weak | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| **Aspect** | the stage 4 drill, ten minutes a day for a fortnight |
| **Listening** | double the volume and halve the difficulty |
| **Speaking** | narrate out loud alone, daily, and stop avoiding conversations |
| **The genitive** | the stage 3 writing exercise, five sentences a day |
| **Vocabulary** | read more, card less |
| **Spelling** | the Spelling track's six-step drill on your own errors |

**The thing most likely to have lapsed** is the writing, because it is the least rewarding. It is also where errors become visible, so it is the one to restart first.

**What stage 7 does.** Connected speech: the complex sentence, the discourse particles that make Greek sound Greek — **λοιπόν, δηλαδή, βρε, μωρέ, ρε** — idiom and proverb, register, and the colloquial speech that no textbook teaches. It is the stage that closes the gap between correct Greek and natural Greek.

**Practice.** Go down all four skill descriptions and judge yourself honestly out loud. Then pick the weakest and do its remedy for a fortnight before starting stage 7.
Review: stage 6:
The end of stage 6, which completes the verb. What should be true, and what stage 7 does.

**What should now be true:**

- The perfect, **έχω** plus one invariable form, and the honest account of how little Greek uses it compared with English.
- The pluperfect for what had already happened, and the future perfect — including **θα έχει** meaning *must have*.
- The conditional, **θα** plus the imperfect, and its three uses: politeness, hypothesis, and the past habitual.
- **θα ήθελα, θα μπορούσατε, θα έπρεπε** — and the understanding of what they are made of.
- All three conditional sentence types, with both halves matching.
- **μακάρι να** with three tenses for hope, wish and regret.
- The passive in every tense, formed by the five endings — **-φτηκα, -χτηκα, -στηκα, -ώθηκα, -ήθηκα** — and **από** for the agent.
- Where Greek uses the passive (signs, news, writing) and where it uses the third-person plural instead (speech).
- Both participles: **-οντας** invariable for simultaneous action, **-μένος** declining for a state.
- Reported speech with no tense shift, and **ότι / να / αν** chosen by meaning.
- The modal system in full, with the **πρέπει / θα έπρεπε / έπρεπε** politeness scale.
- The deponent verbs in all their tenses, and the imperatives of the irregulars.
- The impersonal constructions, including which take the genitive and which the accusative.
- Nominalisation, and the ability to read a headline made of nouns and genitives.
- The formal connectives, and **λόγω** plus the genitive.
- The four workhorse verbs — **κάνω, βάζω, παίρνω, πάω** — with their expressions.
- The church verbs, and the words for a death and a memorial.
- The fifteen errors English speakers make, and which three of them you make.

**What stage 6 really did.** It made written Greek readable. Everything before it was spoken-first; this stage was the one that opens the newspaper, the notice, the official letter and the sermon — and all of it from three stems and four particles, with almost no new morphology.

**What stage 7 does.** The things that make Greek sound Greek rather than correct: the particles (**λοιπόν, ρε, βρε, μωρέ, δηλαδή, τελικά**), the discourse moves, idiom and proverb, the colloquial register, interruption and emphasis, and the complex sentence at speed. It is a stage about naturalness rather than about accuracy.

**And the tracks.** Spelling 3 and 4 and Forms 3 and 4 cover the verb endings and the full tables you have just used. If they are behind, they are now behind on material you need; catch them up during stage 7.

**Practice.** Go down the list. Then narrate something that happened last month in a two-minute turn, using a pluperfect, a conditional, a passive and a participle — and notice that a year ago you had none of them.
Reading: a story, and your first book:
The milestone of this stage: reading something of length, in Greek, for pleasure rather than for study.

**Why now.** With the past tenses, the pluperfect, the passive and the participles you have the grammar of narrative prose. What is left is vocabulary, and vocabulary comes from volume rather than from lists — which means the right move is a book.

**What to read first, in order of difficulty:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Children's chapter books** | Greek editions of what you already know — *Ο Μικρός Πρίγκιπας*, Roald Dahl, Harry Potter's first chapters |
| **Αίσωπος, complete** | the fables, one or two a day, free on Wikisource |
| **Greek folk tales** | **παραμύθια** — formulaic and repetitive, which is ideal |
| **Saints' lives for children** | narrative, short, and your own subject matter |
| **Γλώσσα Ε΄–ΣΤ΄ Δημοτικού** | the later primary readers, with real texts in them |
| **Short stories, modern** | and the next lesson's list |

**Ο Μικρός Πρίγκιπας is the standard first book** in any language and it works here: short chapters, simple past tenses, a story you already know, and a Greek translation that is not archaic.

**Harry Potter's Greek translation** is the other common choice and it is harder — invented words, long sentences — but the familiarity carries you.

**The method for a first book, which is not the method for a page:**

1. **Read a chapter without stopping.** Do not look anything up.
2. **Underline nothing on the first pass.**
3. **Reread the same chapter**, now looking up three to five words — the ones that blocked the sense, not every unknown one.
4. **Move on.** Do not reread a third time.
5. **Expect the first three chapters to be hard** and the rest to get easier, because a book repeats its own vocabulary.

**That last point is the argument for a book over a collection of short pieces**: a novel teaches its own words by repeating them, and by chapter five you are reading rather than decoding.

**How long it will take.** A children's book, two to four weeks at twenty minutes a day. The first one is slow and the second is twice as fast.

**What to do with the words.** Card the ones that recur, as the deck lesson said. A word you meet three times in one book is worth a card; a word you meet once is not.

**Where to get them free:** Greek Wikisource for anything out of copyright, including Aesop and folk tales; **openbook.gr** for free legal ebooks; the school readers at ebooks.edu.gr; and Greek libraries' digital collections. Buying a Greek children's book is also cheap and worth it for the physical object.

**And the target to aim at**, which is the real reward of this stage: by the end of stage 8 you should be reading an adult book — slowly, with a dictionary occasionally, for pleasure. The first children's book is the step that makes that credible.

**Practice.** Choose a book today. Read its first chapter tonight without looking anything up. Then reread it tomorrow with five lookups. Then keep going at twenty minutes a day.
Listening at natural speed:
Television, film and podcasts — native material at native speed, which is the last listening frontier and the one that takes longest.

**Why it is so much harder than the news.** Overlapping speakers, slang, regional accents, background noise, and sentences that are not finished. A news bulletin is designed to be understood; a drama is designed to be natural.

**What to watch, in order of difficulty:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Greek children's cartoons, dubbed** | slow, clear, repetitive. Not beneath you. |
| **Greek documentaries** | one narrator, measured pace, often subtitled |
| **Greek drama series** | *Μαέστρος και οι Λευκοί* (Maestro in Blue) is the common recommendation; Netflix has it with Greek subtitles |
| **Greek films** | and the classics of the 1960s are slower and clearer than modern ones |
| **Talk shows and panel programmes** | the hardest: four people interrupting each other |
| **Greek YouTube** | vloggers speak fast and informally, which is exactly the register you cannot get elsewhere |

**The 1960s films are a genuine tip.** Greek cinema of that period — Lambeti, Vougiouklaki, Hadjichristos — is slow, theatrically enunciated, and culturally foundational: the lines are quoted constantly, so learning them is learning references as well as words.

**Greek subtitles, not English.** This is the rule. English subtitles turn the exercise into reading; Greek ones align the sound with the spelling and teach you to hear word boundaries. Netflix and ERTFLIX both offer them.

**The method for a series, which is the most efficient form of this:**

1. **Watch an episode with Greek subtitles.**
2. **Pick one two-minute scene** and watch it three times: with subtitles, without, with again.
3. **Write down five lines** from that scene and say them aloud until they are fluent.
4. **Next episode.**

**Five lines an episode is a hundred lines in twenty episodes**, and those lines are idiomatic, current and useful — which no textbook sentence is.

**Podcasts**, for listening without a screen:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Easy Greek podcast** | still, at the harder tier |
| **Greek news podcasts** | ERT and Kathimerini both produce them |
| **Greek interview podcasts** | two people, slowly, at length — the best middle ground |
| **Greek music** | and the lyrics on stixoi.info |

**Music deserves its own note at this level.** Greek song lyrics are often poetry — Theodorakis setting Seferis and Elytis, Hadjidakis setting Gatsos — and learning a song is learning vocabulary, rhythm and culture at once. **Το τραγούδι είναι ο ευκολότερος δρόμος**: ask any Greek what song you should learn and you will get a passionate answer and a lesson.

**The honest timeline**: following a Greek drama without subtitles is a stage 8-to-9 achievement. At the end of stage 6 you will follow a cartoon, half a documentary, and the gist of a drama with Greek subtitles. That is normal, and the progress is invisible until it is not.

**Practice.** Pick one series with Greek subtitles and watch one episode this week with the four-step method on one scene. Then ask a Greek to name one song you should learn, and learn it.
What stage 7 is: from correct to natural:
Six stages have made your Greek correct. This one makes it Greek.

**The gap this stage closes.** A learner at the end of stage 6 can say anything, grammatically, and still sounds like a textbook — because what makes speech natural is not grammar. It is the small words, the order, the idiom, the exaggeration, the way a sentence is begun and abandoned, and the noises people make while someone else is talking.

**What is in it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The particles** | **λοιπόν, δηλαδή, βασικά, τελικά, ρε, βρε, μωρέ** |
| **Emphasis** | word order, repetition, the doubled pronoun |
| **Conversation management** | interrupting, holding the floor, backchannelling, changing the subject |
| **Idiom** | the body, food, God, animals — several hundred expressions |
| **Proverbs** | the fifty everyone quotes |
| **Gestures** | including the two that mean something else |
| **Diminutives** | which Greeks use constantly and learners never |
| **Register** | five ways to say one thing, and when each is right |
| **Colloquial grammar** | what people say rather than what the grammar says |
| **Slang and loanwords** | and the Turkish, Italian and English layers |

**Why it comes seventh rather than second.** Every item above is a modification of something you already have: you cannot shade an emphasis you cannot construct, and you cannot use **ρε** before you can use **εσύ** correctly. Idiom learned early is parroted; idiom learned now is placed.

**The honest framing of this stage**: it is the least systematic in the curriculum. There is no paradigm to learn and no rule to apply — it is several hundred small facts and a changed attitude to how you listen. That makes it the stage most dependent on contact with people, which is also why it comes after a stage of conversation.

**What it will do for your listening, which is the bigger half.** Most of what you miss in a Greek conversation now is not grammar or vocabulary but the connective tissue: the **λοιπόν** that starts a point, the **δηλαδή** that restates it, the **ρε** that marks who is being addressed, the idiom that carries the meaning. Learning them is learning to hear the shape of real talk.

**How to work through it.** Differently from the earlier stages:

1. **Read the lesson.**
2. **Listen for the items that week** — in the hall, in a film, in a podcast — and count them.
3. **Adopt two or three at a time**, deliberately, in your own speech.
4. **Do not try to use all of them.** A learner deploying nine idioms in a paragraph sounds like a phrasebook; one who says **λοιπόν** and **δηλαδή** in the right places sounds fluent.

**That last point is the rule for the whole stage.** Recognise everything; adopt slowly.

**Practice.** Read the next lesson. Then listen to ten minutes of any Greek conversation with one aim: count the **λοιπόν**s and the **δηλαδή**s.
The particles: λοιπόν, δηλαδή, βασικά:
The small words that organise a Greek sentence. They carry almost no meaning and they are everywhere, and using three of them correctly does more for your fluency than fifty new nouns.

**λοιπόν — so, well then, right.** It opens, resumes and concludes:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Λοιπόν, τι κάνουμε;** | Right, what are we doing? |
| **Λοιπόν, ξεκινάμε.** | OK, let's start. |
| **Λοιπόν;** | Well? / And so? |
| **Άρα λοιπόν…** | and therefore… |

**It is the single most frequent discourse word in spoken Greek**, and it is what a Greek says when gathering the conversation together. Learning to open with it is worth more than it looks.

**δηλαδή — that is, I mean, so you mean.** It restates, clarifies and questions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δηλαδή, δεν θα έρθεις;** | So you are not coming, then? |
| **…δηλαδή, θέλω να πω ότι…** | …that is, what I mean is… |
| **Δηλαδή;** | Meaning? |

**It is the learner's best friend**, because it legitimises a second attempt at a sentence you have made a mess of.

**βασικά — basically, actually.** It softens and corrects:

- **Βασικά, δεν ξέρω.** — Actually, I do not know.
- **Βασικά, είναι πιο περίπλοκο.** — Basically, it is more complicated.

**τελικά — in the end, as it turns out.**

- **Τελικά δεν πήγαμε.** — In the end we did not go.
- **Τελικά είχες δίκιο.** — You were right after all.

**The rest of the set:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **άρα** | so, therefore |
| **οπότε** | so then, at which point |
| **πάντως** | anyway, in any case |
| **ούτως ή άλλως** | in any case, anyway — slightly formal |
| **εντάξει** | OK — and as a question, *all right?* |
| **έτσι;** | right? — a tag question |
| **ξέρεις;** | you know? |
| **κατάλαβες;** | do you see? |
| **βρε παιδί μου** | an affectionate exasperation, untranslatable |
| **καλά** | fine, OK — and, with the right tone, *oh come on* |
| **μάλιστα** | indeed, I see, yes — formal, and the proper way to answer a superior |
| **ωραία** | lovely, good, fine — as an acknowledgement |
| **έγινε** | done, consider it done |
| **πω πω** | wow, oh dear — tone decides |
| **αμάν** | enough! / oh dear — from Turkish |
| **σιγά** | big deal — ironic, when said flatly |

**καλά and σιγά both reverse with tone**, which is worth knowing before you misread one: **καλά** said warmly is *fine*, said flatly is *oh, come off it*; **σιγά** means *slowly* and, said with a shrug, *so what*.

**The three to adopt this week**: **λοιπόν** at the start of a point, **δηλαδή** when restating, and **εντάξει** as acknowledgement. They are low-risk and immediately audible.

**Practice.** Say the four main particles in five sentences each. Then listen to ten minutes of Greek and count every **λοιπόν**, **δηλαδή** and **βασικά**. Then use **λοιπόν** and **δηλαδή** in your next conversation, deliberately.
ρε, βρε, μωρέ:
Three particles of address that have no English equivalent, that are everywhere in Greek speech, and that a foreigner should understand long before using.

**ρε — the familiar marker.** It attaches to an address and signals closeness:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ρε Γιώργο, τι κάνεις;** | Hey George, how are you? |
| **Τι λες, ρε;** | What are you saying, mate? |
| **Έλα ρε!** | Come on! |
| **Άσε ρε φίλε.** | Leave it, mate. |
| **Ρε συ!** | oi, you! |

**What it does.** Between friends it marks intimacy and warmth. From a stranger it is an intrusion. From a younger person to an older one it is rude. Said in an argument it raises the temperature.

**The rule for you: hear it constantly and use it almost never.** With a close friend of your own age, after they have used it to you, it is fine. With anyone at church who is older than you, with the priest, or with a woman you do not know well, it is not.

**βρε — softer than ρε**, older, and often affectionate:

- **Βρε παιδί μου…** — *my dear fellow*, with a sigh
- **Τι λες βρε;** — *what are you saying?*, gentler than the **ρε** version
- **Βρε Γιώργο…** — mildly remonstrating

**μωρέ — softer still, and old-fashioned.** Common from older speakers and in villages. **Μωρέ παιδί μου**, **μωρέ συ**. The feminine **μωρή** is a different matter: it is rude, often very rude, and should never be used.

**The address words that go with them:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **φίλε** | mate — to a man |
| **φιλενάδα** | — to a woman, but between women |
| **παιδί μου** | my child — used to adults, affectionately or with exasperation |
| **αγόρι μου / κορίτσι μου** | my boy / my girl — to any age, affectionately |
| **κουμπάρε** | the kinship term, used as a friendly address between men |
| **μάστορα** | *boss, chief* — to a tradesman, respectfully |
| **αρχηγέ / καπετάνιε** | chief, captain — jocular respect |
| **αδερφέ μου** | my brother — warm |
| **καρδιά μου / ψυχή μου** | my heart, my soul — to family and intimates |

**αγάπη μου, ψυχή μου and καρδιά μου are used much more widely than their English equivalents** — including by shopkeepers and older women to people they have just met — and they are not flirtatious. An older Greek woman calling you **παιδί μου** is being kind.

**What to do with all this.** Recognise it so that a conversation's temperature is legible to you: **ρε** tells you the register, **βρε** tells you the speaker is softening, **παιδί μου** tells you they are being kind, **μωρή** tells you something has gone wrong.

**And the one safe adoption**: **φίλε** to a man of your own age in an informal setting, and **παιδί μου** never — it is a senior's word.

**Practice.** Listen for **ρε** and **βρε** this week and note who uses them to whom. Then say the nine address words aloud. Then decide, for five people at your church, which of them you could call **φίλε** — and probably conclude none of them yet.
Emphasis: order, repetition and the doub:
How Greek stresses a word without raising the voice — three devices, all of which you have seen and none of which you have been using.

**1. Word order.** From stage 3: moving a word forward topicalises it.

- **Τον καφέ τον θέλω σκέτο.** — The coffee, I want it black.
- **Εμένα μου το είπε.** — It was me he told.
- **Στην Ελλάδα δεν έχω πάει ποτέ.** — Greece I have never been to.

**The doubled pronoun comes with it**, as that lesson said: a fronted noun is echoed by a weak pronoun before the verb. **Τον καφέ τον θέλω.** That doubling is the clearest single marker of natural spoken Greek.

**2. Repetition**, which Greek uses far more than English:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **σιγά σιγά** | slowly, slowly — little by little |
| **λίγο λίγο** | bit by bit |
| **γύρω γύρω** | round and round |
| **πάνω κάτω** | roughly, up and down |
| **ένα ένα** | one by one |
| **καλά καλά** | properly — **δεν ξέρω καλά καλά** |
| **τώρα τώρα** | right now |
| **μέσα μέσα** | right inside |
| **Όχι, όχι!** | no, no! |
| **Έλα, έλα.** | come on, come on |

**Doubling an adjective intensifies it**: **μικρός μικρός** (tiny), **ζεστό ζεστό** (piping hot). It is a real and productive device, not baby talk.

**3. The emphatic pronoun and the strong forms**, from stage 3: **εγώ**, **εμένα**, **δικό μου**.

- **Εγώ δεν ξέρω.** — *I* do not know.
- **Αυτό είναι δικό μου.** — That is *mine*.
- **Ο ίδιος ο παπάς.** — The priest *himself*.

**4. The intensifiers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **πολύ** | very |
| **πάρα πολύ** | very much indeed |
| **τρομερά / φοβερά** | terribly, awfully — and both mean *very* |
| **απίστευτα** | unbelievably |
| **τελείως** | completely |
| **εντελώς** | utterly |
| **κατά βάθος** | deep down |
| **ακριβώς** | exactly |
| **καθόλου** | not at all — with a negative |
| **ούτε λίγο** | not in the least |

**φοβερός and τρομερός both mean *terrible* and are used to mean *great***, exactly as English *terrific* did: **Ήταν φοβερό!** is a compliment.

**5. The cleft-like constructions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Αυτό που θέλω είναι…** | what I want is… |
| **Ο λόγος που…** | the reason why… |
| **Εκείνο που με ενοχλεί είναι…** | the thing that bothers me is… |
| **Δεν είναι ότι… αλλά…** | it is not that… but… |

**Practice.** Say five sentences with a fronted object and a doubled pronoun. Then say ten doubled words and two doubled adjectives. Then take one plain sentence and emphasise three different parts of it, three different ways.
Fillers, hesitation and buying time:
What to say while thinking — because silence while you construct a sentence ends your turn, and a filler keeps it.

**The fillers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **εεε…** | the Greek *er* |
| **λοιπόν…** | well… |
| **δηλαδή…** | that is… |
| **πώς να το πω…** | how shall I put it… |
| **τι να πω…** | what can I say… |
| **ξέρω 'γω…** | I dunno… — **ξέρω εγώ**, contracted |
| **για να δω…** | let me see… |
| **μισό λεπτό** | just a moment |
| **περίμενε** | wait |
| **κάτι σαν…** | something like… |
| **ας πούμε** | let's say, for instance |
| **τέλος πάντων** | anyway |
| **πού είχα μείνει;** | where was I? |
| **τι άλλο…** | what else… |

**ας πούμε is the most useful of them** — *let's say* — and it does duty for *like*, *sort of*, and *for example*, which means it fits almost anywhere.

**The paraphrase kit**, for when the word is gone:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν ξέρω τη λέξη.** | I do not know the word. |
| **Είναι σαν…** | it is like… |
| **Είναι κάτι που…** | it is something that… |
| **Το χρησιμοποιείς για να…** | you use it to… |
| **Πώς το λένε αυτό;** | what is this called? |
| **Το άλλο, εκείνο, αυτό εδώ** | the other one, that one, this one |
| **το πράγμα** | the thing |
| **αυτό το μηχάνημα** | that machine |

**Το πράγμα and αυτό are the universal stand-ins**, and pointing while saying **αυτό** is a complete communicative act.

**The repair moves**, for when the sentence has gone wrong:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Συγγνώμη, ξανά.** | Sorry, again. |
| **Δηλαδή, θέλω να πω…** | That is, what I mean is… |
| **Όχι, κάτσε.** | No, hang on. |
| **Πώς το λένε… α, ναι.** | What's it called… ah, yes. |
| **Ας το πω αλλιώς.** | Let me put it another way. |

**Κάτσε — *sit* — means *hang on*** when said like that, and it is extremely common.

**What not to do**, and this is the whole point of the lesson: do not fill the gap in English. An English *erm* or *you know* in the middle of a Greek sentence breaks the frame and invites the other person to switch languages. **Εεε** and **ας πούμε** keep you in Greek.

**And do not apologise repeatedly.** One **συγγνώμη** is fine; three in a minute makes the conversation about your Greek instead of about the subject.

**The target to aim for**: a two-minute turn with three fillers, two paraphrases and no English. That is what fluency sounds like at this level — not the absence of hesitation but hesitation in Greek.

**Practice.** Say the fourteen fillers aloud. Then describe five objects without naming them, using the paraphrase kit. Then narrate something for two minutes and count your English fillers — then do it again with Greek ones.
Interrupting, and holding the floor:
Greek conversation is more overlapping than English. This lesson is how to join it without rudeness and how to keep your turn when someone joins yours.

**The cultural fact first.** In a Greek conversation, waiting for a gap means never speaking. Overlap is not rudeness; it is engagement, and a conversation where everyone takes neat turns is a conversation where nobody is interested. An English speaker's politeness looks like disengagement.

**Getting in:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Συγγνώμη, μπορώ να πω κάτι;** | Sorry, may I say something? — formal |
| **Να πω κι εγώ κάτι;** | Can I say something too? |
| **Ένα λεπτό…** | one moment… |
| **Κάτσε, κάτσε…** | hang on, hang on… |
| **Ναι, αλλά…** | yes, but… |
| **Σωστά, και…** | right, and… |
| **Θέλω να πω μόνο ότι…** | I just want to say that… |
| **Μια ερώτηση.** | one question |
| **Για να καταλάβω…** | so that I understand… |

**Ναι, αλλά… is the standard way into a conversation** and it is not confrontational — it signals that you were listening and have a point.

**Holding your turn:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Κάτσε να τελειώσω.** | let me finish |
| **Μισό, μισό.** | hang on, hang on |
| **Άσε με να πω.** | let me speak |
| **Δύο πράγματα.** | two things — signposting |
| **Και κάτι άλλο.** | and another thing |
| **Δεν τελείωσα.** | I have not finished |

**Those are all perfectly polite in Greek**, including **άσε με να πω**, which would sound sharp translated into English.

**Signposting, which is the real technique.** Announcing how many points you have reserves the floor for all of them:

- **Θέλω να πω δύο πράγματα. Πρώτον… δεύτερον…**
- **Έχω μια ερώτηση και ένα σχόλιο.**

**πρώτον, δεύτερον, τρίτον** — firstly, secondly, thirdly — are the formal numerals used adverbially and they are the clearest floor-holders there are.

**Yielding gracefully:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πες, πες.** | go on, speak |
| **Σε ακούω.** | I am listening |
| **Ό,τι θες να πεις.** | whatever you want to say |
| **Τελείωσα.** | I have finished |
| **Εσύ τι λες;** | what do you think? |

**Εσύ τι λες; is the move that makes you a good conversationalist** in any language, and in Greek it is also a graceful way to stop talking before your grammar runs out.

**What to do about speed.** When three people are talking at once you will lose it entirely. The honest options are: ask one person to summarise — **Τι λέει;** — or wait and rejoin at the next topic. Both are normal, and **Δεν κατάλαβα, τι λέγατε;** is a perfectly ordinary thing to say.

**Practice.** Say the nine ways in and the six ways to hold your turn, aloud. Then practise a signposted turn: two points, numbered, in Greek, for a minute. Then listen to a Greek panel show and count the interruptions in two minutes.
Backchannelling: showing you are listeni:
The noises and short words that a listener makes, which in Greek are constant — and whose absence makes you look as though you have stopped following.

**The basic set:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ναι… ναι…** | yes… yes… |
| **Μμμ.** | mm |
| **Ωραία.** | good, right |
| **Εντάξει.** | OK |
| **Σωστά.** | right |
| **Βέβαια.** | of course |
| **Καλά.** | fine, I see |
| **Έτσι.** | just so |
| **Ακριβώς.** | exactly |
| **Φυσικά.** | naturally |
| **Μάλιστα.** | I see — formal |
| **Σοβαρά;** | seriously? |
| **Αλήθεια;** | really? |
| **Τι λες!** | you don't say! |
| **Πω πω!** | wow / oh dear |
| **Αμάν!** | oh no! / enough! |
| **Έλα!** | come on! / you're joking! |
| **Μπα!** | no! / surprise |
| **Κρίμα.** | what a shame |
| **Μπράβο.** | well done |
| **Δόξα τω Θεώ.** | thank God |
| **Ο Θεός να βάλει το χέρι του.** | God help us — of a bad situation |

**The frequency is the point.** A Greek listener produces one of these every few seconds. An English speaker's habit of listening in silence and nodding reads, in Greek, as either boredom or incomprehension — and it is one reason people switch to English with you: your silence looks like you are lost.

**So this is the cheapest fluency improvement available.** **Ναι, ναι** and **σωστά** cost nothing, require no grammar, and change how a conversation feels.

**The ones that do specific work:**

- **Αλήθεια; / Σοβαρά;** — invite more, and keep a story going.
- **Και μετά;** — *and then?* — the strongest continuation prompt there is.
- **Τι λες!** — surprise, and not a question.
- **Μπράβο!** — approval, given generously in Greek.
- **Κρίμα** and **Δόξα τω Θεώ** — the two moral reactions, and both expected at the right moment.

**The sympathetic set**, for bad news:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πω πω, κρίμα.** | oh dear, what a shame |
| **Καλά να περάσει.** | may it pass well |
| **Κουράγιο.** | courage |
| **Περαστικά.** | get well |
| **Να 'ναι καλά.** | bless them |
| **Τι να κάνουμε…** | what can you do |

**And the one gesture that goes with all of it**: a slow shake of the head, which in Greece accompanies sympathy rather than denial.

**Practice.** Listen to ten minutes of Greek conversation and count the backchannels. Then watch a scene and say the backchannels along with the listener. Then in your next conversation, produce one every few seconds — **ναι, ναι, σωστά, αλήθεια;** — and notice the difference in how long the other person talks to you.
Diminutives and augmentatives:
How Greek shrinks and enlarges a word, which it does constantly and which learners almost never do — and which carries affection rather than size.

**The diminutive endings:**

| Ending | Gender | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **-άκι** | neuter | παιδάκι, σπιτάκι, καφεδάκι, ψωμάκι, κρασάκι |
| **-ούλα** | feminine | γυναικούλα, μαμούλα, ωρίτσα? no — **αδερφούλα**, **γιαγιούλα** |
| **-ίτσα** | feminine | κοπελίτσα, ωρίτσα, μπιρίτσα |
| **-άκης** | masculine | Γιωργάκης, αδερφάκης |
| **-ούλης** | masculine | μικρούλης |
| **-ούδι / -ούλι** | neuter | αγγελούδι, μικρούλι |

**-άκι is the main one** and it is always neuter, whatever the gender of the original: **ο καφές → το καφεδάκι**, **η γυναίκα → το γυναικάκι**, **το παιδί → το παιδάκι**.

**What they actually mean**, and it is rarely size:

1. **Affection.** **Το παιδάκι μου** is not *my small child* but *my dear child*, and it is said to adults.
2. **Modesty about a request.** **Ένα καφεδάκι;** — *a little coffee?* — is politer and warmer than **ένας καφές**.
3. **Making something manageable.** **Μια δουλίτσα** — *a little job* — minimises what you are asking for.
4. **Pleasantness.** **Ένα κρασάκι, λίγο ψωμάκι, μια ωρίτσα στον ήλιο** — the whole of a Greek good afternoon in three diminutives.
5. **Occasionally, condescension.** Tone decides, and **γυναικούλα** can be dismissive.

**Greeks use them constantly.** A waiter will offer **ένα γλυκάκι**, a friend will suggest **ένα ουζάκι**, your host will press **λίγο φαγητάκι**. Not using them at all makes your Greek flat; using them where a Greek would is one of the clearest signs of a good ear.

**Names take them too**, which is how affection works in a family: **Γιώργος → Γιωργάκης**, **Μαρία → Μαράκι**, **Ελένη → Ελενάκι**, **Κωνσταντίνος → Κωστάκης**. Using a diminutive of someone's name is intimate; wait to be invited.

**The augmentatives**, which are rarer:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **-άρα** | μπιράρα (a big beer), γυναικάρα (a magnificent woman), δουλειάρα |
| **-αράς** | ψηλαράς (very tall man), φαγανάρας |
| **-ούκλα** | σπιτούκλα — a great big house |

**-άρα is admiring** more than it is descriptive: **αυτοκινητάρα** is *a hell of a car*.

**And the pejorative endings**: **-ίλα** for a bad smell (**ψαρίλα**), **-ούρα** for an unpleasant state (**ζεστούρα**, **πλήξη** — no: **βαρεμάρα**).

**The two to adopt immediately**: **καφεδάκι** when offering or ordering coffee socially, and **λίγο** plus a diminutive when asking for something — **λίγο ψωμάκι, λίγο νεράκι**. Both are small, both are instantly natural.

**Practice.** Make diminutives of ten words you use daily. Then order a coffee and a sweet using diminutives. Then listen for them this week and count how many you hear in one conversation — it will be more than you expect.
Idioms: the body:
The first of four idiom lessons. Greek, like English, hangs a great deal of its idiom on the body — and most of these are opaque until someone tells you.

**The head:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μου έφαγε το κεφάλι.** | He drove me mad. (*ate my head*) |
| **Έχω πονοκέφαλο με αυτό.** | It is a headache. |
| **Δεν βάζει μυαλό.** | He will not learn sense. |
| **Του πήρε το κεφάλι.** | It went to his head. |
| **Κουνάω το κεφάλι.** | I shake my head. |
| **Στο κεφάλι μου!** | on my own head — accepting responsibility |

**The eyes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Με τα μάτια μου το είδα.** | I saw it with my own eyes. |
| **Κλείνω τα μάτια σε κάτι.** | I turn a blind eye. |
| **Μάτια μου!** | my dear — a term of endearment |
| **Έχει μάτι.** | he has an eye for it — and also *the evil eye* |
| **Το μάτι** / **το κακό μάτι** | the evil eye — and **ξεματιάζω**, to undo it |
| **Μάτι με μάτι** | face to face |

**το μάτι deserves the note**: belief in the evil eye is widespread and casual, the blue charm against it is everywhere, and **Σε ματιάσανε** — *someone has given you the eye* — is said half-seriously about a headache. The Church disapproves and grandmothers persist.

**The mouth and tongue:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Από το στόμα σου και στον Θεό.** | From your mouth to God's ear. |
| **Μου βγήκε η γλώσσα.** | I was worn out. (*my tongue came out*) |
| **Έχει γλώσσα.** | He has a sharp tongue. |
| **Δεν βάζει γλώσσα μέσα.** | He never stops talking. |
| **Στο στόμα του λύκου** | into the lion's den |

**The hands:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Βάζω το χέρι μου στη φωτιά.** | I would swear to it. |
| **Μου δένει τα χέρια.** | It ties my hands. |
| **Με τα χέρια μου το έκανα.** | I made it with my own hands. |
| **Έχει χέρι.** | He is handy, he has a knack. |
| **Χέρι χέρι** | hand in hand |
| **Δίνω ένα χέρι.** | I lend a hand. |

**The heart and soul:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Με όλη μου την καρδιά.** | with all my heart |
| **Μου ράγισε την καρδιά.** | It broke my heart. |
| **Καρδιά μου / ψυχή μου** | my heart, my soul — endearments |
| **Βάλε τα δυνατά σου.** | Do your utmost. |
| **Με την ψυχή στο στόμα** | out of breath, in a panic |
| **Καλή σου καρδιά.** | bless your kind heart |

**The feet and legs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Με τα πόδια** | on foot |
| **Στα πόδια μου** | under my feet, in my way |
| **Πήρε πόδι.** | He got the sack. |
| **Το πόδι του δεν πάτησε εδώ.** | He never set foot here. |

**How to learn these.** Card them whole, learn ten at a time, and use three. The value of the other seven is recognition: when someone says **μου έφαγε το κεφάλι** you need to know they are exasperated, not hungry.

**Practice.** Say all thirty aloud. Then pick five you would actually use and put each in a sentence. Then ask a Greek friend which of them they say — the answers will surprise you, and the asking is a conversation.
Idioms: food, drink and the table:
The second idiom lesson, and the richest, because Greek thinks about food constantly and says so.

**Bread, salt and oil — the staples, and the deepest idioms:**

| | |
