| --- | --- |
| **Ψωμί και αλάτι** | bread and salt — a shared life, a long friendship |
| **Φάγαμε ψωμί και αλάτι μαζί.** | We have been through a lot together. |
| **Βγάζω το ψωμί μου.** | I earn my living. |
| **Του έκοψε το ψωμί.** | He took away his livelihood. |
| **Λάδι στη φωτιά** | oil on the fire |
| **Τα λάδωσε.** | He greased palms. |
| **Αλάτι στην πληγή** | salt in the wound |

**Eating and drinking:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τρώω τον κόσμο να…** | I search everywhere to… |
| **Μου τα έφαγε όλα.** | He ate up all my money. |
| **Έφαγα πόρτα.** | I was turned away. (*I ate door*) |
| **Έφαγα χυλόπιτα.** | I was rejected, romantically. |
| **Τρώγοντας έρχεται η όρεξη.** | Appetite comes with eating. |
| **Πίνω στην υγειά σου.** | I drink your health. |
| **Τα ήπιε.** | He got drunk. |
| **Το γλυκό και το πικρό** | the sweet and the bitter |

**Έφαγα πόρτα and έφαγα χυλόπιτα are both worth knowing** — being refused entry and being turned down — and both are extremely common.

**The sweet and the sour:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **γλυκό σαν μέλι** | sweet as honey |
| **Μου έγινε ξύδι.** | It turned sour on me. |
| **Του γλυκού νερού** | *of sweet water* — amateurish, soft |
| **αλμυρός λογαριασμός** | a salty bill — an expensive one |
| **Μην τα κάνεις θάλασσα.** | Do not make a mess of it. (*do not make it sea*) |

**Cooking as metaphor:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Σιγοβράζει.** | It is simmering — of a situation. |
| **Ψήνεται.** | He is being roasted — put under pressure; and *it is being cooked up*. |
| **Μαγειρεύουν κάτι.** | They are cooking something up. |
| **Τα έκανε μαντάρα.** | He made a complete hash of it. |
| **Τα κάνω σαλάτα.** | I make a salad of it — I muddle it up. |

**The table phrases, which you will use:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλή όρεξη!** | enjoy your meal |
| **Με γεια!** | — said when someone uses something new, or has a haircut, or starts a meal |
| **Και στα δικά σου!** | may your own come too |
| **Στην υγειά μας!** | our health |
| **Γούρι!** | good luck — on a first drink or a new thing |
| **Ό,τι φάμε, ό,τι πιούμε κι ό,τι αρπάξει ο κώλος μας** | roughly *eat, drink, and grab what you can* — a famously fatalistic toast |

**Με γεια is one to learn and use**: said to someone wearing something new, with a new haircut, or enjoying a new possession. There is no English equivalent and Greeks notice when a foreigner says it.

**And the food words used of people:**

- **γλυκός / γλυκιά** — sweet, as a character
- **ψωμωμένος** — well-built, *bready*
- **ξινός** — sour-faced
- **Είναι ψωμί με ψωμί.** — of a situation with nothing in it

**Practice.** Say all thirty aloud. Then learn **Με γεια**, **Έφαγα πόρτα** and **Μην τα κάνεις θάλασσα** properly. Then use **Με γεια** the next time someone at church has something new.
Idioms: God, saints and the devil:
The third idiom lesson, and the one most relevant to you: religious language is woven through ordinary Greek speech, often with no religious intent at all.

**God in everyday speech:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δόξα τω Θεώ.** | thank God — said constantly, about anything |
| **Πρώτα ο Θεός.** | God first — *if God wills*, before any plan |
| **Ο Θεός βοηθός.** | God help us |
| **Θεού θέλοντος** | God willing |
| **Ο Θεός να δώσει.** | may God grant it |
| **Ο Θεός να μη δώσει.** | God forbid |
| **Ο Θεός να σε φυλάει.** | God keep you |
| **Για τον Θεό!** | for God's sake! |
| **Θεός φυλάξοι.** | God preserve us — learned, and common |
| **Έχει ο Θεός.** | God will provide |
| **Ο Θεός ξέρει.** | God knows |
| **Ο Θεός να βάλει το χέρι του.** | may God intervene |

**Πρώτα ο Θεός is the one to notice.** Any statement about the future gets it: **Θα πάμε το καλοκαίρι, πρώτα ο Θεός.** It is the Greek equivalent of *God willing*, it is said by the devout and the indifferent alike, and omitting it from a plan sounds slightly bald.

**Christ and the Panagia:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Χριστέ μου!** | my Christ! — surprise or dismay |
| **Παναγία μου!** | Holy Mother! — the same |
| **Για την αγάπη του Χριστού** | for the love of Christ |
| **Χριστός κι Απόστολος** | the bare minimum of people present |
| **Να με συγχωρεί η Παναγία** | may the Panagia forgive me |

**The saints:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Έχει τον άγιό του.** | He has his saint — he has protection, connections. |
| **Κάθε άγιος και το θαύμα του.** | every saint has his own miracle — everyone has their speciality |
| **Από τον Άγιο Νικόλα…** | invoked by sailors and travellers |
| **Ο άγιος που δεν τον ξέρεις…** | the saint you do not know… — of unfamiliar authority |

**Έχει τον άγιό του** is a political idiom as much as a religious one: it means someone is protected by a patron.

**The devil:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Στον διάολο!** | to hell with it |
| **Άι στον διάολο.** | go to hell |
| **Ο διάολος να το πάρει.** | the devil take it |
| **Έχει διάολο μέσα του.** | he has the devil in him — of a lively child |
| **Μη λες τον διάολο.** | do not speak of the devil |
| **Του διαόλου κάλτσα** | a crafty one (*the devil's sock*) |
| **Φωτιά και λάβρα** | fire and brimstone |

**The ones used of death, from stage 6:** **Θεός σχωρέσ' τον**, **Αιωνία του η μνήμη**, **Καλό Παράδεισο**, **Ο Θεός να τον αναπαύσει**.

**And the sayings with a church shape:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Κάλλιο αργά παρά ποτέ.** | better late than never |
| **Ό,τι σπείρεις θα θερίσεις.** | as you sow, so shall you reap |
| **Ο Θεός αγαπά τον κλέφτη, αγαπά και τον νοικοκύρη.** | God loves the thief and the householder both |
| **Συν Αθηνά και χείρα κίνει.** | *with Athena, move your hand too* — God helps those who help themselves, and pre-Christian |

**The register note that matters for you.** None of this is blasphemy and most of it is not piety either: **Δόξα τω Θεώ** from a shopkeeper is as automatic as English *thank goodness*. Knowing that stops you over-reading it — and it is also why these phrases are the easiest religious Greek to adopt, because nobody will think you are preaching.

**Practice.** Say all of them aloud. Then adopt **Δόξα τω Θεώ** and **Πρώτα ο Θεός** this week, in the places a Greek would use them. Then listen for how often you hear them — it will be dozens of times.
Idioms: animals, weather and the rest:
The last idiom lesson, and then the proverbs. These are the ones that will stop you dead in a conversation if you have not met them.

**Animals:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Κάνει τη πάπια.** | He plays the duck — pretends not to know. |
| **Σιγά τα λάχανα!** | big deal! (*easy on the cabbages* — not an animal, but the same tone) |
| **Έγινε γάτα.** | He became a cat — he got clever, or he thinned down. |
| **Είναι λύκος.** | He is a wolf — shrewd, ruthless. |
| **Πρόβατο** | a sheep — a follower |
| **Είναι γάιδαρος.** | He is a donkey — rude, boorish. |
| **Με τα κουνέλια** | — of breeding fast |
| **Κάθε πράμα στον καιρό του, κι ο κολιός τον Αύγουστο.** | everything in its season, and mackerel in August |
| **Όποιος βιάζεται σκοντάφτει.** | he who hurries stumbles |
| **Μια χελιδόνα δεν φέρνει την άνοιξη.** | one swallow does not bring the spring |

**Weather and the sea:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Βρέχει καρεκλοπόδαρα.** | It is raining chair legs — cats and dogs. |
| **Μας τα έκανε θάλασσα.** | He made a mess of it. |
| **Είναι θάλασσα.** | it is a sea — chaos |
| **Μπήκε το νερό στο αυλάκι.** | the water is in the channel — things are on track |
| **Πάει καλά ο καιρός.** | the weather is holding |
| **Αέρα!** | the war cry, literally *wind* — used as encouragement |
| **Μπουνάτσα** | a dead calm — of the sea and of life |

**Money and work:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν έχω φράγκο.** | I have not got a penny. |
| **Του κόστισε τα μαλλιά της κεφαλής του.** | It cost him the hair of his head. |
| **Δουλεύω σαν σκυλί.** | I work like a dog. |
| **Τα έκανε φύλλο και φτερό.** | He turned the place upside down. |
| **Είναι πανάκριβο.** | It is horribly expensive. |
| **Τζάμπα** | free, for nothing — from Turkish |
| **Μαύρα** | *black* — cash in hand, undeclared |

**Time:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Του χρόνου** | next year |
| **Στο πιτς φιτίλι** | in a flash |
| **Με το σταγονόμετρο** | with an eyedropper — very slowly, grudgingly |
| **Αύριο-μεθαύριο** | one of these days |
| **Σιγά σιγά** | little by little |
| **Του αγίου Ποτέ** | St Never's day — i.e. never |
| **Έχει καιρό.** | it has been a while |

**Του αγίου Ποτέ is worth having** — the feast of St Never — and it is how Greeks describe a promise that will not be kept.

**People and character:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Είναι εντάξει άνθρωπος.** | He is a decent person. — high praise |
| **Είναι του χεριού μου.** | He is in my pocket. |
| **Τα έχει τετρακόσια.** | He is all there, sharp. |
| **Χάνει τα αυγά και τα καλάθια.** | He loses the eggs and the baskets — he is all at sea. |
| **Του φταίει ο κόσμος.** | He blames the world. |
| **Είναι άλλο πράγμα.** | He / it is something else. |
| **Σπάει πλάκα.** | He is joking, having a laugh. |
| **Μας δούλεψε.** | He had us on. |

**Σπάει πλάκα and μας δούλεψε are the two to know** for recognising when you are being teased, which in a Greek group you will be, affectionately.

**Practice.** Say them all aloud once. Then pick the ten you are most likely to hear and card them. Then ask someone Greek to explain **σιγά τα λάχανα** and **του αγίου Ποτέ** — the explanation will be enjoyable.
Proverbs:
The fifty that get quoted, which is a cultural index as much as a language one — and knowing a dozen of them makes you legible in a way vocabulary does not.

**The ones you will actually hear:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Όπου υπάρχει καπνός, υπάρχει και φωτιά.** | no smoke without fire |
| **Κάλλιο αργά παρά ποτέ.** | better late than never |
| **Ο πνιγμένος από τα μαλλιά του πιάνεται.** | a drowning man clutches at his own hair |
| **Όποιος βιάζεται σκοντάφτει.** | he who hurries stumbles |
| **Η καλή μέρα από το πρωί φαίνεται.** | a good day shows from the morning |
| **Μια χελιδόνα δεν φέρνει την άνοιξη.** | one swallow does not bring the spring |
| **Ό,τι σπείρεις θα θερίσεις.** | as you sow, so shall you reap |
| **Φασούλι το φασούλι γεμίζει το σακούλι.** | bean by bean the sack is filled |
| **Ο καλός ο μύλος όλα τα αλέθει.** | a good mill grinds everything |
| **Στου κουφού την πόρτα όσο θέλεις βρόντα.** | knock all you like at the deaf man's door |
| **Το μήλο κάτω από τη μηλιά θα πέσει.** | the apple falls under the apple tree |
| **Άλλαξε ο Μανωλιός κι έβαλε τα ρούχα αλλιώς.** | Manolis changed — and put his clothes on differently. (*nothing has changed*) |
| **Όποιος δεν θέλει να ζυμώσει, δέκα μέρες κοσκινίζει.** | he who does not want to knead sieves for ten days |
| **Κάθε εμπόδιο για καλό.** | every obstacle is for the good |
| **Σιγά σιγά πάει μακριά.** | slowly goes far |
| **Μάτια που δεν βλέπονται γρήγορα λησμονιούνται.** | eyes that do not see each other soon forget |
| **Τα πολλά λόγια είναι φτώχεια.** | many words are poverty |
| **Όποιος καεί στο χυλό φυσάει και το γιαούρτι.** | burnt by porridge, he blows on the yoghurt |
| **Η γλώσσα κόκαλα δεν έχει και κόκαλα τσακίζει.** | the tongue has no bones and breaks bones |
| **Αγάλι αγάλι γίνεται η αγουρίδα μέλι.** | slowly, slowly the unripe grape becomes honey |
| **Ο κόσμος το 'χει τούμπανο κι εμείς κρυφό καμάρι.** | the world has it as a drum and we as a secret pride |
| **Όπου ακούς πολλά κεράσια, κρατά μικρό καλάθι.** | where you hear of many cherries, take a small basket |
| **Έχει ο καιρός γυρίσματα.** | time has its turns |
| **Το καλό πράγμα αργεί να γίνει.** | a good thing takes time |
| **Οι τοίχοι έχουν αυτιά.** | the walls have ears |

**Κάθε εμπόδιο για καλό** is the one said to you when something goes wrong, and **Αγάλι αγάλι γίνεται η αγουρίδα μέλι** is the one said to you about learning Greek. Both are kind and both are worth recognising.

**The ones about speech and silence**, which recur in a culture that talks:

- **Τα πολλά λόγια είναι φτώχεια.**
- **Η γλώσσα κόκαλα δεν έχει…**
- **Ο σιωπών δοκεί συναινείν.** — *he who is silent seems to consent*, in the learned register and still quoted.

**The ones that are Ancient Greek and still current:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γνώθι σαυτόν.** | know thyself |
| **Μέτρον άριστον.** | moderation is best |
| **Εν οίδα ότι ουδέν οίδα.** | I know one thing: that I know nothing |
| **Νους υγιής εν σώματι υγιεί.** | a healthy mind in a healthy body |
| **Αρχή άνδρα δείκνυσι.** | office reveals the man |
| **Συν Αθηνά και χείρα κίνει.** | with Athena, move your hand too |

**Those are quoted in their ancient form**, by ordinary people, in ordinary conversation — which is one of the genuinely distinctive things about Greek and a glimpse of the later curriculum.

**How many to learn.** Ten to use and thirty to recognise. The use is the smaller half: deploying a proverb correctly in a conversation is a party trick and a good one, but recognising the one being said to you matters more.

**Practice.** Read all of them aloud. Pick five you like and learn them properly. Then ask a Greek for their favourite — everyone has one — and learn that too.
Gestures:
A short lesson with practical consequences: Greek gestures, including the two that an English speaker will get badly wrong.

**The two that matter most:**

**1. Yes and no are reversed from what you expect.**

- **Yes** is a single downward nod — a quick dip of the head.
- **No** is a single upward tilt of the head, often with raised eyebrows and a small *tsk*.

**That upward tilt reads to an English speaker as *what?* or as haughtiness.** It means no. Likewise the Greek **no** sound — a sharp intake through the teeth, written **ττ** or heard as *ts* — is a complete and polite negative.

**2. The open palm — η μούντζα — is an insult.**

Holding up an open hand with the fingers spread, palm towards someone, is deeply rude in Greece — the equivalent of a raised middle finger, and worse with two hands. So:

- **Do not wave with an open palm facing someone.** Wave with the palm turned slightly or with the fingers together.
- **Do not hold up five fingers to mean *five***. Use the thumb and fingers folded differently, or just say **πέντε**.

**That one is worth real care**, because an English wave or an English *five* is a genuine insult delivered by accident, and it is noticed.

**The rest of the useful set:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Head tilt up + eyebrows** | no |
| **Single downward nod** | yes |
| **Hand shaken side to side, fingers spread** | so-so, roughly |
| **Fingers pinched and drawn together** | delicious, or *exactly* |
| **Both hands raised, palms up, shaken** | what do you want me to do? |
| **Flat hand chopped downwards** | enough, that's final |
| **Index finger wagged** | no, don't |
| **Hand on the heart** | sincerity, thanks |
| **Kissing the fingers** | something is beautiful |
| **Tapping the temple** | he is clever — or, with a different motion, mad |
| **Hand swept over the shoulder** | the past, or *forget it* |
| **Three fingers crossed over the chest** | crossing oneself — right shoulder first |

**Crossing oneself is right shoulder first**, with thumb and first two fingers joined, and it happens on passing a church, at a blessing, at a difficult moment, and before eating. You are not obliged to and it is noticed warmly if you do.

**The spitting**, which you will see and should not be alarmed by: a small triple *ftou ftou ftou*, often with a gesture, to avert the evil eye — especially after praising a child. It is affectionate, it is universal, and declining to join in is fine.

**Physical distance.** Greeks stand closer, touch more, and kiss on both cheeks between friends and relatives — including men. A handshake is for first meetings and formal settings; after that, expect the two kisses, right cheek first.

**Practice.** Practise the up-tilt *no* and the down-nod *yes* until they are not confusing. Then make sure you never wave with a flat open palm again. Then watch a Greek film for ten minutes with the sound off and count the gestures you now recognise.
The colloquial grammar:
What people actually say, as against what the grammar says — and all of it is standard spoken Greek rather than error.

**1. Longer verb endings.** Spoken Greek adds a syllable:

| Written | Spoken |
| --- | --- |
| έχουν | **έχουνε** |
| είναι | **είναι / ένε** |
| ήμουν | **ήμουνα** |
| ήταν | **ήτανε** |
| γράφουν | **γράφουνε** |
| μπορούν | **μπορούνε** |

**Those -νε endings are everywhere in speech** and in song lyrics, and they are not sloppy — they are the older forms surviving.

**2. Dropped final syllables and vowels:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **είμαστε → είμαστ'** | |
| **θα → θ'** | **θ' ακούσω** |
| **και → κι** | before a vowel: **κι εγώ** |
| **σε → σ'** | **σ' αγαπώ** |
| **μου → μ'** | **μ' αρέσει** |
| **να → ν'** | **ν' ακούσω** |
| **πού είναι → πού 'ναι** | |
| **θα είμαι → θα 'μαι** | |

**Those apostrophes from stage 1's punctuation lesson are what spoken Greek looks like written down**, and song lyrics are full of them.

**3. The relative que-like που for everything**, as stage 3 said: **ο άντρας που μίλησα μαζί του** rather than the formal **με τον οποίο**.

**4. Pronoun doubling**, from the emphasis lesson: **Τον Γιώργο τον είδα.**

**5. Resumptive and loose syntax.** Spoken Greek starts a sentence, abandons it and restarts — **Ο αδερφός μου… δηλαδή, ο μεγάλος… αυτός μου το είπε.** That is normal and it is what a transcript of any language looks like.

**6. The present for the past, in narrative:**

- **Και πάω εγώ στο μαγαζί, και τι να δω…** — *So I go to the shop, and what do I see…*

**The historic present is the standard way to tell a lively story**, exactly as in English, and it is worth adopting because it is easier than the aorist.

**7. Double marking of the negative**, from stage 2: **Δεν ξέρω τίποτα.**

**8. The vocative with ρε and the article dropped**, from earlier in this stage.

**9. Aorist for the perfect**, from stage 6: **Έφαγες;**

**10. Questions as statements** with rising intonation: **Θα έρθεις;** — and in speech often just **Θα έρθεις.** with the tone doing the work.

**11. The emphatic double negative με το ούτε**: **Ούτε ξέρω ούτε θέλω να ξέρω.**

**12. να instead of an imperative**, which is softer and extremely common: **Να μου πεις** rather than **Πες μου**.

**What to do with this lesson.** All twelve are for recognition, and three or four are worth adopting: the **-νε** endings, the elisions, the historic present, and **να** instead of the imperative. Adopting the elisions in particular makes your speech sound less recited.

**And the honest note**: what you have been taught in stages 2 to 6 is standard written and spoken Greek, and none of it is wrong. This lesson is the difference between a well-formed sentence and the way a sentence actually comes out of a mouth.

**Practice.** Say ten sentences with the long **-νε** endings. Then say five with elisions — **σ' αγαπώ, μ' αρέσει, πού 'ναι, θα 'μαι, κι εγώ**. Then tell a thirty-second story in the historic present.
Register: five ways to say one thing:
The same meaning at five levels, which is what register is — and knowing where you are on the scale is as important as being correct.

**Take *I would like to ask you something*:**

| Level | |
| --- | --- |
| **Intimate** | **Ρε, άκου κάτι.** |
| **Casual** | **Θέλω να σε ρωτήσω κάτι.** |
| **Neutral** | **Θα ήθελα να σε ρωτήσω κάτι.** |
| **Polite** | **Θα ήθελα να σας ρωτήσω κάτι.** |
| **Formal / written** | **Θα ήθελα να σας υποβάλω ένα ερώτημα.** |

**And *he died*:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Blunt** | **πέθανε** |
| **Neutral** | **έφυγε από τη ζωή** |
| **Church** | **εκοιμήθη** |
| **Formal notice** | **απεβίωσε** |
| **Euphemistic** | **μας άφησε** |

**The five registers of Modern Greek, in practice:**

1. **Intimate and slang** — **ρε, μαλάκα** between friends, elisions, no formality.
2. **Casual spoken** — the Greek of this curriculum's stages 2 to 5.
3. **Neutral standard** — what you write in an email and say to a stranger.
4. **Formal** — the polite plural, the conditional, longer vocabulary: **παρακαλείσθε, οφείλετε, δύνασθε**.
5. **Learned** — the fossils and the katharevousa remnants: **εν τω μεταξύ, ως προς, άνευ, περί**.

**The fifth is the one this curriculum deliberately skips**, by your ruling — it is the later classical curriculum's material — and the practical approach to it is: recognise, do not produce. If you write **άνευ** in an email you will sound like a notary.

**How to tell which register a text is in**, which is the reading skill:

| Marker | Register |
| --- | --- |
| **που** as relative, elisions, **ρε** | casual |
| **ο οποίος**, passives, perfects | formal |
| **εν, ως, άνευ, περί, διά** | learned |
| **-ωσις, -ότης, -μένως** endings | learned |
| Participles in **-ων, -ούσα** | learned |
| Diminutives, idiom, doubling | casual |

**Where each belongs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Parish hall** | casual, with the polite plural for elders |
| **Email to a stranger** | neutral to formal |
| **Official letter** | formal |
| **A shop** | casual with the polite plural |
| **A notice** | formal, with passives |
| **A church service** | learned and liturgical — not your register, and not expected to be |

**The mistake to avoid**, and learners make it both ways: over-formal in the hall (which is stiff and distancing) and over-casual in writing (which reads as uneducated). The rule of thumb: **speak one notch less formally than you write.**

**Practice.** Take one sentence — *can you help me* — and say it at all five levels. Then read three Greek texts and place each on the scale. Then write one email at the neutral register and say the same content out loud at the casual one.
Loanwords: Turkish, Italian, English:
Where a lot of everyday Greek vocabulary came from, which explains the words that look like nothing else in the language.

**Turkish, from four centuries of Ottoman rule.** Mostly food, household, trade and emotion:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **το τζάκι** | fireplace | **το ντουλάπι** | cupboard |
| **ο τενεκές** | tin | **το γιαούρτι** | yoghurt |
| **ο καφές** | coffee | **το κέφι** | good spirits, mood |
| **ο μεζές** | small plate | **το ντέρτι** | sorrow, longing |
| **το μαχαλάς** | neighbourhood | **ο μπακάλης** | grocer |
| **το χαρτζιλίκι** | pocket money | **ο μάστορας** | craftsman |
| **τζάμπα** | free | **μπράβο** — no, that is Italian | |
| **γλέντι** | celebration | **σόι** | clan, extended family |
| **μπουνάτσα** — Italian | | **αμάν** | oh dear, enough |
| **γιαπί** | building site | **ζόρι** | difficulty, force |

**κέφι and ντέρτι are the two with no translation** — the first is the pleasure of an occasion, the second a sweet melancholy — and both are central to how Greeks talk about music and feeling.

**Italian and Venetian**, from the trading centuries and the Ionian islands. Mostly sea, music, and the house:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **η μπάντα** | band, side | **το μπαλκόνι** | balcony |
| **η πόρτα** | door | **το κανάλι** | channel |
| **η σκάλα** | stairs | **το κουζίνα** — η κουζίνα | kitchen |
| **το μαντολίνο** | mandolin | **η μπύρα** | beer |
| **φρέσκος** | fresh | **μπράβο** | well done |
| **ο καπετάνιος** | captain | **το μπαρκάρω** | to embark |
| **η φουρτούνα** | rough sea | **τα μακαρόνια** | pasta |

**English, from the last fifty years.** Technology, business and youth language:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το κομπιούτερ / ο υπολογιστής** | computer — and the Greek coinage competes |
| **το ίντερνετ / το διαδίκτυο** | internet — likewise |
| **το κινητό** | mobile — a Greek word, from *moving* |
| **το μέιλ / το ηλεκτρονικό ταχυδρομείο** | email |
| **τα σπορ** | sport |
| **το πάρτι** | party |
| **ο μάνατζερ** | manager |
| **κάνω λάικ / σέρφινγκ / ζάπινγκ** | the verbs made from English nouns |
| **τζιν, σορτς, τοστ, σάντουιτς, τσεκ** | the obvious ones |

**Greek resists English more actively than most languages**, with official coinages that sometimes win: **διαδίκτυο** for internet, **υπολογιστής** for computer, **κινητό** for mobile, **ιστοσελίδα** for website. Both forms circulate and the Greek one is commoner in writing.

**The giveaway for a loanword**: it does not inflect. **Το ταξί, το μετρό, το πάρτι, το σορτς, το ευρώ** keep one form for everything, which is the sign that a word arrived recently.

**Why this lesson is useful.** Because when a word looks unlike Greek, there is usually a reason, and knowing the reason makes it stick: **τζάκι** is Turkish, **μπαλκόνι** is Italian, **πάρτι** is English, and none of them will yield to a Greek etymology.

**Practice.** Sort twenty words you know by likely origin. Then learn **κέφι** and **ντέρτι** properly, because both will be used about music in your hearing. Then list five English words Greek has taken and five Greek coinages that resist them.
Slang, the internet and youth language:
The register you will hear from anyone under thirty and read in every message — and which no textbook includes.

**The general-purpose slang:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **τέλειο / τέλεια** | perfect, brilliant |
| **φοβερό** | great (*terrible*) |
| **χάλια** | awful |
| **κουλό** | weird, daft |
| **άσχετο** | irrelevant — and *clueless* of a person |
| **χαζό** | silly |
| **μπερδεμένο** | confusing |
| **κομμάτι** | *a bit* — **κομμάτι δύσκολο** |
| **πλάκα** | a joke — **για πλάκα**, for fun |
| **φάση** | *a situation, a vibe* — **τι φάση;** what's going on? |
| **καψούρα** | infatuation |
| **ξενέρωτο** | a let-down, uncool |
| **χαλαρά** | easily, relaxed |
| **άνετα** | comfortably, easily |
| **στα παπάρια μου** | — vulgar; *I don't care*. Recognise, do not say. |
| **δεν παίζει** | no chance (*it doesn't play*) |
| **το πήρα** | I get it |
| **έχει ψωμί** | there is potential in it (*it has bread*) |
| **σκίζει** | it's outstanding (*it tears*) |
| **τα σπάει** | it's brilliant (*it breaks things*) |

**τι φάση; is the current all-purpose question** among younger speakers — *what's going on, what is this* — and **φάση** has become a universal noun for a situation.

**The messaging conventions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τπτ** | τίποτα |
| **Τι κανς;** | τι κάνεις |
| **Καλημ** | καλημέρα |
| **Ευχ** | ευχαριστώ |
| **Δστχ** | δυστυχώς |
| **Σ'σγπ / σ'αγαπώ** | σε αγαπώ |
| **Λοπν** | λοιπόν |
| **ΟΚ / οκ / εντ** | εντάξει |
| **χαχαχα / χαχα** | laughing |
| **:) 😊 ❤️** | as everywhere |

**Greeklish**, from stage 1: Greek in Latin letters, used constantly in messages by older people and increasingly less by the young, who have Greek keyboards. You should read it: **kalimera, ti kaneis, tha se paro, s'agapo**.

**The internet vocabulary:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το προφίλ** | profile |
| **η ανάρτηση / το ποστ** | post |
| **κάνω λάικ / μου αρέσει** | to like |
| **το σχόλιο** | comment |
| **ο κωδικός** | password |
| **η οθόνη** | screen |
| **το πληκτρολόγιο** | keyboard |
| **κατεβάζω / ανεβάζω** | download / upload |
| **στέλνω μήνυμα** | to message |
| **μπλοκάρω** | to block |
| **η εφαρμογή** | app |
| **ο λογαριασμός** | account — the same word as *bill* |

**κατεβάζω and ανεβάζω are the Greek words that won** — literally *take down* and *take up* — and they are what everyone says.

**The register warning.** Slang dates fast, it varies by city and age, and a foreigner using it slightly wrong sounds worse than a foreigner not using it at all. **Τέλειο**, **πλάκα** and **χαλαρά** are safe; the rest is for recognition.

**And the one thing to avoid completely**: the vulgar items. You will hear **μαλάκα** used between friends as punctuation — it is the commonest word in young male speech — and it is not available to you until a Greek friend uses it to you first. The next lesson deals with that properly.

**Practice.** Read ten Greek Instagram or Facebook comments and work out every abbreviation. Then learn **τι φάση;**, **τέλειο**, **πλάκα** and **χαλαρά**. Then write a message in Greek with two abbreviations in it.
What you need to recognise and not say:
A short, clinical lesson on swearing and insult — for comprehension, because you will hear all of it, and for the sake of not using it by accident.

**Why this lesson exists.** Greek swears freely and inventively, including in company where English would not. Not knowing the words means missing the temperature of a conversation and occasionally missing the content. Knowing them does not mean using them.

**The one you will hear most: μαλάκα.** Literally vulgar, functionally a vocative between male friends meaning roughly *mate* — and used as sentence filler by young men dozens of times an hour. From a stranger, or in anger, it is a real insult. **It is not available to you** until a Greek friend uses it to you, and even then, not at church.

**The general-purpose expletives:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **γαμώτο** | damn — vulgar, very common, mild in effect |
| **σκατά** | shit |
| **άντε / άι** | oh come on — mild, and **άι στο διάολο** is *go to hell* |
| **να πάρει η οργή** | damn it — the mild, old-fashioned version |
| **πω πω** | not swearing at all, but it covers the same ground |

**Να πάρει η οργή is the one you can actually use** — it is what your grandmother's generation said — and it is the safe equivalent of *for heaven's sake*.

**The blasphemy taboo, which is the part that matters for you.** Greek has a class of oaths against the sacred — against the Cross, the Virgin, the candle, the icon — and these are genuinely offensive in a way that **γαμώτο** is not. They are not used in front of older people, and in a parish context they are unthinkable. You will occasionally hear them in traffic.

**The distinction is the useful knowledge**: ordinary vulgarity in Greek is mild and ubiquitous; religious vulgarity is serious and bounded. An English speaker, used to the reverse weighting, can misjudge both.

**Insults you may hear directed at others**, for recognition only: **βλάκας** (fool), **ηλίθιος** (idiot), **άχρηστος** (useless), **ψώνιο** (full of himself), **κουτός** (dim), **παλιάνθρωπος** (scoundrel), **αλήτης** (thug). Most are no stronger than their English equivalents.

**The gesture**, from the gestures lesson: the open-palm **μούντζα** is the physical equivalent, and it is worse than most of the words.

**What to do instead.** Greek has a rich stock of exasperation that is not vulgar at all, and using it marks you as someone with manners:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Έλα τώρα!** | oh come on |
| **Μα τι λες;** | what on earth are you saying |
| **Δεν γίνεται αυτό.** | this is not on |
| **Αμάν πια!** | enough already |
| **Πω πω, τι κάνεις;** | good grief |
| **Ο Θεός να βάλει το χέρι του.** | God help us |
| **Τι να πω…** | what can I say |
| **Αυτό πάει πολύ.** | that is going too far |

**Those eight cover every situation** in which an English speaker would swear, and all eight are usable in front of anyone.

**Practice.** Read the lesson once. Learn **Να πάρει η οργή** and the eight non-vulgar alternatives. Then do not use anything else from this lesson, and recognise it when you hear it.
Regional accents and what varies:
What changes from place to place, so that an unfamiliar accent is a known quantity rather than a wall — and so that Cypriot, which is stage 10, has a context.

**Standard Modern Greek is based on Athens** and is what broadcast, education and this curriculum teach. Everything below is a deviation from it, and all of it is normal speech for millions of people.

**Northern Greek — Macedonia, Thrace, Thessaly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Unstressed vowels are dropped** | **το παιδί → τ' πδί**, **μου λέει → μ' λέει** |
| **-ε and -ο endings weaken** | which makes the words shorter and faster |
| **The accusative replaces the genitive for pronouns** | **σε λέω** rather than **σου λέω** |
| **A distinctive intonation** | a rising, almost sung contour |

**That pronoun difference is the one to know**: in the north, **με είπε** and **σε λέω** are normal where Athens says **μου είπε** and **σου λέω**. It is not an error; it is a dialect feature with a long history.

**Cretan:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **κ before e/i becomes a *tch* sound** | **και → τσαι**, **καιρός → τσαιρός** |
| **λ before i palatalises** | |
| **Distinctive vocabulary** | **κοπέλι** (boy), **μπάλε** no — **ίντα** (what), **μουδέ** (nor) |
| **The ancient *-ν* endings survive** in some words |

**Cretan also has its own literature** — the *Erotokritos* — and a strong musical tradition, and Cretans are proud of the dialect in a way that makes it a conversational subject.

**Peloponnesian and the islands:** closest to the standard, which is historically why the standard sounds like that.

**The Dodecanese and the eastern Aegean:** double consonants are pronounced, as in Cypriot, and some words keep older forms.

**Pontic**, from the Black Sea: a genuinely separate dialect, barely intelligible to a standard speaker, still spoken by descendants of the 1923 exchange. If you meet it you will know, because you will understand none of it.

**Cypriot** is stage 10 and is the largest divergence of all: geminate consonants, **sh** and **ch** sounds the standard lacks, different vocabulary, a different pronoun syntax, and a genuine diglossia with the standard.

**The diaspora**, which matters to you most: Greek spoken in Britain, Australia, South Africa and the United States has its own features — English loanwords, simplified morphology in the second generation, and older village forms preserved from the time of emigration. Your parish may speak a Greek that is forty years behind Athens and mixed with English, and that is its own authentic variety.

**What this means practically:**

1. **An accent you cannot follow is probably northern or Cretan**, and asking **Από πού είστε;** usually explains it and starts a conversation.
2. **Do not correct anyone's Greek**, ever, on the basis of this curriculum.
3. **Learn the standard**, which is what you are doing, and understand the rest.
4. **Expect the diaspora Greek around you to be its own thing**, and learn its words too.

**Practice.** Listen to one clip each of northern, Cretan and Cypriot Greek — Easy Greek and YouTube both have them — and note one feature of each. Then ask three people at church where their family is from, and listen for what varies.
The learned fossils in daily speech:
A recognition lesson. Katharevousa and older forms survive inside ordinary modern Greek as fixed phrases, and you need to know what they are — while the system behind them stays in the later curriculum, as you ruled.

**Why they are there.** Until 1976, formal Greek was **katharevousa** — a deliberately archaised written language — and the modern standard replaced it. But hundreds of its phrases stayed, frozen, in law, administration, the Church and everyday speech, with grammar the modern language no longer has: datives, old participles, and prepositions that take cases Greek has lost.

**The ones in ordinary speech:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δόξα τω Θεώ** | glory to God — a dative |
| **εν τω μεταξύ** | meanwhile — a dative |
| **εν τάξει** → **εντάξει** | *in order* — a dative, now one word meaning OK |
| **εν πάση περιπτώσει** | in any case |
| **εν ολίγοις** | in short |
| **τοις εκατό** | per cent — a dative |
| **εξ αρχής** | from the start |
| **εκ των προτέρων** | in advance |
| **εν γνώσει** | knowingly |
| **καθ' όλα** | in every respect |
| **διά βίου** | lifelong |
| **άνευ όρων** | unconditionally |
| **ως προς** | as regards |
| **περί ορέξεως** | a matter of taste |
| **Θεού θέλοντος** | God willing — a genitive absolute |
| **Αιωνία η μνήμη** | eternal be the memory |
| **Ευλογείτε** | bless — an imperative of the old conjugation |
| **Κύριε ελέησον** | Lord have mercy |

**You have been using several of them since stage 2** — **εντάξει**, **δόξα τω Θεώ** — without knowing they were anything but words.

**Where you will meet more of them:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Official documents** | **υποβάλλεται, δύναται, άνευ, περί, διά** |
| **Legal and academic writing** | the same, systematically |
| **Church texts and notices** | **υπέρ αναπαύσεως, τελεσθήσεται, εις μνήμην** |
| **Shop and institution names** | **Τράπεζα της Ελλάδος**, **Ιερά Μονή** |
| **Mottoes and inscriptions** | everywhere |

**The honest instruction, which is your ruling:** recognise and do not produce. If a phrase is in the list above, use it — they are part of modern Greek. Anything beyond that is the other curriculum's work, and attempting to construct new katharevousa sentences from these fragments produces nonsense.

**How to recognise the register in two seconds**: look for **εν, εις, εκ, εξ, διά, περί, υπέρ, άνευ, ως, τοις** and for endings in **-ωσις, -ότης, -ουσα, -ων**. Any of those and you are reading the learned layer.

**And the thing worth knowing about it historically**, in one paragraph: the **γλωσσικό ζήτημα** — the language question — was a real political conflict for a century and a half, with riots, careers and governments turning on whether Greek should be written as it was spoken. Demotic won in 1976. The fossils are the battlefield's remains, and a Greek of any education knows exactly what they are.

**Practice.** Read the eighteen phrases aloud and note which five you already use. Then find three learned forms on one church notice. Then read one official Greek sentence and mark every learned marker in it.
Loanwords in the other direction:
Greek in English, which is thousands of words you already half-know — and the single largest vocabulary advantage an English speaker has in this language.

**The three layers of Greek in English:**

**1. The learned layer** — science, medicine, philosophy, politics. Tens of thousands of words, built from Greek roots, often coined in English or Latin from Greek parts:

| English | Greek source | Modern Greek meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| telephone | τῆλε + φωνή | **το τηλέφωνο** — the same word |
| democracy | δῆμος + κράτος | **η δημοκρατία** |
| psychology | ψυχή + λόγος | **η ψυχολογία** |
| geography | γῆ + γράφω | **η γεωγραφία** |
| biology, biography | βίος | **η βιολογία** |
| hypothesis | ὑπό + θέσις | **η υπόθεση** |
| sympathy | σύν + πάθος | **η συμπάθεια** |
| programme | πρό + γράμμα | **το πρόγραμμα** |
| problem | πρό + βάλλω | **το πρόβλημα** |
| school | σχολή | **το σχολείο** |
| idea | ἰδέα | **η ιδέα** |
| music, theatre, drama, chorus | — | **η μουσική, το θέατρο, το δράμα, ο χορός** |

**The practical consequence**: an abstract or technical word in English is a good bet in Greek. **Η ανάλυση, η σύνθεση, η κρίση, η θεωρία, το σύστημα, η μέθοδος, η ενέργεια, η πολιτική, η οικονομία** — all of them say what you expect.

**2. The Church layer**, which came through Latin into every European language:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο άγγελος** | angel |
| **ο απόστολος** | apostle |
| **ο επίσκοπος** | bishop — through *episcopus* |
| **ο πρεσβύτερος** | priest — through *presbyter* |
| **η εκκλησία** | ecclesiastical |
| **το βάπτισμα** | baptism |
| **η ευχαριστία** | eucharist |
| **ο ύμνος** | hymn |
| **η λειτουργία** | liturgy |
| **το μαρτύριο / ο μάρτυρας** | martyr — and the word means *witness* |
| **η μετάνοια** | metanoia — repentance, *change of mind* |
| **ο μοναχός** | monk |
| **το μυστήριο** | mystery — and *sacrament* |

**That list is worth studying for its own sake**, because the Greek meanings are often more precise than the English: **μάρτυρας** is a *witness*, **μετάνοια** is a *change of mind*, **εκκλησία** is an *assembly*. The theology is in the etymology, which is one of the reasons the later curriculum exists.

**3. The everyday layer**, which is smaller and surprising: **ο χάρτης** (chart), **το κέντρο** (centre), **η ζώνη** (zone), **ο κίνδυνος** (no English cousin), **το πανικός** (panic), **ο ήρωας** (hero), **ο γίγαντας** (giant), **το ταλέντο** — Italian, in fact.

**The false friends, which are the trap:**

| Greek | Looks like | Actually means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **η συμπάθεια** | sympathy | liking, fondness |
| **η εμπάθεια** | empathy | **animosity** — the opposite |
| **το σύμπτωμα** | symptom | symptom, and *coincidence* |
| **η ιδιωτικός** | idiotic | **private** |
| **το μανιφέστο** | manifesto | — the same, but **ο μανιακός** is a *maniac* |
| **η παράκληση** | — | a request, and a church service |
| **ο δραματικός** | dramatic | dramatic, and *theatrical* in a bad sense |
| **ο φανατικός** | fanatic | fanatic, and *a devoted fan* |

**η εμπάθεια is the dangerous one**: it means hostility, not empathy, and using it as a compliment would be an error worth avoiding.

**What to do with this lesson.** Use it as a guessing strategy, deliberately: when you need an abstract word, try the Greek-looking English one with a Greek ending, and you will be right surprisingly often. **Η πληροφορία** is *information*, **η οργάνωση** is *organisation*, **η κατάσταση** is *situation* — the last two by analogy rather than by cognate, which is the limit of the trick.

**Practice.** Write down twenty English words of Greek origin and give the modern Greek of each. Then learn the eight false friends. Then try the guessing strategy on five abstract words you do not know and check them in the dictionary.
Telling a joke, and being teased:
Humour, which is where a foreigner is most excluded and where being included matters most — and most of it is a matter of recognising what is happening.

**Greek humour, in general terms**: fast, verbal, affectionate, and heavily based on teasing people who are present. A group that likes you will tease you, and the correct response is to tease back or to take it well — not to be hurt.

**The words for it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **η πλάκα** | a joke, a laugh — **για πλάκα**, for fun |
| **κάνω πλάκα** | I am joking |
| **σπάω πλάκα** | I am having a laugh |
| **το ανέκδοτο** | a joke, a story with a punchline |
| **πειράζω** | I tease |
| **με δουλεύεις;** | are you having me on? |
| **σοβαρά;** | seriously? |
| **γελάω** | I laugh |
| **αστείο** | funny, a joke |
| **χαζό** | silly |

**Κάνω πλάκα is the phrase to have cold**, because you will need it after your Greek produces something unintentionally funny — which it will.

**When you are being teased**, which you will be:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Με δουλεύεις;** | Are you pulling my leg? |
| **Πλάκα κάνεις.** | You are joking. |
| **Α, καλά!** | Oh, right! — with the right tone |
| **Σε πιάσαμε!** | We got you! — what they will say |
| **Έλα ρε, πλάκα κάνω.** | Come on, I'm joking — what they will add |

**The right response is to laugh and return it.** Being teased in a Greek group is inclusion; responding stiffly reads as not getting it, which is the only real failure available.

**Telling a joke**, which is harder in a second language than anything else — the timing is the joke, and timing is the last thing to arrive. So:

1. **Start with the short forms.** A one-line observation beats a three-minute anecdote.
2. **Use the historic present**, from the colloquial lesson: **Και πάω εγώ και του λέω…**
3. **Signpost it.** **Να σου πω ένα ανέκδοτο** — let me tell you a joke — and the group will wait.
4. **Expect to be rescued.** If it fails, **έλα, δεν πέτυχε** and move on.

**The structure of a Greek anecdote**, which is worth recognising: setup, a repeated line, and a punchline that is often a pun or a reversal. Puns do not translate, which means a large part of the humour around you will be inaccessible for a long time — and that is a vocabulary problem rather than a cultural one.

**Self-deprecation about your Greek is the safest joke available** and it works every time:

- **Τα ελληνικά μου είναι… σιγά σιγά.**
- **Μιλάω ελληνικά σαν παιδί τριών χρονών.**
- **Ξέρω τρεις λέξεις: καλημέρα, ευχαριστώ και νηστίσιμο.**

**That last kind of line does real work**: it is funny, it is modest, it signals that you are trying, and it invites help. Have one ready.

**And the cultural fact worth knowing**: there is a large stock of jokes about regional stereotypes — Pontians especially, who tell them about themselves with enthusiasm — about politicians, and about priests. The priest jokes are told by the devout and are not disrespectful. If you are included in them, you are in.

**Practice.** Learn **κάνω πλάκα** and **με δουλεύεις;** cold. Then prepare one self-deprecating line about your Greek and use it this week. Then, when you are teased, laugh and say something back.
Complaining, sympathising and arguing:
Three social functions that need the same machinery and that English speakers handle very differently from Greeks.

**Complaining**, which in Greece is a recognised conversational genre rather than a breach of manners:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι να σου πω…** | what can I tell you |
| **Χάλια τα πράγματα.** | things are terrible |
| **Δεν πάει άλλο.** | it cannot go on |
| **Είναι απαράδεκτο.** | it is unacceptable |
| **Έχω βαρεθεί.** | I am fed up |
| **Μας έχουν τρελάνει.** | they have driven us mad |
| **Πάει από το κακό στο χειρότερο.** | it is going from bad to worse |
| **Όλο τα ίδια.** | always the same |
| **Τι κόσμος!** | what a world |

**Complaining about the state, the economy, the weather, bureaucracy and the neighbours is a shared pastime**, and joining in is social participation. The expected response is agreement and escalation, not solutions.

**Sympathising:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Σε καταλαβαίνω.** | I understand you |
| **Έχεις δίκιο.** | you are right |
| **Κρίμα.** | what a shame |
| **Πω πω.** | oh dear |
| **Τι να κάνεις…** | what can you do |
| **Κουράγιο.** | courage |
| **Θα περάσει.** | it will pass |
| **Είμαι εδώ.** | I am here |
| **Αν χρειαστείς κάτι, πες μου.** | if you need anything, tell me |
| **Ο Θεός να βάλει το χέρι του.** | may God intervene |

**Note what is not on that list**: advice. Greek sympathy is agreement and presence, and offering a solution too early reads as dismissal — exactly as in English, but the threshold is later.

**Complaining effectively, which is different from venting** — in a shop, to a landlord, to an official:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Υπάρχει ένα πρόβλημα.** | there is a problem |
| **Αυτό δεν είναι σωστό.** | this is not right |
| **Θα ήθελα να μιλήσω με τον υπεύθυνο.** | I would like to speak to the person in charge |
| **Έχω την απόδειξη.** | I have the receipt |
| **Τι μπορείτε να κάνετε;** | what can you do? |
| **Θα κάνω καταγγελία.** | I will make a formal complaint |
| **Δεν είναι δική μου ευθύνη.** | it is not my responsibility — what you may hear |
| **Πού πρέπει να απευθυνθώ;** | where should I apply? |

**Ο υπεύθυνος — the person responsible — is the key word** in any Greek complaint, and asking for them politely is the whole technique.

**Arguing**, from stage 5 and now with the tools:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν συμφωνώ καθόλου.** | I do not agree at all |
| **Από μια πλευρά…** | in one way |
| **Ναι, αλλά σκέψου ότι…** | yes, but consider that |
| **Το θέμα δεν είναι αυτό.** | that is not the point |
| **Εντάξει, δέχομαι ότι…** | all right, I accept that |
| **Ας συμφωνήσουμε να διαφωνούμε.** | let's agree to disagree |
| **Τέλος πάντων.** | anyway — the exit |

**And the four things to remember about a Greek argument**, from stage 5's lesson: volume is not anger, interruption is engagement, nobody expects to be persuaded, and coffee follows.

**Practice.** Complain about three things for a minute, out loud, in the venting register. Then sympathise with three problems without offering advice. Then make one formal complaint, politely, asking for **τον υπεύθυνο**.
Toasts, speeches and set pieces:
The occasions when Greek requires you to say something — and the formulas that mean you can.

**At the table**, from stage 5 and now in full:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Στην υγειά μας!** | our health |
| **Στην υγειά σου / σας!** | your health |
| **Γεια μας!** | cheers |
| **Και στα δικά σας!** | may your own come too |
| **Να ζήσετε!** | long life — to a couple |
| **Βίον ανθόσπαρτον!** | a life strewn with flowers — the full wedding toast, learned |
| **Καλή όρεξη!** | enjoy the meal |
| **Με γεια!** | — for anything new |
| **Γούρι!** | good luck — on a first drink |
| **Εις υγείαν!** | the learned version of *to health* |

**At a wedding:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Να ζήσετε!** | long life |
| **Καλούς απογόνους!** | good descendants |
| **Και στα δικά σας!** | — to the unmarried guests |
| **Ο Θεός να σας ευλογεί.** | God bless you |
| **Να σας χαιρόμαστε.** | may we rejoice in you |

**At a baptism:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Να σας ζήσει!** | may the child live for you |
| **Πάντα άξιος!** | — to the godfather, *always worthy* |
| **Καλοφώτιστος!** | *well-enlightened* — of the newly baptised |

**Πάντα άξιος to the godparent is the specific formula**, and it is the kind of detail that marks someone who has been paying attention.

**At a name day or a feast:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Χρόνια πολλά!** | many years |
| **Να τα εκατοστήσεις!** | may you reach a hundred |
| **Χρόνια πολλά και ευλογημένα!** | many and blessed years |
| **Και του χρόνου!** | and next year too |

**At a death**, from stage 6: **Συλλυπητήρια**, **Ζωή σε λόγου σας**, **Αιωνία του η μνήμη**, **Καλό Παράδεισο**.

**On arriving and leaving anywhere:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλώς ήρθατε! — Καλώς σας βρήκα.** | welcome — and the guest's reply |
| **Καλή συνέχεια!** | a good continuation |
| **Καλό βράδυ / Καλή νύχτα.** | good evening / good night |
| **Στο καλό.** | go well |
| **Με το καλό.** | may it go well — of a journey or an undertaking |
| **Καλή δύναμη.** | strength to you |

**And the short speech**, which you may be asked for at a table — Greeks do this readily and briefly:

> **Θέλω να πω λίγα λόγια. Ευχαριστώ πολύ για τη φιλοξενία. Χαίρομαι πολύ που είμαι εδώ μαζί σας. Στην υγειά σας, και να 'στε όλοι καλά!**

**Four sentences is a complete Greek toast** — thanks, pleasure, health, blessing — and having them ready means you are never caught out.

**The structure of any set piece**: thank, say you are glad, wish health, bless. In that order, briefly, and sit down.

**Practice.** Learn the four-sentence toast until it is automatic. Then say the right formula for: a wedding, a baptism, a name day, a death, a new coat, and someone leaving on a journey. Then deliver the toast out loud, standing up, once — it is less ridiculous now than it will be on the night.
Emphasis and intonation:
The music of the sentence, which carries meaning that the words do not — and which is the last thing a learner acquires and the first thing a listener notices.

**What Greek intonation does:**

**1. Questions rise at the end.** Since the word order does not change, the rise is the question:

- **Θα έρθεις.** — You will come. · **Θα έρθεις;** — Will you come?

**Practising that pair is the single most useful intonation exercise** at this level, because an unraised question in Greek is simply a statement.

**2. The stressed syllable is louder and longer**, and the rest of the word is not reduced — stage 1's rule, and the one that makes a Greek accent Greek.

**3. Emphasis is placed by pitch, on the word that matters:**

- **ΕΓΩ δεν το είπα.** — *I* did not say it.
- **Δεν το είπα ΕΓΩ.** — It was not me who said it.
- **Δεν ΤΟ είπα.** — I did not say *that*.

**4. The list contour**, which rises on each item and falls on the last — the same as English.

**5. The exclamation contour**, which starts high: **Τι ωραία!**, **Μπράβο!**, **Πω πω!**

**6. The tag questions**, which fall:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **έτσι;** | right? |
| **σωστά;** | correct? |
| **εντάξει;** | OK? |
| **δεν είναι;** | isn't it? |
| **ναι;** | yes? |

**What varies by meaning rather than by grammar:**

| Said this way | Means |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλά** flat | fine, whatever |
| **Καλά!** rising | oh come on! |
| **Καλά, καλά** quickly | all right, all right — placating |
| **Σιγά** flat | big deal |
| **Σιγά!** sharp | slow down! |
| **Ναι** drawn out | yes, but… |
| **Έλα** rising | come on / you're joking |
| **Έλα** falling | come here / hello on the phone |

**Έλα on the telephone means *hello*** — specifically to someone you know — and it falls. The same word rising is disbelief. That pair is worth hearing a dozen times.

**The three things to practise:**

1. **The question rise**, on statements you turn into questions.
2. **Full vowels throughout**, with no English reduction.
3. **One pitch peak per sentence**, on the word you mean.

**How to practise them.** Shadowing, from stage 2 — which is the only exercise that trains intonation, because intonation cannot be learned from a description. Ten seconds of audio, spoken along with, repeatedly.

**And the honest note**: intonation is the last thing to arrive and the thing that most marks a foreign accent even when every word is right. It is also the thing Greeks are most charmed by when you get it, because it signals that you have been listening rather than studying.

**Practice.** Say five statements and then the same five as questions, with the rise. Then say **καλά**, **σιγά** and **έλα** in both their meanings. Then shadow ten seconds of audio with attention only to the melody, not the words.
Keeping up at speed:
The practical problem of this stage: Greeks talk fast, and knowing the language is not the same as processing it in real time.

**Why speed is a separate problem.** Your comprehension is built on a slower parse than a native's. The words are known; the time to retrieve them is too long, so by the time you have understood the first clause the speaker is three clauses further on.

**It is a processing problem, not a knowledge problem** — which means the cure is volume and exposure, not more study.

**The seven strategies, in order of usefulness:**

**1. Listen for the stressed syllables.** Greek is stress-timed and the stressed syllables carry the content. Hearing **ΠΗ-γα στην εκ-κλη-ΣΙ-α** as two peaks is faster than hearing eight syllables.

**2. Predict.** Most of a conversation is predictable: after **θα** comes a verb, after **που** a clause, after **δηλαδή** a restatement. Prediction is most of native-speed listening.

**3. Let the small words go.** The articles, the particles and the pronouns can be inferred. The nouns and verbs cannot.

**4. Hold the topic, not the sentence.** If you have the subject, you can lose two sentences and rejoin.

**5. Use the backchannels**, from earlier in this stage, which buy you processing time and keep the speaker going.

**6. Ask for repair, specifically.** Not **δεν κατάλαβα** (which gets the whole thing repeated at the same speed) but:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ποιος;** | who? |
| **Πού;** | where? |
| **Τι είπες για τον…;** | what did you say about the…? |
| **Την Κυριακή;** | on Sunday? — checking one item |
| **Πιο αργά, παρακαλώ.** | more slowly, please |
| **Μία λέξη δεν κατάλαβα: «…».** | one word I did not get: "…" |

**That last one is the best repair move there is** — naming the single word you missed — because it is quick, specific and shows you followed the rest.

**7. Accept partial understanding.** Native speakers do this constantly in their own language. Following 70 per cent of a conversation is participating in it.

**What actually builds the speed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Volume of listening** | hours, not techniques — and at a level where you understand most of it |
| **Shadowing** | which trains production speed, which feeds comprehension |
| **Reading aloud** | the same |
| **Repeated listening** to the same material | which converts decoding into recognition |
| **Being in the room** | an hour a week of real conversation is worth ten of media |

**The honest timeline.** Native-speed comprehension of a conversation between two Greeks is a stage 8-to-9 achievement, arriving two to four years in for most adult learners, and it arrives suddenly after long apparent stasis.

**And the thing not to do**: do not ask people to speak slowly all the time. Slowed speech does not train the skill that fast speech requires. Ask for it when you need the content; otherwise let the fast version wash over you and train on it.

**Practice.** Listen to two minutes of fast Greek and write down only the stressed-syllable words you caught. Then listen again and see how much of the content those words already gave you. Then use the one-word repair move in your next conversation.
Greek music, and why it matters:
A cultural lesson with a practical use: music is the fastest route into Greek idiom, and it is a conversational subject on which everyone has strong views.

**The genres, and knowing the names is most of it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το ρεμπέτικο** | rebetiko — the urban music of the 1920s to 50s, bouzouki, hashish dens and refugees from Asia Minor |
| **το λαϊκό** | laiko — popular song, the mainstream of the 50s to 80s |
| **το έντεχνο** | *art song* — composers setting poets: Theodorakis, Hadjidakis |
| **το δημοτικό** | folk, regional, with each area's own forms |
| **το σκυλάδικο** | the derogatory word for cheap bouzouki-club music |
| **η καντάδα** | the Ionian serenade tradition |
| **το νησιώτικο** | island music |
| **το κρητικό** | Cretan — lyra, and a living tradition |
| **η βυζαντινή μουσική** | Byzantine chant — the Church's music, and a different system |

**The names everyone knows:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μίκης Θεοδωράκης** | Theodorakis — Zorba, and the settings of Seferis and Ritsos |
| **Μάνος Χατζιδάκις** | Hadjidakis — *Never on Sunday*, and the settings of Gatsos |
| **Βασίλης Τσιτσάνης** | Tsitsanis — the great rebetiko composer |
| **Μαρκος Βαμβακάρης** | Vamvakaris — the patriarch of rebetiko |
| **Γιώργος Νταλάρας** | Dalaras — the voice of several generations |
| **Χάρις Αλεξίου** | Alexiou — likewise |
| **Στέλιος Καζαντζίδης** | Kazantzidis — the voice of the emigration years, and still revered |
| **Νίκος Ξυλούρης** | Xylouris — Cretan, and a national figure |
| **Δημήτρης Μητροπάνος** | Mitropanos |
| **Νίκος Παπάζογλου, Θανάσης Παπακωνσταντίνου** | the northern songwriters |

**Καζαντζίδης deserves the note for your purposes**: he is the voice of the Greek diaspora, of the people who left in the 1950s and 60s, and in a diaspora parish his songs are the emotional soundtrack of the generation that built it. Knowing one of them is worth a great deal socially.

**Why music is the best idiom teacher:**

1. **The lyrics are poetry**, often literally — Theodorakis set Seferis, Elytis and Ritsos, so learning those songs is learning the national poets.
2. **Repetition.** You hear a chorus twenty times and it stays.
3. **The register is colloquial**, with the elisions and the **-νε** endings from the colloquial lesson.
4. **The vocabulary is emotional**, which is the part textbooks cover worst: **καημός, ντέρτι, λαχτάρα, ξενιτιά, μοναξιά, καρδιά**.
5. **stixoi.info has every lyric**, free and searchable.

**η ξενιτιά is the word to learn from this lesson** — the condition of being abroad, away from home, with the grief that goes with it. It has no English equivalent and it is the subject of hundreds of songs, because a third of the nation left. In a diaspora parish it is not a historical term.

**The conversational use.** Ask anyone what song you should learn. You will get an answer, an argument, a recommendation of a singer, and probably a phone held up to play it. It is the single most reliable conversation-starter available to you, and the answers will tell you where people are from and how old they are.

**Practice.** Ask one person at church what Greek song you should learn. Learn it: lyrics on stixoi.info, sung along with until you can follow it. Then learn the word **ξενιτιά** and listen to one song about it.
The history everyone refers to:
The shared references a Greek conversation assumes — because a conversation about anything will eventually touch one of these, and not recognising them means losing the thread.

**The dates that are named out loud:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το 1821** | the Revolution against the Ottomans. **Η 25η Μαρτίου** is the national day, and it coincides with the Annunciation — the Church and the nation celebrate together. |
| **η Μικρασιατική Καταστροφή, 1922** | the Asia Minor Catastrophe: the end of the Greek presence in Anatolia and the arrival of a million and a half refugees. The single most consequential event in modern Greek history. |
| **το 1940 / η 28η Οκτωβρίου** | the **ΟΧΙ** — the refusal of Mussolini's ultimatum. The other national day, celebrated with school parades. |
| **η Κατοχή** | the Occupation, 1941–44, and the famine in Athens |
| **ο Εμφύλιος** | the Civil War, 1946–49 — still a live subject in families |
| **η Χούντα, 1967–74** | the colonels' dictatorship |
| **το Πολυτεχνείο, 17 Νοεμβρίου 1973** | the Polytechnic uprising — a public holiday, and a date said as a word |
| **η Κύπρος, 1974** | the Turkish invasion and the division of the island. For Cypriots, the central fact of their lives. |
| **η Μεταπολίτευση** | the restoration of democracy after 1974 |
| **η κρίση** | the financial crisis from 2009 — and *the* crisis, with no further specification needed |

**The two national days are in the Church's calendar too.** 25 March is the Annunciation and the Revolution; 28 October is **ΟΧΙ** day and the feast of the Protection of the Mother of God in Greek practice. Both are marked at church as well as at school, and both involve a **δοξολογία** — a thanksgiving service — after which people go to the parade.

**The 1922 refugee descent matters socially.** A large share of Greeks — and of any diaspora parish — descend from Asia Minor refugees, and the family's town of origin is often known and named: **Σμύρνη** (Smyrna), **Κωνσταντινούπολη** (Constantinople — never *Istanbul* in Greek), **Πόντος**, **Καππαδοκία**. Asking **Από πού είναι η οικογένειά σας;** can produce a story of a hundred years.

**Κωνσταντινούπολη, η Πόλη** — *the City* — is what Greeks call Istanbul, and **η Αγιά Σοφιά** needs no explanation. The usage is not political posturing; it is simply the Greek name.

**The names you will hear:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Κολοκοτρώνης, Μπότσαρης, Καραϊσκάκης** | the Revolution's generals |
| **Βενιζέλος** | Venizelos, the great modern statesman |
| **Μεταξάς** | who said no in 1940 |
| **Καραμανλής, Παπανδρέου, Μητσοτάκης** | the political dynasties |
| **Μακάριος** | Cyprus's archbishop-president |

**What to do with this lesson.** Not to have opinions — you are not required to and a foreigner's judgement on the Civil War is not wanted. But to recognise a reference, know roughly when it was, and ask rather than guess:

- **Συγγνώμη, τι έγινε τότε;** — what happened then?
- **Δεν ξέρω την ιστορία καλά. Μου λέτε;** — I do not know the history well. Will you tell me?

**That second sentence will get you an hour of excellent listening practice** from almost anyone over fifty, delivered slowly because they want you to understand.

**Practice.** Learn the ten dates. Then ask one person where their family is from and listen to the answer. Then watch a 28 October parade on video and listen for **ΟΧΙ**.
Politics and football, carefully:
The two subjects Greeks argue about most, and how to be present for them without being drawn in.

**Politics first, and the honest framing**: Greek political conversation is frequent, loud, informed and partisan, and it reaches into family history — the Civil War and the Junta are within living memory, and allegiances are inherited.

**The vocabulary you need to follow it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **η κυβέρνηση / η αντιπολίτευση** | government / opposition |
| **το κόμμα** | party |
| **οι εκλογές** | elections |
| **η Βουλή** | parliament |
| **ο πρωθυπουργός** | prime minister |
| **ο Πρόεδρος της Δημοκρατίας** | the President |
| **δεξιά / αριστερά / κέντρο** | right / left / centre |
| **ψηφίζω** | I vote |
| **η ψήφος** | the vote |
| **το δημοψήφισμα** | referendum |
| **η διαφθορά** | corruption |
| **τα μέτρα** | the measures — i.e. austerity |
| **το μνημόνιο** | the bailout memorandum |
| **ο λαός** | the people |
| **η Ευρώπη / η ΕΕ** | Europe / the EU |

**The parties**, so that names mean something: **Νέα Δημοκρατία** (centre-right), **ΠΑΣΟΚ** (centre-left, historic), **ΣΥΡΙΖΑ** (left), **ΚΚΕ** (communist, with a long and distinct culture), and several smaller.

**How to be present without taking sides:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν ξέρω αρκετά για την ελληνική πολιτική.** | I do not know enough about Greek politics. |
| **Είμαι ξένος, ακούω και μαθαίνω.** | I am a foreigner, I listen and learn. |
| **Τι πιστεύεις εσύ;** | What do you think? |
| **Είναι περίπλοκο.** | It is complicated. |
| **Δεν θέλω να πω κάτι λάθος.** | I do not want to say something wrong. |

**Those five are a complete and respectable position** and nobody will press you. Asking rather than asserting also produces the better conversation.

**One thing to avoid**: the Macedonia naming question, Turkey, and Cyprus are subjects where a casual foreign opinion lands badly. Listening is fine; summarising a BBC article is not.

**Football, the other national subject:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **η ομάδα** | the team |
| **ο αγώνας / το ματς** | the match |
| **το γκολ** | goal |
| **ο παίκτης** | player |
| **ο προπονητής** | coach |
| **ο διαιτητής** | referee — and the object of most of the conversation |
| **το πρωτάθλημα** | the championship |
| **ο τελικός** | the final |
| **τα αποτελέσματα** | the results |
| **ισοπαλία** | a draw |
| **Πόσο τελείωσε;** | What was the score? |
| **Με ποιον είσαι;** | Who do you support? |

**The teams**: Ολυμπιακός and Παναθηναϊκός (the Athens rivalry), ΠΑΟΚ and Άρης (Thessaloniki), ΑΕΚ (the Asia Minor refugees' club, which is why its badge is a double-headed eagle). Those affiliations are inherited and taken seriously; **ΑΕΚ**'s refugee origin ties straight back to the history lesson.

**Basketball matters as much as football** in Greece — **το μπάσκετ**, and the 1987 European championship is a national memory.

**Με ποιον είσαι; is the question you will be asked**, and the acceptable answers are a team, or **Δεν παρακολουθώ πολύ** — I do not follow it much — which is received with disappointment and no offence.

**Practice.** Learn the fifteen political words and the twelve football ones. Then say the five neutral positions aloud until they are automatic. Then ask someone **Με ποιον είσαι;** and listen to the answer.
Where people are from: the village and t:
One of the first things a Greek will tell you about themselves, and a subject that opens more conversation than any other.

**Why it matters.** Greeks identify with a place — a village, an island, a region — often one they do not live in and sometimes one their grandparents left. **Είμαι από…** may mean *I was born in*, *my family is from*, or *my village is*, and all three are live answers.

**The vocabulary:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το χωριό** | the village — and **στο χωριό** means *at the family place* |
| **η πατρίδα** | the homeland — of a country and of a village both |
| **ο τόπος** | the place, one's own region |
| **η ιδιαίτερη πατρίδα** | *one's particular homeland* — the formal phrase for your region |
| **ο συμπατριώτης** | someone from the same place |
| **ντόπιος** | local |
| **ξένος** | foreign, a stranger — and what you are |
| **η ξενιτιά** | being abroad, from the music lesson |
| **ο μετανάστης / ο ομογενής** | emigrant / a Greek of the diaspora |

**ο ομογενής is the word for you if you become part of this world** — *of the same descent*, used of diaspora Greeks — and **ο φιλέλληνας**, a lover of Greece, is the word for a foreigner who takes it seriously. Both are compliments.

**The regions, which are named constantly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **η Πελοπόννησος** | the Peloponnese |
| **η Μακεδονία / η Θράκη** | northern Greece |
| **η Θεσσαλία / η Ήπειρος** | central and north-west |
| **η Στερεά Ελλάδα** | central Greece |
| **η Κρήτη** | Crete |
| **τα Επτάνησα** | the Ionian islands |
| **οι Κυκλάδες / τα Δωδεκάνησα** | the Cyclades / the Dodecanese |
| **η Κύπρος** | Cyprus |
| **ο Πόντος / η Μικρά Ασία** | the Black Sea / Asia Minor — ancestral, not current |

**The questions to ask, in order of productiveness:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Από πού είστε;** | where are you from? |
| **Από πού είναι η οικογένειά σας;** | where is your family from? |
| **Πηγαίνετε στο χωριό το καλοκαίρι;** | do you go to the village in the summer? |
| **Έχετε σπίτι εκεί;** | do you have a house there? |
| **Πότε πήγατε τελευταία φορά;** | when were you last there? |
| **Τι έχει το χωριό σας;** | what is your village known for? |

**That last question is the best one in this lesson.** Every Greek village is known for something — an oil, a cheese, a wine, a saint, a festival — and asking produces an enthusiastic answer and often a gift.

**August and the village.** The country empties in August: people go to the village or the island, the Dormition on the 15th is celebrated with a **πανηγύρι**, and anyone with roots goes home for it. In a diaspora parish the same thing happens in miniature: people fly out in August, and asking **Θα πάτε στην Ελλάδα το καλοκαίρι;** is a natural question that will be answered at length.

**And the thing that places you.** You will be asked where you are from, repeatedly. A fuller answer — your town, your country, how long you have been where you are, and why Greek — turns a two-line exchange into a conversation, and you now have the Greek to give it.

**Practice.** Prepare a four-sentence answer to **Από πού είστε;** Then ask three people at church where their family is from and what their village is known for. Then learn the names of the regions until you can place one when it is said.
Names: what they mean and how they work:
Greek names, which are a system rather than a list — and understanding it makes a parish legible.

**Nearly every Greek first name is a saint's name**, which is why the name day works. The commonest, with their feasts, from stage 5's list — and here is what they mean:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Γεώργιος** | *farmer* — and the warrior saint |
| **Δημήτριος** | of Demeter |
| **Κωνσταντίνος** | *constant* — the emperor |
| **Ελένη** | Helen — his mother, who found the Cross |
| **Βασίλειος** | *royal* |
| **Ιωάννης** | John — *God is gracious* |
| **Μαρία** | and its variants **Μαριάνθη, Μαρίνα** |
| **Παναγιώτης / Παναγιώτα** | *of the All-Holy* — the Panagia's own name day, 15 August |
| **Σταύρος / Σταυρούλα** | *cross* — feast 14 September |
| **Αναστάσιος / Αναστασία** | *resurrection* |
| **Χρήστος / Χριστίνα** | of Christ |
| **Θεόδωρος / Δώρα** | *gift of God* |
| **Σοφία** | *wisdom* |
| **Ειρήνη** | *peace* |
| **Αθανάσιος** | *immortal* |
| **Παρασκευή** | *preparation*, i.e. Friday |
| **Ευαγγελία / Ευάγγελος** | *good news* — feast 25 March, the Annunciation |

**The naming custom**: the first son is traditionally named after the paternal grandfather and the first daughter after the paternal grandmother, which is why the same four or five names repeat down a family and why cousins share them. If you meet three Γιώργος in one family, that is the reason.

**The diminutives from earlier in this stage** are how they are actually used: **Γιώργος → Γιωργάκης, Τζώρτζης**; **Κωνσταντίνος → Κώστας, Κωστάκης, Ντίνος**; **Παναγιώτης → Πάνος, Τάκης**; **Ελένη → Ελενίτσα, Λένα**; **Μαρία → Μαράκι, Μαίρη**; **Αναστάσιος → Τάσος**; **Ευάγγελος → Βαγγέλης**.

**Those short forms are what people are called.** Nobody says **Κωνσταντίνος** except in church and on documents; he is **Κώστας**.

**Surnames**, which carry information:

| Ending | Origin |
| --- | --- |
| **-ópoulos** (-όπουλος) | Peloponnese — *son of* |
| **-ákis** (-άκης) | Crete |
| **-ídis / -ádis** (-ίδης, -άδης) | Pontos and Asia Minor |
| **-éllis / -ákos** | Lesvos / Mani |
| **-átos / -áto** | the Ionian islands |
| **-óglou** (-όγλου) | Turkish *-oğlu*, *son of* — Asia Minor |
| **Παπα-** | *priest's* — Παπαδόπουλος, Παπαγιάννης: descended from a priest |

**So a surname often tells you where a family is from**, which ties straight to the previous lesson: **-ίδης** suggests Pontos, **-άκης** Crete, **Παπα-** a clerical ancestor.

**And the feminine genitive**, from stage 3: **Παπαδόπουλος / Παπαδοπούλου**, because a woman's surname is the genitive of her father's or husband's.

**How to use all this:**

1. **Learn the name days of the people you know.** Five is enough to start.
2. **Use the short form once invited**, and **κυρία** or **κύριε** plus the first name with elders.
3. **Ask about a surname** — **Από πού είναι το επώνυμό σας;** — and you will get a family history.

**Practice.** Learn what five names you know mean. Then work out from the surnames at your church which families came from where. Then learn five people's name days and put them in your calendar.
Hospitality: the whole system:
φιλοξενία, which is a social institution with rules — and the thing you will encounter most often and understand least.

**The word: φιλοξενία**, *stranger-loving*, and **ο φιλόξενος** is one of the highest compliments available about a person or a place.

**The obligations, which run both ways:**

**The host must:**

1. **Offer food and drink immediately**, before any conversation.
2. **Press it again after refusal** — at least twice.
3. **Over-provide.** Running out is a disgrace; too much is correct.
4. **Pay**, if the meeting is outside.
5. **Refuse any offer of payment or help**, at least twice.
6. **Send you away with something** — fruit, a jar, leftovers.

**The guest must:**

1. **Bring something**, whatever was said.
2. **Accept the first offer**, at least in part.
3. **Compliment the food specifically.**
4. **Refuse the third helping twice and accept once.**
5. **Offer to pay or help, and be refused.**
6. **Leave in three rounds**, as stage 5 said.
7. **Reciprocate**, within a reasonable period.

**The reciprocity is the part foreigners miss.** Hospitality received and never returned reads as taking. The return need not match in scale — a coffee, a small invitation, a lift, a gift from your own country — but it has to happen.

**The phrases of the system:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Περάστε!** | come in! |
| **Καθίστε!** | sit down! |
| **Τι θα πάρετε;** | what will you have? |
| **Τίποτα, ευχαριστώ. — Όχι, κάτι θα πάρετε.** | the obligatory exchange |
| **Σας έφερα κάτι μικρό.** | I have brought you something small |
| **Μη φέρνεις τίποτα!** | do not bring anything — said, not meant |
| **Έχει και άλλο.** | there is more |
| **Φάε, φάε.** | eat, eat |
| **Χόρτασα, αλήθεια.** | I am full, really |
| **Πάρε και αυτό για το σπίτι.** | take this home too |
| **Εγώ κερνάω.** | my treat |
| **Την άλλη φορά εγώ.** | next time me |
| **Να 'στε καλά.** | be well |

**Την άλλη φορά εγώ is how you take your turn** without an argument, and it is the sentence that resolves the paying contest gracefully.

**Where it is strongest**: villages, islands, monasteries and among older people. A village house will feed a stranger; a monastery will give you a bed. Refusing it outright is the error, and the more remote the place, the stronger the obligation on both sides.

**At a monastery**, specifically: **η φιλοξενία** is formalised — a guestmaster, **ο αρχοντάρης**, a cell, meals in silence or with reading, and the expectation that you attend the services. There is no charge and a donation is appropriate. **Δι' ευχών** is the farewell.

**The thing to understand about all of it.** This is not politeness in the English sense, where the forms protect distance. It is an exchange that creates obligation deliberately — you are being brought inside something. Accepting it, and returning it, is how a stranger becomes **δικός μας** — *one of ours* — which is the phrase you want said about you.

**Practice.** Say the thirteen phrases aloud. Then plan one act of reciprocity for the hospitality you have already received at church, and do it this month. Then learn **Την άλλη φορά εγώ** and use it the next time someone pays.
Time, lateness and the Greek clock:
A short practical lesson on when things happen, because the written time and the real time are different and knowing the gap prevents a great deal of confusion.

**The day's shape:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **το πρωί** | until about 12 |
| **το μεσημέρι** | 12 to 5 — and the rest period within it |
| **το απόγευμα** | 5 to 8 |
| **το βράδυ** | 8 onwards |
| **η νύχτα** | late |

**το μεσημέρι is an institution.** Shops shut, offices empty, people eat the main meal and sleep. Telephoning between about 2 and 5 is an intrusion — it is the **ώρα κοινής ησυχίας**, the legally recognised quiet period — and so is ringing a doorbell.

**Meal times**: lunch 2 to 3, dinner 9 to 10 or later. An invitation for dinner at 9 means arriving at 9.15 and eating at 10.

**Punctuality, honestly:**

| Occasion | Expectation |
| --- | --- |
| **A doctor's or official appointment** | be on time; they may not be |
| **A business meeting** | on time |
| **A church service** | the start time is the start; people arrive throughout, and this is normal and not disapproved of |
| **Dinner at someone's house** | fifteen to thirty minutes after the stated time |
| **A social meeting in a café** | ten to twenty minutes late is unremarkable |
| **A party** | an hour after the stated time |

**The church case is worth knowing**: in Greek practice people arrive at the Liturgy over the course of the first half hour, stand where they like, light candles and move about. Arriving twenty minutes in is not rudeness. Leaving before the end is slightly different, and leaving immediately after communion is common.

**The phrases:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Θα αργήσω λίγο.** | I will be a bit late |
| **Έρχομαι σε δέκα λεπτά.** | I'm coming in ten minutes |
| **Σε λίγο.** | shortly |
| **Τώρα-τώρα.** | right now — which may mean ten minutes |
| **Σε μισή ώρα.** | in half an hour |
| **Έφτασα.** | I have arrived — said when still in the car |
| **Όπου να 'ναι.** | any minute now |
| **Μας πρόλαβες.** | you caught us in time |
| **Αργήσαμε.** | we are late |
| **Δεν πειράζει, κάθισε.** | never mind, sit down — the response |

**Έφτασα said on the phone means *I am nearly there***, not *I have arrived*, and the gap can be twenty minutes. Learning to interpret it saves irritation.

**The scheduling vagueness**, from stage 5: **θα τα πούμε**, **τα κανονίζουμε**, **κάποια στιγμή** and **αύριο-μεθαύριο** all mean *no time has been fixed*. If a time matters, fix it explicitly and confirm by message — and that is normal practice among Greeks too for anything that matters.

**And the fatalism about it**: **Σιγά, δεν χάθηκε ο κόσμος** — *slowly, the world has not ended* — is the standard response to someone's anxiety about being late, and it is worth internalising rather than resisting.

**Practice.** Learn the ten time phrases. Then say what time you would actually arrive for: a dinner invitation at nine, a coffee at five, a Liturgy at ten, and a doctor at eleven. Then use **Θα αργήσω λίγο** by message the next time it is true.
Money, generosity and who pays:
A short lesson on the social economics of Greek life, because getting it wrong is the commonest way a foreigner causes quiet offence.

**The rule: one person pays for everyone, and the turn rotates.**

Splitting a bill — **πάμε μισά-μισά**, or the dreaded itemised division — is done among students and young people and is otherwise avoided. Between adults who know each other, somebody pays and somebody else pays next time.

**How to take your turn:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Εγώ κερνάω.** | my treat |
| **Σήμερα εγώ.** | today it's me |
| **Την άλλη φορά εγώ.** | next time me |
| **Άσε, το έχω.** | leave it, I've got it |
